article_meta.title: Primary Sources and Classical Commentaries on Hadith Transmission
article_meta.subtitle: An Examination of 25 Cases from Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Early Compilations, and Classical Sunni Commentaries
article_meta.plain_english_intro: More than two centuries after the Prophet Muhammad's death, Sunni scholars compiled oral reports (hadiths) into collections such as Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. These 25 cases examine specific reports in those books alongside early Islamic biographical works and the classical commentaries written by Sunni masters.
article_meta.hub_intro: Sunni Islam regards Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim as the most authentic books after the Qurʾān. These cases look at specific reports in those books and at what classical scholars, many of them the books' defenders, wrote about them. Each case quotes its sources and links to them, so you can read the full text and judge for yourself. Where classical scholars proposed a reconciliation, the case presents it beside the texts. Start with the first case, or choose any question below.
article_meta.tone: Archive reading-room tone: neutral, primary-source-led, attributing every judgment to named classical scholars
article_meta.primary_link_policy: 100% of inline citation links and primary_references point strictly to authoritative Islamic repositories (sunnah.com, quran.com, shamela.ws, www.islamweb.net, bukhari.islamweb.net, ketabonline.com, ar.wikisource.org).

ranking_methodology.overview: Cases are ordered for a sincere Muslim reader on a mobile screen using five criteria: (1) survival against classical reconciliations (such as rounding, multiple events, or abrogation), (2) direct reliance on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, or explicit statements by classical masters (such as al-Bukhārī, Muslim, al-Nawawī, Ibn Taymiyyah, al-Dhahabī, and Ibn Ḥajar), (3) immediate clarity in two sentences without requiring a technical glossary, (4) relevance to the foundational question of how the Prophet's words were preserved, and (5) thematic progression from opening primary-text cases to corpus tallies, classical grading rules, reciter evaluations, and detailed textual comparisons.
ranking_methodology.sequencing_rule: Section 1 (Cases #1-#3) opens with three foundational primary-text cases in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim; Section 2 (Cases #4-#6) examines the classical Companion narration tallies and corpus selection figures; Section 3 (Cases #7-#11) presents what the classical hadith masters wrote about their own grading criteria and epistemic certainty; Section 4 (Cases #12-#13) examines how those biographical grading rules were applied to the transmitters of the canonical Qurʾān readings; and Sections 5 and 6 (Cases #14-#25) provide twelve detailed comparisons of parallel versions across compilations and differing reports of single events.

classical_reconciliation_checks.standard_reconciliation: Oral rounding (e.g., 63 rounded to 60 or 65) or counting distinct sub-periods.
classical_reconciliation_checks.primary_text_comparison: Explicit sub-period arithmetic (such as '7 + 8 = 15' in Muslim 2353e) and classical commentary by Ibn Ḥajar and al-Nawawī attributing the variant numbers to narrator oversight (wahm).

classical_reconciliation_checks.category: Divergent eyewitness accounts of public events
classical_reconciliation_checks.primary_text_comparison: Events anchored to a single historical occasion (such as the solar eclipse on the day Ibrāhīm died, where al-Bukhārī and Ibn Taymiyyah noted that Ibrāhīm died once) or four different dates for the final prohibition of mutʿah.

classical_reconciliation_checks.standard_reconciliation: Transmission by meaning (al-riwāyah bi-al-maʿnā) or scribal abbreviation.
classical_reconciliation_checks.primary_text_comparison: Direct textual comparison between Muslim 1370a ('Mount Thawr') and Bukhārī 1870 ('such-and-such', kadhā), or sayings attributed to Successors in 8th-century compilations appearing with prophetic chains in 9th-century collections.

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 2 Wordings of the Hadith That the Hour Comes Before a Boy Grows Old
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see both wordings side by side: three chains from Anas (Bukhārī 6167; Muslim 2953) read “the Hour,” and Bukhārī 6511 and Muslim 2952 read “your hour.” Which wording came first?
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Ṣaḥīḥ chains tie the Hour to a boy's lifetime; a variant reads “your hour.”
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Comparing 'The Hour' (Bukhārī 6167; Muslim 2953) and 'Your Hour' (Bukhārī 6511)
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Which Words in the Ṣaḥīḥs Come From the Prophet?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 4 Abū Hurayrah Reports in the Ṣaḥīḥs, One al-Bukhārī Traced to Kaʿb
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Muslim 2789 (which al-Bukhārī traced to Kaʿb al-Aḥbār), a ruling traced to al-Faḍl (Muslim 1109a), a gloss from “Abū Hurayrah's bag” (Bukhārī 5355), and a report he later denied narrating (Bukhārī 5771).
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Al-Bukhārī and later critics traced Muslim 2789 to Kaʿb al-Aḥbār and noted added commentary in Bukhārī 136.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Classical Commentary on Attribution and Intermediaries in Muslim 2789 and Bukhārī 136
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Which Words in the Ṣaḥīḥs Come From the Prophet?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 4 Early Statements on Writing Hadith, From the Prophet to the Umayyads
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Muslim 3004's instruction not to write from the Prophet except the Qurʾān, Ibn ʿAbbās on what he left in writing, ʿUmar limiting narration, and al-Zuhrī on rulers requiring hadith to be written.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Sources record early reluctance to write hadith; al-Zuhrī linked its writing to the demands of Umayyad rulers.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Early Reports on Writing Hadith, Caliphal Policy, and Umayyad-Era Compilation
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Which Words in the Ṣaḥīḥs Come From the Prophet?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 5 Classical Hadith Tallies, From Abū Hurayrah to Abū Bakr
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see classical counts (5,374 for Abū Hurayrah, 1,660 for Ibn ʿAbbās, 1,361 for the four caliphs), assessments that Ibn ʿAbbās heard 4–10 hadiths directly, and ʿĀʾishah and ʿUmar on Abū Hurayrah.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Classical tallies credit Abū Hurayrah with 5,374 hadiths and the four caliphs together with 1,361.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Abū Hurayrah (5,374) & Ibn ʿAbbās (1,660) vs. Senior Companions (1,361)
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Who Narrated the Most, and How Much Circulated?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 4 Figures From al-Bukhārī's Selection, From 600,000 Reports to 2,602
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see the classical figures for al-Bukhārī's book (600,000 reports, 100,000 he called ṣaḥīḥ, 7,397 entries, 2,602 unique texts), Muslim's 300,000, and what scholars say was counted.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Ibn Ḥajar said each chain was counted; by al-Bukhārī's own count, two-thirds of what he knew was not ṣaḥīḥ.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Al-Bukhārī's Reported 600,000 Corpus Figures and ~2,602 Unique Texts
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Who Narrated the Most, and How Much Circulated?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Narrators Classical Critics Discussed for Old Age or Long Life
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see al-Dhahabī and Ibn Ḥajar on Hishām ibn ʿUrwah's later years in Iraq, the chain note in Bukhārī 5765, and the Kūfan narrators Zirr and Suwayd, recorded as living 122 and up to 130 years.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Several chains pass through narrators who taught in old age or were said to have lived past 120.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Hishām ibn ʿUrwah's Late-Life Memory Decline & Centenarian Narrators
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Who Narrated the Most, and How Much Circulated?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 4 Early Critics on Unintended Falsehood and the First Chain Requests
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see al-Qaṭṭān, quoted in Muslim's introduction, on unintended falsehood among the pious, Shuʿbah's estimate of false reports, and Ibn Sīrīn and al-Nakhaʿī dating the first requests for chains.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Muslim's introduction notes unintended falsehood; Ibn Sīrīn dates the first asking for chains to the fitnah.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Unintended Falsehood in Pious Reports, Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān, & the Rise of the Isnād
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: What Did Hadith Masters Say About Their Own Criteria?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Classical Statements on Keeping Disputed Narrators and Single Chains
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see al-Dhahabī on retaining disputed narrators to preserve the corpus, Ibn Ḥibbān on chains lacking two witnesses at every link, and Judge ʿUmar ibn Ḥabīb on exempting Companions from review.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Al-Dhahabī and Ibn Ḥibbān gave practical reasons for retaining disputed narrators and single-witness chains.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Pragmatic Retention of Disputed Narrators & Solitary Reports (Āḥād)
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: What Did Hadith Masters Say About Their Own Criteria?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Theorists on Single-Chain Hadith as Ẓann, Beside Qurʾānic Verses
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see al-Shāfiʿī, al-Ghazālī and Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ on single-chain reports yielding probable belief (ẓann), set beside Qurʾān 10:36 and 53:28 on conjecture and 9:101 and 49:6 on verifying reports.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Classical theorists held that single-chain reports yield probable belief (ẓann), not certainty.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Quranic Epistemology (Q. 9:101, 10:36) vs. Narrator Grading & Conjecture
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: What Did Hadith Masters Say About Their Own Criteria?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: Omitting a Link (Tadlīs) in the Ṣaḥīḥs and 3 Critics Who Questioned It
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see narrators in both Ṣaḥīḥs whom Ibn Ḥajar ranked as mudallisūn (omitting an intermediary), Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ's presumption that their hearing was verified, and 3 Mamluk specialists who called it assumption.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Later scholars presumed hearing was verified in these two books; some Mamluk specialists called it assumption.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: How Scholars Treated 'From' (Muʿanʿan) Links by Mudallis Narrators in the Ṣaḥīḥayn
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: What Did Hadith Masters Say About Their Own Criteria?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: Imām Muslim on Whether Narrators Must Meet, and 2 Chains Examined
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Imām Muslim's introduction accepting contemporaries without a recorded meeting, al-Bukhārī's reported stricter rule, and two chains where classical scholars questioned whether the narrators met.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Al-Bukhārī is reported to have required a meeting; Imām Muslim held that contemporaries suffice for a chain.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Muslim's Muqaddimah on Contemporaneity (*Muʿāṣarah*) vs. Verified Meeting (*Liqāʾ*)
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: What Did Hadith Masters Say About Their Own Criteria?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 4 Hadith Critics' Verdicts on Ḥafṣ, Whose Qurʾān Most Muslims Read
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Ibn Maʿīn, al-Bukhārī, Muslim and al-Nasāʾī on Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān as a hadith narrator, reports that he copied books without hearing them, and how ʿadālah and ḍabṭ are defined.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Hadith critics graded Ḥafṣ “abandoned” in hadith; most printed Qurʾāns follow his transmission.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān in Rijāl and the Separation of Qirāʾah from Ḥadīth
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: How Did Hadith Critics Grade the Qurʾān's Reciters?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 5 Canonical Qurʾān Reciters in Hadith Critics' Books, and al-Ṭabarī
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see biographical records on Hishām ibn ʿAmmār, ʿĀṣim, Shuʿbah, al-Bazzī and Qālūn on narration and recitation, plus al-Ṭabarī's comments on readings later counted as canonical.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Hadith critics graded several canonical Qurʾān transmitters as weak narrators in hadith.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Biographical Critiques Across Canonical Qurʾān Reciters & al-Ṭabarī
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: How Did Hadith Critics Grade the Qurʾān's Reciters?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 5 Versions of ʿAlī's Scroll and the Name “Thawr” as a Medina Boundary
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see five chains giving different contents for the one short scroll in ʿAlī's scabbard, and Muslim 1370a naming Thawr as a Medina boundary where Bukhārī 1870 reads “such-and-such.” How do the versions compare?
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Ibn Ḥajar cited a small Thawr near Uḥud; Abū ʿUbayd said Medina had no mountain of that name.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: The 'Scroll of ʿAlī' Reports and 'Mount Thawr' Across Parallel Versions
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Does a Report Keep Its Wording From Book to Book?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Bukhārī Versions of Cave Ḥirāʾ and 2 Lists of Ten Promised Paradise
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Bukhārī 6982 (which includes al-Zuhrī's clause “according to what reached us” on mountain peaks) beside shorter versions in Bukhārī 4953 and 3, plus al-Tirmidhī comparing 2 lists of ten promised Paradise.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Bukhārī 6982 marks an unchained addition by al-Zuhrī that the version in Bukhārī 3 does not include.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Comparing Parallel Versions of the Cave Ḥirāʾ Account and the Ten Promised Paradise
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Does a Report Keep Its Wording From Book to Book?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Reports on the Desert-Army Prophecy: 2 Name Ibn al-Zubayr, 1 Omits
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Muslim 2882–2883, where people in Ibn al-Zubayr's Mecca apply a prophecy of an army swallowed by the desert to the Syrian forces of their day, and Bukhārī 2118, which omits that setting.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Commentators refer the prophecy to a future army; narrators in Muslim applied it to Ibn al-Zubayr's war.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: The Desert-Swallowing Report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2882–2884 and Bukhārī 2118
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Does a Report Keep Its Wording From Book to Book?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 2 Sayings Found as Others' Words Early and as the Prophet's Later
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see the “fire from the Ḥijāz,” recorded as al-Zuhrī's words in ʿAbd al-Razzāq's Muṣannaf and as the Prophet's in Bukhārī 7118, and a parable found as Ibn Masʿūd's words before it appears as a hadith.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Some sayings appear as a Successor's or Companion's words in early books and as the Prophet's in later ones.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Comparing Companion and Successor Sayings in Early Books with Later Prophetic Chains
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Does a Report Keep Its Wording From Book to Book?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: “Arabia Will Become Meadows”: 1 Chain and 2 Translations of a Verb
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Muslim 157c and its single narrator Suhayl, Sufyān al-Thawrī's doubt that Suhayl attributed it to the Prophet, classical readings of taʿūd as “becomes,” and sunnah.com's 2020 change to “reverts to.”
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Sufyān al-Thawrī doubted the attribution; classical commentators read taʿūd as “becomes.”
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: The 'Green Arabia' Hadith: Attribution Doubts & 2020 Translation Shift
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Does a Report Keep Its Wording From Book to Book?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 2 Prophecy Groups on Constantinople and Basra With 8th-Century Details
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see reports in Muslim and Bukhārī on taking Constantinople, Musnad Aḥmad 18957 being cited for Maslamah's 717 AD siege, and Basra reports that run through Saʿīd ibn Jumhān (d. 136 AH).
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Commentators link some reports to 1453; others carry 8th-century details such as Maslamah's 717 AD siege.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Eighth-Century Constantinople and Basra Contexts Preserved in Hadiths
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Does a Report Keep Its Wording From Book to Book?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Ṣaḥīḥ Reports Giving Different Ages for the Prophet at His Death
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see reports via Ibn ʿAbbās and others giving 60, 63 and 65 years, the rounding explanation commentators proposed, and where Ibn Ḥajar and al-Nawawī attributed some versions to narrator error (wahm).
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Ṣaḥīḥ reports give ages 60, 63 and 65; Ibn Ḥajar and al-Nawawī attributed some to narrator error (wahm).
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Three Conflicting Timelines (Age 60, 63, or 65) via Identical Ṣaḥīḥ Chains
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Do Ṣaḥīḥ Reports of the Same Event Agree?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Ṣaḥīḥ Reports Giving 4, 6 and 8 Bowings for One Eclipse Prayer
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see ʿĀʾishah's, Jābir's and Ibn ʿAbbās's reports of the eclipse prayer on the day Ibrāhīm died, and al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī and Ibn Taymiyyah judging the higher counts narrator error.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī and Ibn Taymiyyah judged the higher counts in Muslim to be narrator error.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Three Conflicting Bowing Counts in the Eclipse Prayer on the Day Ibrāhīm Died
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Do Ṣaḥīḥ Reports of the Same Event Agree?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Pilgrimage Modes and 2 Kaʿbah Accounts From the Prophet's One Hajj
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Companions in Bukhārī and Muslim describing the Farewell Pilgrimage as Ifrād, Tamattuʿ and Qirān, and Bilāl and Ibn ʿAbbās differing on whether he prayed inside the Kaʿbah.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Ṣaḥīḥ reports describe three pilgrimage modes; al-Nawawī attributed one Kaʿbah account to conjecture (ẓann).
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Eyewitness Contradictions on the Farewell Pilgrimage and Kaʿbah Prayer
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Do Ṣaḥīḥ Reports of the Same Event Agree?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Ṣaḥīḥ Accounts of the First Revelation and 4 of the Last
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see reports naming Sūrah 96, Sūrah 74 or a sūrah on Paradise and the Fire as the first, and two verses and two sūrahs as the last, with the explanations commentators offered.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Ṣaḥīḥ reports name different first and last revelations; al-Nawawī judged Jābir's literal claim weak.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Conflicting Ṣaḥīḥ Reports on the First and Last Qurʾānic Revelations
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Do Ṣaḥīḥ Reports of the Same Event Agree?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 4 Accounts of When Temporary Marriage (Mutʿah) Was Prohibited
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see reports placing the prohibition at Khaybar, the Conquest of Mecca and Awṭās, Jābir's report that it was practised until ʿUmar, and the repeated-abrogation explanation scholars proposed.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Scholars proposed repeated abrogation; Muslim 1406 calls the ban binding “until the Day of Resurrection.”
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Four Conflicting Eyewitness Timelines in Muslim on Temporary Marriage
global_subpoint_leaderboard.parent_argument_short_title: Do Ṣaḥīḥ Reports of the Same Event Agree?

global_subpoint_leaderboard.short_title: 3 Wordings of What the Prophet Left Behind: Book, Household, Sunnah
global_subpoint_leaderboard.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Muslim 1218a (“the Book of God”), Muslim 2408a (“the Book of God and my household”), and the wording “the Book of God and my Sunnah,” which appears in Mālik's Muwaṭṭaʾ without a chain.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.takeaway: Muslim records two wordings of the bequest; “and my Sunnah” is absent from the Six Books.
global_subpoint_leaderboard.title: Wordings of the Farewell Bequest Across Muslim, Tirmidhī, and the Muwaṭṭaʾ

arguments.header: Which Words in the Ṣaḥīḥs Come From the Prophet?
arguments.short_title: Which Words in the Ṣaḥīḥs Come From the Prophet?
arguments.reader_question: What do variant wordings, critics' attributions and early writing practice show?
arguments.plain_english_hook: The canonical collections preserve reports on the Hour, Companion narrations reviewed by critics, and early views on writing hadith. What do variant wordings and attributions show?
arguments.title: Early Transmission Practices, Attribution Questions, and Written Records
arguments.executive_summary: This opening section examines three foundational reports in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: the statement tying the coming of the Hour to a young boy's lifetime alongside its variant wording, classical commentators' attribution of the seven-day creation report in Muslim 2789 to Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, and early accounts regarding the writing down of hadith. How do these primary texts describe the earliest stage of transmission?
arguments.methodological_significance: Comparing parallel wordings and classical commentary in al-Bukhārī's al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr, Fatḥ al-Bārī, and Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim clarifies how early scholars distinguished prophetic speech from Companion or Successor commentary and how written compilation developed. What do these records indicate about how reports circulated before the canonical books were compiled?

subpoints.short_title: 2 Wordings of the Hadith That the Hour Comes Before a Boy Grows Old
subpoints.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see both wordings side by side: three chains from Anas (Bukhārī 6167; Muslim 2953) read “the Hour,” and Bukhārī 6511 and Muslim 2952 read “your hour.” Which wording came first?
subpoints.takeaway: Ṣaḥīḥ chains tie the Hour to a boy's lifetime; a variant reads “your hour.”
subpoints.title: Comparing 'The Hour' (Bukhārī 6167; Muslim 2953) and 'Your Hour' (Bukhārī 6511)

a.text: Asked "When will the Hour be established?" the Prophet points to a young boy: "If this boy lives, he will not reach decrepit old age before [[the Hour]] (al-Sāʿah) is established."

b.text: Asked "When will the Hour be?" he looks at the youngest of them: "If this one lives, he will not reach old age before [[your hour]] (sāʿatukum) is established." Hishām added: meaning their death.

showcase.note: Two wordings of one answer: three Basran chains from Anas read "the Hour" (al-Sāʿah), while Hishām ibn ʿUrwah's chain from ʿĀʾishah reads "your hour" (sāʿatukum).

subpoints.summary_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6167](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6167) and three independent Basran chains from **Anas ibn Mālik** in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2953a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2953a), [2953b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2953b), and [2953c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2953c), a questioner asks when the Hour will come (`مَتَى تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ`) and the Prophet points to a young boy, stating that he will not reach decrepit old age before **the Hour** (`حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ`) is established. A parallel Medinan chain via **Hishām ibn ʿUrwah** from **ʿĀʾishah** ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6511](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6511); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2952](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2952)) reads **"your hour"** (`سَاعَتُكُمْ`), which Hishām and classical commentators interpreted as the passing of that generation.

evidence_items.label: Three Chains from Anas Reading 'Until the Hour Is Established' (Bukhārī 6167 & Muslim 2953a–c)
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6167](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6167) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2953a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2953a), [2953b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2953b), and [2953c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2953c) (transmitted through Qatādah, Maʿbad ibn Hilāl, and Thābit al-Bunānī from **Anas ibn Mālik**), a man asks the Prophet, *"When will the Hour be established (`مَتَى تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ`)?"* Looking at a young boy of Anas's age from Azd Shanūʾah (or a page of al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah), the Prophet replies that should the youth live long, old age (*al-haram*) will not overtake him prior to the establishment of **the Hour** (`السَّاعَةُ`, carrying the definite article *al-*).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: إِنْ عُمِّرَ هَذَا لَمْ يُدْرِكْهُ الْهَرَمُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ — "If this boy lives, he will not reach decrepit old age before the Hour is established." ([Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2953b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2953b))

key_arabic_quote_structured.arabic: إِنْ عُمِّرَ هَذَا لَمْ يُدْرِكْهُ الْهَرَمُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ
key_arabic_quote_structured.english: If this boy lives, he will not reach decrepit old age before the Hour is established.

evidence_items.label: The 'Your Hour' (Sāʿatukum) Wording and Hishām's Gloss (Bukhārī 6511 & Muslim 2952)
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6511](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6511) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2952](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2952), a Medinan route transmitted via **Hishām ibn ʿUrwah** from his father from **ʿĀʾishah** recounts that when bedouins asked the Prophet, *"When will the Hour be (`مَتَى السَّاعَةُ`)?"* he looked at the youngest among them and said: *"If this one lives, he will not reach old age before your hour (`سَاعَتُكُمْ`) is established upon you."* Directly after the report, the sub-narrator Hishām adds the explanatory remark: *"meaning their death"* (`قَالَ هِشَامٌ يَعْنِي مَوْتَهُمْ`). Classical commentators such as **al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ** and **al-Nawawī** read Anas's unmodified wording (`السَّاعَةُ`) in light of Hishām's suffixed wording (`سَاعَتُكُمْ`).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: إِنْ يَعِشْ هَذَا لاَ يُدْرِكْهُ الْهَرَمُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ عَلَيْكُمْ سَاعَتُكُمْ ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالَ هِشَامٌ يَعْنِي مَوْتَهُمْ — "If this one lives, he will not reach old age before your hour is established upon you. Hishām said: meaning their death." ([Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6511](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6511))

key_arabic_quote_structured.arabic: إِنْ يَعِشْ هَذَا لاَ يُدْرِكْهُ الْهَرَمُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ عَلَيْكُمْ سَاعَتُكُمْ ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالَ هِشَامٌ يَعْنِي مَوْتَهُمْ
key_arabic_quote_structured.english: If this one lives, he will not reach old age before your hour is established upon you. Hishām said: meaning their death.

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical commentators such as al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ and al-Nawawī explained the unmodified phrase "until the Hour is established" in Anas's three chains (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6167; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2953a–c) by interpreting it through the suffixed wording "your hour" (sāʿatukum) in Hishām ibn ʿUrwah's chain from ʿĀʾishah (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6511; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2952), understanding "the Hour" as the lesser hour—the passing away of the generation being addressed.
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: Comparing the two recensions side by side highlights a textual question across the canonical chains: in all three Basran routes from Anas ibn Mālik, both the question ("When will the Hour be established?") and the answer ("until the Hour is established") use the definite noun al-Sāʿah without a possessive pronoun, whereas the pronoun -kum ("your hour") and the gloss "meaning their death" appear in the single Medinan route transmitted by Hishām ibn ʿUrwah.

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
### 1. First-Generation Apocalyptic Imminence vs. Qurʾānic Agnosticism
Throughout the Qurʾānic corpus, the Prophet is commanded to disclaim foreknowledge of the unseen (*al-ghayb*) and of when the Last Hour (*al-Sāʿah*) will arrive (Qurʾān 7:187–188, alongside 46:9). In tension with that scriptural stance, the *Ṣaḥīḥayn* preserve two divergent layers of eschatological material: a later panoramic layer in which the Prophet surveys every civil war (*fitnah*) and leader down to the end of time (*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6604; *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2891a), and an earlier apocalyptic stratum expecting the cosmic Hour within a single human lifespan.

In Bukhari's corpus (report 6167) and three independent Basran routes from **Anas ibn Mālik** in Muslim's compilation (reports 2953a through 2953c) (transmitted via Thābit al-Bunānī, Maʿbad ibn Hilāl, and Qatādah), an interlocutor asks directly when the Hour will occur (`مَتَى تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ؟`). Pointing to a youth in the gathering, the Prophet states that if the boy lives on, he will not reach decrepit old age (*al-haram*) before **the Hour** (`السَّاعَةُ`, with the definite article) is established.

### 2. Post-First-Century Reinterpretations and the ~800 AD Historical Horizon
While all three Basran chains from Anas retain the unmodified noun `السَّاعَةُ`, a separate Medinan branch via `Hishām ibn ʿUrwah ← ʿUrwah ← ʿĀʾishah` (*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2952; *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6511) alters the predicate to *"your hour"* (`سَاعَتُكُمْ`), supplying the metaphorical gloss that *"the Hour"* merely meant the death of that generation. A parallel sequence of secondary reinterpretation surrounds the 100-year oath in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2538a (and 2539), where Jābir reports the Prophet answering an explicit inquiry about the Hour (`تَسْأَلُونِي عَنِ السَّاعَةِ`) by swearing—without the word *"today"*—that no living soul on earth would have a hundred years pass over it. Once the year 110 AH passed with humanity intact, transmitters appended competing corrective glosses: Ibn ʿUmar and al-Zuhrī in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2537a (cf. *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 116; *Sunan Abī Dāwūd* 4348) asserted that listeners misconstrued the statement and added the qualifier *"today"* (`الْيَوْمَ`), whereas ʿAbd al-Raḥmān in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2538c interpreted it as a gradual shortening of human lifespans (`نَقْصَ الْعُمُرِ`). Together with political prophecies that track seventh- and eighth-century dynastic events with high specificity before abruptly terminating around ~800 AD (late second century AH), these traditions mark the historical window in which the canonical Hadith corpus crystallized. The survival of both the literal first-century apocalyptic horizon and its subsequent exegetical reinterpretation highlights the tension between early expectations and historical time.

I have not seen him forget a hadith other than it.

subpoints.summary_markdown: Abū Hurayrah is credited with 5,374 *Musnad* reports (517 in the *Ṣaḥīḥayn*) according to classical tallies ([IslamWeb Fatwa #174903](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/174903/); [al-Dhahabī, *Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 2/632](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/267/أبو-هريرة)). Within the canonical collections and their commentaries, classical scholars discussed four specific cases in his transmissions: a creation report in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2789](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2789) that al-Bukhārī and Ibn Taymiyyah attributed to Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, a ruling in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1109a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1109a) traced to al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās, a closing phrase in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 136](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:136) that Ibn Ḥajar identified as added commentary (*mudraj*), and Abū Salamah's remark in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2221a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2221a) (cf. [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5771](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5771); [*Muslim* 2220a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2220a)) regarding the differing 'no contagion' texts.

evidence_items.label: Al-Bukhārī and Ibn Taymiyyah on the Seven-Day Creation Report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2789
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2789](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2789), Abū Hurayrah narrates—under the explicit formula *"The Messenger of God ﷺ took me by my hand and said"*—a seven-day terrestrial creation sequence (*"God created the soil on Saturday... and created Adam after ʿAṣr on Friday"*) that stands in textual tension with the Qurʾānic six-day creation account ([Qurʾān 7:54](https://quran.com/7/54), [10:3](https://quran.com/10/3), [50:38](https://quran.com/50/38)). Rather than harmonizing the two accounts, **al-Bukhārī** (*al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr* 1/413–414, cited in [IslamWeb Fatwa #137773](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/137773/)), **Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn**, **ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī**, **al-Bayhaqī**, **Ibn Taymiyyah** ([*Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā* 18/18–19](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=18&bk_no=22&pageno=18); cf. [IslamWeb Fatwa #35560](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/35560/)), and **Ibn Kathīr** (*al-Bidāyah wa-l-Nihāyah* 1/20) concluded that this report is defective (*maʿlūl*) and represents the speech of the Jewish convert **Kaʿb al-Aḥbār** erroneously elevated (*ghuliṭa fī rafʿihi*) to the Prophet.
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «أَخَذَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم بِيَدِي فَقَالَ خَلَقَ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ التُّرْبَةَ يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ» — "The Messenger of God ﷺ took me by my hand and said: 'God, Mighty and Majestic, created the soil on Saturday...'" (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2789; cf. Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā 18/18–19)

evidence_items.label: The Fasting Report via al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās Compared with ʿĀʾishah and Umm Salamah (Muslim 1109a; Bukhārī 1925–1926)
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1109a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1109a) (cf. [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 1925](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1925)–[1926](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1926)), Abū Hurayrah reported that whoever reaches dawn in major ritual impurity (*janābah*) should not fast. When Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam sent ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith to ask **ʿĀʾishah** and **Umm Salamah**, both widows reported that the Prophet used to fast in that state, and Abū Hurayrah stated that he had heard the report from al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās rather than directly from the Prophet.

evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5355](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5355), Abū Hurayrah followed a Prophetic statement on charity with an illustrative dialogue and clarified when asked by listeners: *'No, this is from Abū Hurayrah\'s own bag [his own words].'* In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 136](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:136), **Ibn Ḥajar** ([*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 1/236](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/269/)), **al-Mundhirī**, **Ibn Taymiyyah**, and **Ibn al-Qayyim** concluded that the closing exhortation (*'whoever is able to lengthen his radiance, let him do so'*) was an added remark (*mudraj*) of Abū Hurayrah's speech.

He said: 'No, this is from Abū Hurayrah's own bag [i.e., his own words].'" (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5355)

key_arabic_quote_structured.english: They said: 'O Abū Hurayrah, did you hear this from the Messenger of God ﷺ?' He said: 'No, this is from Abū Hurayrah's own bag [i.e., his own words].'

evidence_items.label: Abū Salamah's Question on the 'No Contagion' Report Alongside the Cloak Hadith (Bukhārī 5771; Muslim 2221a)
evidence_items.content_markdown: Although Abū Hurayrah accounted for his prolific narration through the 'Cloak Hadith' ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:118)–[119](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:119); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2492a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2492a)), stating that he *"never forgot anything afterwards"* (`فَمَا نَسِيتُ شَيْئًا بَعْدَهُ`), [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5771](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5771) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2221a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2221a) (cf. [2220a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2220a)) record that he subsequently ceased transmitting his earlier report *"There is no contagion (lā ʿadwā),"* spoke in Ethiopic when reminded of it, and denied ever narrating it. His student **Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān** and cousin **al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Dhubāb** witnessed this exchange, leading Abū Salamah to observe: *"I do not know whether Abū Hurayrah forgot (`a-nasiya Abū Hurayrah`), or whether one statement abrogated the other"* ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2221a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2221a); cf. [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5771](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5771): `فَمَا رَأَيْتُهُ نَسِيَ حَدِيثًا غَيْرَهُ`).

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical and modern commentators maintain that a Companion's omitted intermediary (*mursal al-Ṣaḥābī*) remains presumptively reliable ([IslamWeb Fatwa #174903](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/174903/)), that the cloak narrative ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 119](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:119)) did not preclude isolated memory lapses, and that a downstream transmitter rather than Abū Hurayrah may have elevated Kaʿb al-Aḥbār's statement in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2789](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2789).
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1109a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1109a), Abū Hurayrah's report via al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās differed from the household practice reported by ʿĀʾishah and Umm Salamah, leading him to return to their account. Likewise, **Ibn Taymiyyah** ([*Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā* 18/18–19](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=18&bk_no=22&pageno=18)) and **Ibn Kathīr** (*al-Bidāyah wa-l-Nihāyah* 1/20, cited in [IslamWeb Fatwa #137773](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/137773/)) trace the seven-day creation report in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2789](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2789) to traditions Abū Hurayrah heard from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, even though it appears in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* with the opening phrase *'The Messenger of God ﷺ took me by my hand.'*

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
#### 1. Mechanics of Commentary Fusion (*Idrāj*) and Unstated Sources (*Irsāl*)

In classical *ʿulūm al-ḥadīth*, interpolation (*idrāj*) arises whenever a transmitter attaches personal homiletic remarks or legal deductions to a Prophetic text (*matn*) without a clear verbal boundary, causing downstream students to transmit both segments as unified revelation. During public instruction in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5355](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5355) (*Kitāb al-Nafaqāt*), Abū Hurayrah followed a Prophetic maxim on charity with a dramatic dialogue illustrating household maintenance claims; only direct questioning from his listeners separated the two layers. Regarding [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 136](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:136), analyzing its pathways in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* ([vol. 1, p. 236](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/269/)), **Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī** notes that ten other Companions and every parallel pupil of Abū Hurayrah transmitted the core Prophetic statement without the closing appendage, concluding it was an added remark (*mudraj*).

A parallel dynamic governed second-hand Companion reporting (*irsāl al-ṣaḥābī*). In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1109a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1109a) alongside [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 1926](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1926) (and [no. 1925](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1925)), Abū Hurayrah's initial invalidation of fasting for anyone waking in *janābah* was updated after Governor Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam dispatched an envoy to ask **ʿĀʾishah** and **Umm Salamah**. Following their clarification from household observation, Abū Hurayrah clarified that his initial report was traced to al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās.

#### 2. The 'No Contagion' Reports and Classical Criticism of Muslim 2789

Canonical records likewise document mnemonic discussion alongside the Cloak narrative of [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 119](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:119) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2492a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2492a). In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2221a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2221a) as well as [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5771](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5771), Abū Hurayrah initially paired two differing dictums on contagion (`«لاَ عَدْوَى»`) and quarantining diseased camels, but subsequently dropped the first clause and repudiated it in Ethiopic when confronted by al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Dhubāb, leaving Abū Salamah unable to distinguish memory failure from abrogation. Finally, in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2789](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2789), the chain `Ibn Jurayj ← Ismāʿīl ibn Umayyah ← Ayyūb ibn Khālid ← ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rāfiʿ ← Abū Hurayrah` attributes a seven-day terrestrial creation schedule directly to the Prophet against the six-day creation of [Qurʾān 7:54](https://quran.com/7/54) and [50:38](https://quran.com/50/38). Early *ʿilal* masters—referenced by [Fatwa #137773 on IslamWeb](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/137773/) and **Ibn Taymiyyah** in *Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā* ([vol. 18, pp. 18–19](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=18&bk_no=22&pageno=18))—concluded that this narrative originated in study sessions where Abū Hurayrah exchanged lore with **Kaʿb al-Aḥbār**, and that it was erroneously elevated (*ghuliṭa fī rafʿihi*) to the Prophet.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «لاَ، هَذَا مِنْ كِيسِ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "No, this is from Abū Hurayrah's own bag [i.e., his own words]."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «سَمِعْتُ ذَلِكَ مِنَ الْفَضْلِ وَلَمْ أَسْمَعْهُ مِنَ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ — قَالَ: فَرَجَعَ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ عَمَّا كَانَ يَقُولُ فِي ذَلِكَ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "[Abū Hurayrah] said: 'I heard that from al-Faḍl [ibn ʿAbbās], and I did not hear it from the Prophet ﷺ.' Thus Abū Hurayrah retracted what he used to say regarding that."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «فَضَمَمْتُهُ فَمَا نَسِيتُ شَيْئًا بَعْدَهُ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "So I gathered it to my chest, and I never forgot anything afterwards."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «وَلَعَمْرِي لَقَدْ كَانَ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ يُحَدِّثُنَا أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ قَالَ: لاَ عَدْوَى، فَلاَ أَدْرِي أَنَسِيَ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ أَوْ نَسَخَ أَحَدُ الْقَوْلَيْنِ الآخَرَ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "By my life, Abū Hurayrah certainly used to narrate to us that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, 'There is no contagion'—so I do not know whether Abū Hurayrah forgot (a-nasiya Abū Hurayrah), or whether one of the two statements abrogated the other."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «أَخَذَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِيَدِي فَقَالَ: خَلَقَ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ التُّرْبَةَ يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ، وَخَلَقَ فِيهَا الْجِبَالَ يَوْمَ الأَحَدِ، وَخَلَقَ الشَّجَرَ يَوْمَ الاِثْنَيْنِ، وَخَلَقَ الْمَكْرُوهَ يَوْمَ الثُّلاَثَاءِ، وَخَلَقَ النُّورَ يَوْمَ الأَرْبِعَاءِ، وَبَثَّ فِيهَا الدَّوَابَّ يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ، وَخَلَقَ آدَمَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلاَمُ بَعْدَ الْعَصْرِ مِنْ يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ...»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "The Messenger of God ﷺ took me by my hand and said: 'God, Mighty and Majestic, created the soil on Saturday, and created the mountains therein on Sunday, and created the trees on Monday, and created unpleasant things on Tuesday, and created light on Wednesday, and dispersed the beasts therein on Thursday, and created Adam (peace be upon him) after ʿAṣr on Friday...'"

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «وَمِثْلُهُ حَدِيثُ مُسْلِمٍ: إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَلَقَ التُّرْبَةَ يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ... فَإِنَّ هَذَا طَعَنَ فِيهِ مَنْ هُوَ أَعْلَمُ مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ مِثْلُ يَحْيَى بْنِ مَعِينٍ وَمِثْلُ الْبُخَارِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِمَا وَذَكَرَ الْبُخَارِيُّ أَنَّ هَذَا مِنْ كَلَامِ كَعْبِ الْأَحْبَارِ وَطَائِفَةٌ اعْتَبَرَتْ صِحَّتَهُ مِثْلُ أَبِي بَكْرٍ ابْنِ الْأَنْبَارِيِّ وَأَبِي الْفَرَجِ ابْنِ الْجَوْزِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِمَا وَالْبَيْهَقِيُّ وَغَيْرُهُ وَافَقُوا الَّذِينَ ضَعَّفُوهُ وَهَذَا هُوَ الصَّوَابُ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "And similar to it is the hadith of Muslim: 'Indeed, God created the soil on Saturday...' For this was criticized by those more knowledgeable than Muslim, such as Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn, al-Bukhārī, and others; and al-Bukhārī stated that this is from the speech of Kaʿb al-Aḥbār. A group considered it authentic, such as Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī, Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī, and others, while al-Bayhaqī and others agreed with those who declared it weak, and this is what is correct."

subpoints.summary_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 3004](https://sunnah.com/muslim:3004) (cf. [*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 2665](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:2665)), the Prophet instructs Companions not to write from him anything other than the Qurʾān, and [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5019](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5019) records Ibn ʿAbbās stating that the Prophet left nothing written outside the *muṣḥaf*. Subsequent reports from the caliphate of ʿUmar record his decision not to codify the *Sunan* ([*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* 20484](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19529/)) and his instruction to narrate sparingly ([*al-Mustadrak* 1/102 #382–383](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/358/)), while **Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī** (d. 124 AH) reported that scholars disliked writing down knowledge until Umayyad rulers required it ([*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* 20486](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19531/); [*Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm* 1/333 #443](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1040/405/)).

evidence_items.label: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 3004 on Not Writing Non-Qurʾānic Speech
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 3004](https://sunnah.com/muslim:3004), Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī narrates the Prophet's command not to transcribe his non-Qurʾānic words and to erase existing copies, adding in [*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 2665](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:2665) (cf. [*Tuḥfat al-Aḥwadhī* 7/5113](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/56/5113/)) that the Prophet declined to grant them permission to write hadiths.
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: لاَ تَكْتُبُوا عَنِّي وَمَنْ كَتَبَ عَنِّي غَيْرَ الْقُرْآنِ فَلْيَمْحُهُ — "Do not write anything from me; and whoever has written anything from me other than the Qurʾān, let him erase it." (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 3004)

key_arabic_quote_structured.arabic: لاَ تَكْتُبُوا عَنِّي وَمَنْ كَتَبَ عَنِّي غَيْرَ الْقُرْآنِ فَلْيَمْحُهُ
key_arabic_quote_structured.english: Do not write anything from me; and whoever has written anything from me other than the Qurʾān, let him erase it.

evidence_items.label: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5019 and 3047 on What the Prophet Left Behind
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5019](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5019), **Ibn ʿAbbās** and **Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah** testify that the Prophet *"did not leave anything except what is between the two covers [of the Qurʾān],"* alongside **ʿAlī's** oath in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3047](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3047) (cf. [111](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:111)), the Farewell Sermon bequest of *"the Book of God"* ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1218a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1218a)), and **ʿUmar's** statement (*"We have with us the Book of God; it is sufficient for us"*) in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 114](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:114) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1637c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1637c).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «مَا تَرَكَ إِلاَّ مَا بَيْنَ الدَّفَّتَيْنِ» — "He did not leave anything except what is between the two covers [of the Qurʾān]." (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5019)

key_arabic_quote_structured.arabic: مَا تَرَكَ إِلاَّ مَا بَيْنَ الدَّفَّتَيْنِ
key_arabic_quote_structured.english: He did not leave anything except what is between the two covers [of the Qurʾān].

evidence_items.label: Reports on Caliph ʿUmar's Policy Toward Writing the Sunan and Multiplying Narration
evidence_items.content_markdown: After the Prophet's death—when Qurʾānic revelation had already ceased—Caliph **ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb** declined to codify the *Sunan* ([*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* 20484](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19529/); Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, [*Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm* #343](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1040/316/)), ordered provincial copies erased ([*Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm* #345](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1040/318/)), burned collected scrolls as *"a Mishnah like the Mishnah of the People of the Book"* (al-Dhahabī, [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 5/59](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/717/)), and detained senior Companions (Ibn Masʿūd, Abū al-Dardāʾ, Abū Dharr) in Medina while instructing delegations to *"keep the Qurʾān pure and minimize narration"* (al-Ḥākim, [*al-Mustadrak* 1/102, #353](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/330/) & [#382–383](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/358/), graded *ṣaḥīḥ* on *Ṣaḥīḥayn* criteria; cf. early authorities on keeping the Qurʾān pure in [*Muṣannaf Ibn Abī Shaybah* 7/4420](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/10/4420/)).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: جردوا القرآن ، وأقلوا الرواية عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ، وامضوا ، وأنا شريككم — "Keep the Qurʾān pure and minimize narrating from the Messenger of God; go forth, and I am your partner in this." (Mustadrak al-Ḥākim 353)

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical Sunni commentators (Ibn Qutaybah, al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, al-Nawawī, Ibn Ḥajar) propose that the prohibition on writing Hadith in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 3004](https://sunnah.com/muslim:3004) was an early precaution against conflating Qurʾānic verses with Hadith on the same parchment that was subsequently abrogated during the Prophet's lifetime once the Qurʾānic text was secure.
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: Alongside the lifetime-abrogation reading, primary sources from the decades **after the Prophet's death**—once Qurʾānic revelation had concluded—record continuing reluctance to write hadith. **Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī (d. 124 AH)** stated via the `ʿAbd al-Razzāq ← Maʿmar ← al-Zuhrī` chain ([*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* 20486](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19531/); [*Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm* 1/333 #443](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1040/405/)): *'We used to dislike writing down knowledge [Hadith], until these [Umayyad] rulers compelled us to do so.'* Likewise, Caliph **ʿUmar's** decision not to write down the *Sunan* ([*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* 20484](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19529/)) and his instruction to Kūfan Companions to *'keep the Qurʾān pure and narrate little from the Messenger of God ﷺ'* ([*al-Mustadrak* #353](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/330/) & [#382–383](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/358/), graded *ṣaḥīḥ* by al-Ḥākim on the criteria of al-Bukhārī and Muslim) date to his caliphate, alongside the early *mursal* report in Ibn Saʿd's *al-Ṭabaqāt* and al-Khaṭīb's *Taqyīd al-ʿIlm* describing his erasure of gathered scrolls as 'a Mishnah like the Mishnah of the People of the Book.'

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
#### 1. Reports on Not Writing Non-Qurʾānic Speech and Companion Scriptural Sufficiency

Canonical Sunni collections preserve foundational reports establishing that the Prophet prohibited transcribing his non-Qurʾānic speech and that senior Companions recognized no binding written revelation outside the Qurʾānic codex. Through Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* ([no. 3004](https://sunnah.com/muslim:3004)), the Prophet issued the instruction forbidding scribes from recording anything beyond the Qurʾān and ordering the erasure (`fa-l-yamḥuhu`) of existing notes, corroborated in *Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* ([no. 2665](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:2665)) and *Tuḥfat al-Aḥwadhī* ([vol. 7, #5113](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/56/5113/)) where Companions repeatedly petitioned for permission to write hadiths and were refused.

Consistent with this policy, when Shaddād ibn Maʿqil asked **Ibn ʿAbbās** and **Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah** in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5019](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5019) whether the Prophet left behind any authoritative heritage, both declared that he left only what lies between the two covers of the *muṣḥaf* (`mā bayna al-daffatayn`). The same boundary appears in **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib's** oath in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* ([no. 3047](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3047); see [no. 111](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:111)) denying any private revelation apart from Qurʾānic comprehension and a brief municipal scroll on blood-money, in Jābir's Farewell Pilgrimage report ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1218a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1218a)) naming solely the Book of God, and in **ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's** Thursday deathbed intervention in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* ([no. 1637c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1637c)) alongside *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* ([no. 114](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:114)) (`ḥasbunā Kitābu Allāh`).

#### 2. Reports from the Caliphate of ʿUmar and the Statement of al-Zuhrī

Although Ibn Qutaybah and al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī proposed that the ban was an early precaution against confusing Hadith with ongoing Qurʾānic revelation, the strictest enforcement occurred **after the Prophet's death** once revelation had ceased. Caliph **ʿUmar** enforced a systematic state policy against codifying or multiplying traditions. Via `ʿAbd al-Razzāq ← Maʿmar ← al-Zuhrī ← ʿUrwah` in *Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* ([vol. 11, #20484](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19529/)) and **Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr's** *Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm* ([vol. 1, #343](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1040/316/)), ʿUmar abandoned plans to write the *Sunan* lest Muslims neglect scripture, ordered provincial copies erased ([entry #345](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1040/318/)), and burned collected notebooks while comparing them to the rabbinic *Mishnah* ([*Siyar* vol. 5, p. 59](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/717/)). In two traditions graded *ṣaḥīḥ* in **al-Ḥākim's** *al-Mustadrak* ([report #353](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/330/) and [reports #382–383](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/358/)), ʿUmar detained senior Companions for prolific narration and ordered Qaraẓah ibn Kaʿb's Kūfan delegation to keep the Qurʾān pure (`jarridū al-Qurʾān`; see *Muṣannaf Ibn Abī Shaybah* [vol. 7, #4420](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/10/4420/)). This scholarly aversion endured across the first century (*Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm* [report #344](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1040/317/) and [report #346](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1040/319/))—unlike [Qurʾān 2:282](https://quran.com/2/282) mandating written debt contracts—until **al-Zuhrī (d. 124 AH)** testified in *Sharḥ al-Sunnah* ([vol. 1, p. 294, #137](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1009/138/)), *Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm* ([vol. 1, p. 333, #443](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1040/405/)), and *Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* ([entry #20486](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19531/)) that Umayyad princes required scholars to compile books.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: حَدَّثَنَا هَدَّابُ بْنُ خَالِدٍ الأَزْدِيُّ، حَدَّثَنَا هَمَّامٌ، عَنْ زَيْدِ بْنِ أَسْلَمَ، عَنْ عَطَاءِ بْنِ يَسَارٍ، عَنْ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ الْخُدْرِيِّ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ: «لاَ تَكْتُبُوا عَنِّي وَمَنْ كَتَبَ عَنِّي غَيْرَ الْقُرْآنِ فَلْيَمْحُهُ وَحَدِّثُوا عَنِّي وَلاَ حَرَجَ وَمَنْ كَذَبَ عَلَىَّ — قَالَ هَمَّامٌ أَحْسِبُهُ قَالَ — مُتَعَمِّدًا فَلْيَتَبَوَّأْ مَقْعَدَهُ مِنَ النَّارِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reported that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Do not write anything from me; and whoever has written anything from me other than the Qurʾān, let him erase it (fa-l-yamḥuhu). Narrate from me, for there is no harm in it; and whoever lies upon me—Hammām said: I think he said: 'intentionally'—let him take his seat in the Fire."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: عَنْ عَطَاءِ بْنِ يَسَارٍ، عَنْ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ الْخُدْرِيِّ قَالَ: «اسْتَأْذَنَّا النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي الْكِتَابَةِ فَلَمْ يَأْذَنْ لَنَا»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: From Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who said: "We asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to write [hadiths], and he did not grant us permission."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 2665; Musnad Aḥmad 11109; Taqyīd al-ʿIlm p. 32

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: حَدَّثَنَا قُتَيْبَةُ بْنُ سَعِيدٍ، حَدَّثَنَا سُفْيَانُ، عَنْ عَبْدِ الْعَزِيزِ بْنِ رُفَيْعٍ، قَالَ: دَخَلْتُ أَنَا وَشَدَّادُ بْنُ مَعْقِلٍ عَلَى ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا، فَقَالَ لَهُ شَدَّادُ بْنُ مَعْقِلٍ: أَتَرَكَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْ شَىْءٍ؟ قَالَ: «مَا تَرَكَ إِلاَّ مَا بَيْنَ الدَّفَّتَيْنِ». قَالَ: وَدَخَلْنَا عَلَى مُحَمَّدِ ابْنِ الْحَنَفِيَّةِ فَسَأَلْنَاهُ فَقَالَ: «مَا تَرَكَ إِلاَّ مَا بَيْنَ الدَّفَّتَيْنِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: Narrated ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rufayʿ: Shaddād ibn Maʿqil and I entered upon Ibn ʿAbbās. Shaddād ibn Maʿqil asked him: "Did the Prophet ﷺ leave anything behind?" He replied: "He did not leave anything except what is between the two covers [of the Qurʾān] (mā taraka illā mā bayna al-daffatayn)." Then we entered upon Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah and asked him, and he replied: "He did not leave anything except what is between the two covers [of the Qurʾān]."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «وَقَدْ تَرَكْتُ فِيكُمْ مَا لَنْ تَضِلُّوا بَعْدَهُ إِنِ اعْتَصَمْتُمْ بِهِ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "And I have left among you that after which you will never go astray if you hold fast to it: the Book of God."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: عَنْ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ، عَنِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، قَالَ: لَمَّا اشْتَدَّ بِالنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَجَعُهُ قَالَ: «ائْتُونِي بِكِتَابٍ أَكْتُبْ لَكُمْ كِتَابًا لاَ تَضِلُّوا بَعْدَهُ». قَالَ عُمَرُ: إِنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ غَلَبَهُ الْوَجَعُ وَعِنْدَنَا كِتَابُ اللَّهِ حَسْبُنَا. فَاخْتَلَفُوا وَكَثُرَ اللَّغَطُ، قَالَ: «قُومُوا عَنِّي، وَلاَ يَنْبَغِي عِنْدِي التَّنَازُعُ». فَخَرَجَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ يَقُولُ: إِنَّ الرَّزِيَّةَ كُلَّ الرَّزِيَّةِ مَا حَالَ بَيْنَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَبَيْنَ كِتَابِهِ
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: Narrated Ibn ʿAbbās: When the ailment of the Prophet ﷺ became severe, he said: "Bring me writing material so that I may write for you a document after which you will not go astray." ʿUmar said: "The Prophet ﷺ is overcome by pain, and we have with us the Book of God; it is sufficient for us (wa-ʿindanā Kitābu Allāhi ḥasbunā)." They differed and raised a clamor, whereupon the Prophet ﷺ said: "Get up and leave me; quarreling in my presence is not fitting." Ibn ʿAbbās went out saying: "Indeed, the calamity of all calamities is what intervened between the Messenger of God ﷺ and his writing."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: أَخْبَرَنَا عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ، عَنْ مَعْمَرٍ، عَنِ الزُّهْرِيِّ، عَنْ عُرْوَةَ، أَنَّ عُمَرَ بْنَ الْخَطَّابِ أَرَادَ أَنْ يَكْتُبَ السُّنَنَ، فَاسْتَشَارَ أَصْحَابَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي ذَلِكَ، فَأَشَارُوا عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَكْتُبَهَا، فَطَفِقَ يَسْتَخِيرُ اللَّهَ فِيهَا شَهْرًا، ثُمَّ أَصْبَحَ يَوْمًا وَقَدْ عَزَمَ اللَّهُ لَهُ، فَقَالَ: «إِنِّي كُنْتُ أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَكْتُبَ السُّنَنَ، وَإِنِّي ذَكَرْتُ قَوْمًا كَانُوا قَبْلَكُمْ كَتَبُوا كُتُبًا، فَأَكَبُّوا عَلَيْهَا وَتَرَكُوا كِتَابَ اللَّهِ، وَإِنِّي وَاللَّهِ لَا أَلْبِسُ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ بِشَيْءٍ أَبَدًا»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: ʿAbd al-Razzāq reported from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwah, that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb intended to write down the Sunan, so he consulted the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ regarding that, and they advised him to write them down. Then he began praying istikhārah (seeking God's guidance) concerning it for a month. Then one morning he awoke, God having resolved his determination, and said: "I had intended to write down the Sunan, and then I remembered a people who came before you who wrote books, devoted themselves to them, and abandoned the Book of God. By God, I will never mingle/obscure the Book of God with anything ever (wa-innī wa-Allāhi lā albisu Kitāba Allāhi bi-shayʾin abadan)!"
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq 11/257–258 (#20484); Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm 1/274–275 (#343)

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: أَنَّ عُمَرَ بْنَ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَرَادَ أَنْ يَكْتُبَ السُّنَّةَ، ثُمَّ بَدَا لَهُ أَنْ لَا يَكْتُبَهَا، ثُمَّ كَتَبَ فِي الْأَمْصَارِ: «مَنْ كَانَ عِنْدَهُ شَيْءٌ فَلْيَمْحُهُ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb intended to write down the Sunnah, then it appeared right to him not to write it down; then he wrote to the provincial garrison cities (al-amṣār): 'Whoever has anything [written] in his possession, let him erase it (man kāna ʿindahu shayʾun fa-l-yamḥuhu).'"
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm wa-Faḍlihi 1/275 (#345)

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: حَدَّثَنَا عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ الْعَلَاءِ قَالَ: سَأَلْتُ الْقَاسِمَ أَنْ يُمْلِيَ عَلَيَّ أَحَادِيثَ فَمَنَعَنِي، وَقَالَ: إِنَّ الْأَحَادِيثَ كَثُرَتْ عَلَى عَهْدِ عُمَرَ، فَنَاشَدَ النَّاسَ أَنْ يَأْتُوهُ بِهَا، فَلَمَّا أَتَوْهُ بِهَا، أَمَرَ بِتَحْرِيقِهَا، ثُمَّ قَالَ: «مَثْنَاةٌ كَمَثْنَاةِ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: "I asked al-Qāsim [ibn Muḥammad] to dictate hadiths to me, but he forbade me and said: 'Indeed, hadiths multiplied during the time of ʿUmar, so he adjured the people to bring them to him. When they brought them to him, he ordered that they be burned (amara bi-taḥrīqihā), and then said: "A Mishnah like the Mishnah of the People of the Book (mathnātun ka-mathnāti Ahl al-Kitāb)!"'"
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 5/59; Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā 5/188; Taqyīd al-ʿIlm pp. 50–52

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: عَنْ شُعْبَةَ، عَنْ سَعْدِ بْنِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ، عَنْ أَبِيهِ، أَنَّ عُمَرَ بْنَ الْخَطَّابِ قَالَ لِابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ وَلِأَبِي الدَّرْدَاءِ وَلِأَبِي ذَرٍّ: «مَا هَذَا الْحَدِيثُ عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ؟» وَأَحْسِبُهُ حَبَسَهُمْ بِالْمَدِينَةِ حَتَّى أُصِيبَ... قَالَ الْحَاكِمُ: «هَذَا حَدِيثٌ صَحِيحٌ عَلَى شَرْطِ الشَّيْخَيْنِ، وَإِنْكَارُ عُمَرَ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ عَلَى الصَّحَابَةِ كَثْرَةَ الرِّوَايَةِ عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِيهِ سُنَّةٌ، وَلَمْ يُخْرِجَاهُ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: From Shuʿbah, from Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said to Ibn Masʿūd, Abū al-Dardāʾ, and Abū Dharr: "What is all this hadith [narration] from the Messenger of God ﷺ?" And I think he detained them in Medina until he was fatally stabbed... Al-Ḥākim said: "This hadith is authentic according to the criteria of the Two Shaykhs [al-Bukhārī and Muslim], and the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar's denunciation of the Companions for prolific narration from the Messenger of God ﷺ establishes a precedent (sunnah), though they did not include it."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Ḥākim, al-Mustadrak ʿalā al-Ṣaḥīḥayn 1/102 (#382–383); Al-Dhahabī, Tadhkirat al-Ḥuffāẓ 1/7

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: عَنْ عَامِرٍ الشَّعْبِيِّ، عَنْ قَرَظَةَ بْنِ كَعْبٍ، قَالَ: خَرَجْنَا نُرِيدُ الْعِرَاقَ فَمَشَى مَعَنَا عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ إِلَى صِرَارٍ، فَتَوَضَّأَ، ثُمَّ قَالَ: «أَتَدْرُونَ لِمَ مَشَيْتُ مَعَكُمْ؟» قَالُوا: نَعَمْ، نَحْنُ أَصْحَابُ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مَشَيْتَ مَعَنَا. قَالَ: «إِنَّكُمْ تَأْتُونَ أَهْلَ قَرْيَةٍ لَهُمْ دَوِيٌّ بِالْقُرْآنِ كَدَوِيِّ النَّحْلِ فَلَا تُبْدُونَهُمْ بِالْأَحَادِيثِ فَيَشْغَلُونَكُمْ، جَرِّدُوا الْقُرْآنَ، وَأَقِلُّوا الرِّوَايَةَ عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ، وَامْضُوا، وَأَنَا شَرِيكُكُمْ». فَلَمَّا قَدِمَ قَرَظَةُ قَالُوا: حَدِّثْنَا، قَالَ: نَهَانَا ابْنُ الْخَطَّابِ
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: From ʿĀmir al-Shaʿbī, from Qaraẓah ibn Kaʿb, who said: "We set out for Iraq, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb walked with us as far as Ṣirār... Then he said: 'Do you know why I walked with you?' They said: 'Yes, we are the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, so you walked with us.' He said: 'Indeed, you are coming to the people of a town whose humming with the Qurʾān is like the humming of bees; so do not divert/preoccupy them with hadiths, lest they distract you. Keep the Qurʾān pure/unadulterated (jarridū al-Qurʾān), and minimize narration from the Messenger of God ﷺ. Go forth, and I am your partner in this.' When Qaraẓah arrived [in Kufa], they said: 'Narrate hadiths to us!' He replied: 'Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb forbade us.'"
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Ḥākim, al-Mustadrak ʿalā al-Ṣaḥīḥayn 1/102 (#353); cf. Muṣannaf Ibn Abī Shaybah 7/4420

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: أَخْبَرَنَا عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ، عَنْ مَعْمَرٍ، عَنِ الزُّهْرِيِّ، قَالَ: «كُنَّا نَكْرَهُ كِتَابَ الْعِلْمِ حَتَّى أَكْرَهَنَا عَلَيْهِ هَؤُلَاءِ الْأُمَرَاءُ، فَرَأَيْنَا أَلَّا نَمْنَعَهُ أَحَدًا مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: ʿAbd al-Razzāq reported from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, who said: "We used to dislike/abhor writing down knowledge [hadith], until these [Umayyad] rulers compelled us to do so (ḥattā akrahanā ʿalayhi hāʾulāʾi al-umarāʾ), so we decided not to withhold it from any of the Muslims."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq 11/258 (#20486); Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm 1/333 (#443); Al-Baghawī, Sharḥ al-Sunnah 1/294 (#137)

arguments.title: Companion Narration Counts, Corpus Selection Ratios, and Biographical Records
arguments.executive_summary: Following the early accounts on oral transmission and the century before formal compilation, this section examines three quantitative and biographical records: Baqī ibn Makhlad's Musnad counts for Abū Hurayrah (5,374), Ibn ʿAbbās (1,660), and the first four Caliphs (1,361 combined), al-Bukhārī's selection of ~2,602 unique texts from 600,000 circulating chains (and 100,000 authentic reports), and biographical notices on Hishām ibn ʿUrwah's later Iraqi transmissions alongside Kūfan narrators recorded as living past 120 years. How do these figures shape our picture of transmission?
arguments.methodological_significance: These biographical and quantitative notices come directly from Ibn Ḥajar, al-Dhahabī, Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, and al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī. How did classical compilers account for the distribution of reports across Companions and the memory changes of senior transmitters?

subpoints.summary_markdown: Across classical *Musnad* tallies preserved from Baqī ibn Makhlad ([IslamWeb Fatwa #174903](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/174903/) citing Ibn al-Jawzī's *Talqīḥ Fuhūm Ahl al-Athar*; [al-Dhahabī, *Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 2/632](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/267/أبو-هريرة) and [3/359](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/347/عبد-الله-بن-عباس-البحر)), the volume of traditions attributed to a Companion stands in inverse proportion to their duration of proximity to the Prophet. While lifelong senior Companions account for comparatively few reports, late-converting and younger Companions such as Abū Hurayrah ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:118), [2047](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2047), [3568](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3568)) and Ibn ʿAbbās account for thousands of traditions that classical authorities acknowledged were acquired predominantly through unstated intermediaries ([al-Ghazālī, *al-Mustaṣfā* 1/169](https://shamela.ws/book/5459/133); [Ibn Ḥajar, *Fatḥ al-Bārī* 11/378](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/11955/باب-كيف-الحشر)).

evidence_items.label: Classical Assessments of How Many Hadiths Ibn ʿAbbās Heard Directly Alongside 1,660 Attributed Reports
evidence_items.content_markdown: According to his own testimony in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5035](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5035)–[5036](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5036) (cf. [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 1357](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1357); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 3/332–341](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/345/عبد-الله-بن-عباس-البحر)), **ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās** resided in Mecca until 8 AH and was ten to thirteen years old when the Prophet died, yet **1,660 hadiths** (including 204 in the *Ṣaḥīḥayn*: 75 agreed upon, 120 Bukhārī-only, 9 Muslim-only per [*Siyar* 3/359](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/347/عبد-الله-بن-عباس-البحر)) are attributed to him ([IslamWeb Fatwa #174903](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/174903/)). Classical Sunni scholars noted that over 99% of this corpus was acquired via intermediaries rather than direct audition: **al-Ghazālī** states in [*al-Mustaṣfā* (1/169)](https://shamela.ws/book/5459/133) that *"he did not hear directly from the Messenger of God ﷺ except **four hadiths** due to his young age,"* while **Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān**, **Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn**, **Abū Dāwūd**, and **Ghundar** (quoted in [*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 11/378](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/11955/باب-كيف-الحشر) and Ibn al-Mulaqqin's [*al-Iʿlām* 1/508](https://shamela.ws/book/13769/505); cf. [*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 1/170](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/150/باب-متى-يصح-سماع-الصغير)) estimated his direct auditions at **nine** or **under ten hadiths**.
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «تُوُفِّيَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَأَنَا ابْنُ عَشْرِ سِنِينَ وَقَدْ قَرَأْتُ الْمُحْكَمَ» — "The Messenger of God ﷺ died when I was a boy of ten years, and I had already read the Muḥkam [of the Qurʾān]." (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5035; cf. al-Mustaṣfā 1/169)

evidence_items.label: Canonical Critiques and Restrictions of Abū Hurayrah's Narration Volume by ʿĀʾishah and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3567](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3567)–[3568](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3568) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2493](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2493), **ʿĀʾishah** objected to the pace and volume of Abū Hurayrah's narration, stating: *"Had I caught up with him, I would have refuted him: 'Indeed, the Messenger of God ﷺ did not rattle off speech the way you rattle it off (`lam yakun yasrudu al-ḥadītha ka-sardikum`)!'"* Similarly, **ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb** physically restrained Abū Hurayrah from public proclamation in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 31](https://sunnah.com/muslim:31) and warned him in al-Dhahabī's [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* (2/600–601)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/263/أبو-هريرة)—*"You shall cease narrating abundantly from the Messenger of God ﷺ, or I shall send you back to the land of Daws!"*—prompting Abū Hurayrah to remark that had he narrated at such volume during ʿUmar's lifetime, *"he would have split my head open (`la-shajja raʾsī`)."*
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «إِنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم لَمْ يَكُنْ يَسْرُدُ الْحَدِيثَ كَسَرْدِكُمْ» — "Indeed, the Messenger of God did not reel off speech rapidly the way you do." (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3568)

evidence_items.label: Inverse Statistical Distribution: Abū Hurayrah (5,374 in ~3 Years) vs. All Four Rāshidūn Caliphs Combined (1,361 Across 18–23 Years)
evidence_items.content_markdown: In Baqī ibn Makhlad's *Musnad* tallies ([IslamWeb Fatwa #174903](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/174903/) citing Ibn al-Jawzī's *Talqīḥ Fuhūm Ahl al-Athar*; [al-Dhahabī, *Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 2/632](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/267/أبو-هريرة)), the four lifelong senior Companions and Rightly Guided Caliphs—**Abū Bakr** (142 total; 17 in *Ṣaḥīḥayn*), **ʿUmar** (537; 81 in *Ṣaḥīḥayn*), **ʿUthmān** (146; 14 in *Ṣaḥīḥayn*), and **ʿAlī** (536; 82 in *Ṣaḥīḥayn*)—account for **1,361 hadiths combined** (194 in the *Ṣaḥīḥayn*). Conversely, **Abū Hurayrah**, who arrived at Khaybar in Muḥarram 7 AH and accompanied the Prophet for roughly three years ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:118), [2047](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2047); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 2/632](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/267/أبو-هريرة)), is credited with **5,374 hadiths** (517 in the *Ṣaḥīḥayn*: 326 agreed upon, 93 Bukhārī-only, 98 Muslim-only per [*Siyar* 2/632](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/267/أبو-هريرة))—nearly four times the combined total of all four Caliphs and 38 times that of Abū Bakr.
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «إِنَّ النَّاسَ يَقُولُونَ أَكْثَرَ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ، وَلَوْلاَ آيَتَانِ فِي كِتَابِ اللَّهِ مَا حَدَّثْتُ حَدِيثًا» — "People say Abū Hurayrah narrates too much; were it not for two verses in the Book of God, I would not have narrated a single hadith." (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 118)

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical and modern commentators note that the four Caliphs narrated fewer reports because they died earlier or were occupied with governance while Abū Hurayrah taught until c. 58 AH ([IslamWeb Fatwa #174903](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/174903/) citing Ibn al-Jawzī's *Talqīḥ Fuhūm Ahl al-Athar*), that a young Companion's audition is valid ([Ibn Ḥajar, *Fatḥ al-Bārī* 1/170](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/150/باب-متى-يصح-سماع-الصغير)), and that Ibn ʿAbbās's ~1,650 non-heard reports represent disconnected Companion transmissions (*marāsīl al-Ṣaḥābah*) acquired from senior Companions ([Ibn Ḥajar, *Fatḥ al-Bārī* 11/378](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/11955/باب-كيف-الحشر); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 3/359](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/347/عبد-الله-بن-عباس-البحر)).
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: However, administrative duties and death dates do not fully account for why **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib** (d. 40 AH, raised by the Prophet for 23 years; [IslamWeb Fatwa #174903](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/174903/) citing Baqī ibn Makhlad's *Musnad* and Ibn al-Jawzī's *Talqīḥ Fuhūm Ahl al-Athar*) has ten times fewer narrations than Abū Hurayrah, nor why **ʿĀʾishah** ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:118), [2047](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2047), [3568](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3568)) and **ʿUmar** ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 2/600–601](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/263/أبو-هريرة)) explicitly contested Abū Hurayrah's narration rate. Furthermore, as **al-Ghazālī** observed in [*al-Mustaṣfā* (1/169)](https://shamela.ws/book/5459/133), early legal theorists questioned unconditional reliance on *mursal al-Ṣaḥābī* *"because Companions sometimes narrate from non-Companions among the desert Arabs (`al-aʿrāb`)"* as well as Successors and scriptural converts.

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
#### 1. Chronological Constraints and Early Medinan Objections to Prolific Narration

Statistical tallies from the third-century *Musnad* of **Baqī ibn Makhlad** (d. 276 AH)—preserved by Ibn Ḥazm, Ibn al-Jawzī, and **al-Dhahabī** in *Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* ([vol. 2, p. 632](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/267/أبو-هريرة) and [vol. 3, p. 359](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/347/عبد-الله-بن-عباس-البحر); cf. [IslamWeb Fatwa #174903](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/174903/) recording the top Companion totals from **Ibn al-Jawzī's** *Talqīḥ Fuhūm Ahl al-Athar*)—exhibit a pronounced inverse relationship between a Companion's years of physical proximity to the Prophet and the volume of canonical traditions later transmitted in their name. Although the four Caliphs accompanied the Prophet across two decades, their combined *Musnad* output totals 1,361 reports. By contrast, **Abū Hurayrah** embraced Islam at Khaybar in Muḥarram 7 AH and spent roughly thirty-eight months in Prophetic company, a window further curtailed by his administrative posting to Bahrain under al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥaḍramī. Dividing his 5,374 attributed traditions across his maximum residence in Medina corresponds to roughly five Baqī ibn Makhlad *musnad* entries per day of his three-year Medina stay (a total that counts distinct transmission pathways alongside unique texts).

Canonical texts confirm that senior Companions viewed this rapid output as anomalous during Abū Hurayrah's own lifetime. In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2493](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2493) as well as *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* nos. [3568](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3568) and [3567](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3567), Mother of the Believers **ʿĀʾishah** contrasted his rapid-fire recitation style beside her chamber with the Prophet's measured speech, while **ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb** physically halted his public preaching in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 31](https://sunnah.com/muslim:31) and threatened him with deportation to Daws in *Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* ([vol. 2, pp. 600–601](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/263/أبو-هريرة)). Abū Hurayrah himself conceded after ʿUmar's assassination that he could not have circulated such volumes while the second Caliph lived without facing corporal punishment (`la-shajja raʾsī`).

#### 2. Juvenile Audition Limits and Secondary Accretion in the Corpus of Ibn ʿAbbās

An analogous chronological bottleneck governs **ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās** (d. 68 AH), the fifth largest source in Sunni Hadith with 1,660 attributed traditions (204 in the *Ṣaḥīḥayn* per [*Siyar* vol. 3, p. 359](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/347/عبد-الله-بن-عباس-البحر)). By his own testimony in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* nos. [5036](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5036), [5035](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5035), [1357](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1357), and [76](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:76) (with [*Siyar* vol. 3, pp. 332–341](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/345/عبد-الله-بن-عباس-البحر)), he resided in Mecca with his mother Umm al-Faḍl until the eve of the Conquest in 8 AH and was a boy of ten to thirteen when the Prophet died. Consequently, classical authorities including **al-Ghazālī** in [*al-Mustaṣfā* (1/169)](https://shamela.ws/book/5459/133) and early *ḥuffāẓ* quoted in **Ibn al-Mulaqqin's** [*al-Iʿlām* (vol. 1, p. 508)](https://shamela.ws/book/13769/505) and **Ibn Ḥajar's** *Fatḥ al-Bārī* ([vol. 1, p. 170](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/150/باب-متى-يصح-سماع-الصغير); [vol. 11, p. 378](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/11955/باب-كيف-الحشر)) concluded that he heard between four and ten reports directly from the Prophet, meaning over 99% of his corpus depends on unstated intermediaries (*marāsīl*) including non-Companions (`al-aʿrāb`), Successors, and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, an observation explicitly affirmed by al-Ghazālī and Ibn Ḥajar.
