subpoints.summary_markdown: Classical biographical sources including al-Dhahabī's [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* (12/402)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=402) and Ibn Ḥajar's *Hady al-Sārī* ([p. 468](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/463), [p. 477](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/472), [p. 489](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/484)) report that **al-Bukhārī** selected his canonical *Ṣaḥīḥ* (~2,602 unique texts; 7,275–7,563 with repetitions, 7,397 per Ibn Ḥajar) from **600,000 circulating hadiths**, while **Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj** ([*Siyar* 12/565](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=565)) compiled his *Ṣaḥīḥ* from **300,000 heard narrations**. Alongside al-Bukhārī's statement that he memorized **100,000 *Ṣaḥīḥ* and 200,000 non-*Ṣaḥīḥ* traditions** ([*Siyar* 12/415](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=415); [*Hady al-Sārī* p. 487](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/482); [IslamWeb Fatwa #129325](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/129325/)), these third-century AH compilation metrics record the proportion of circulating chains selected for inclusion in the written collections alongside the reported size of al-Bukhārī's memorized repertoire.

evidence_items.label: Reported Circulating Narrations (600,000 and 300,000) and Reports Selected in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* (12/402)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=402) and [*Hady al-Sārī* (p. 489)](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/484), **al-Bukhārī** stated that he compiled his *Ṣaḥīḥ* over sixteen years from **600,000 hadiths**, retaining 7,275–7,563 narrations with repetitions (7,397 per Ibn Ḥajar in [*Hady al-Sārī* p. 468](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/463), reducing to **2,602 unique connected texts** in [*Hady al-Sārī* p. 477](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/472)), while **Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj** ([*Siyar* 12/565](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=565)) selected his *Ṣaḥīḥ* (~3,033–4,000 unique reports) from **300,000 heard hadiths**. These canonical compilation figures indicate that **98.8% (including repetitions) to 99.57% (unique texts)** of the traditions circulating two centuries after the Prophet were excluded by the compilers as unverified, defective (*maʿlūl*), or weak ([*Siyar* 12/402](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=402); [*Hady al-Sārī* pp. 477, 489](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/484)).

evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* (12/415)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=415) and [*Hady al-Sārī* (p. 487)](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/482) (cf. scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical and modern commentators explain that early traditionists counted every distinct transmission pathway (*ṭarīq*) and post-prophetic report as a separate "hadith" (**Ibn Ḥajar**, [*Hady al-Sārī* pp. 477, 487](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/482)), while **al-Bukhārī** omitted many valid traditions to keep his compilation concise ([IslamWeb Fatwa #129325](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/129325/)) and included *ḥasan* reports within his 100,000 count under an early binary classification ([IslamWeb Fatwa #31442](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/31442/)).
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: In historical-critical scholarship, defining the 600,000 figure as individual transmission chains (*ṭuruq*) highlights a major diachronic corollary: if a core repertoire of ~2,602–4,000 accepted Prophetic texts generated **600,000 circulating chains** within two centuries—of which **two-thirds (200,000 vs. 100,000) were non-*Ṣaḥīḥ*** in al-Bukhārī's own memory ([*Siyar* 12/415](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=415)) and **98.8% were excluded** from his canon ([*Siyar* 12/402](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=402); [IslamWeb Fatwa #129325](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/129325/))—the primary metrics attest to the large-scale proliferation of uncorroborated *isnād* pathways during the second and third centuries AH.

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
#### 1. Third-Century Compilation Metrics and the Scale of Corpus Filtering

Biographical notices preserved in *Tārīkh Baghdād* (2/8–10), **Ibn Ḥajar** in *Hady al-Sārī* ([p. 489](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/484)), and **al-Dhahabī** in *Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* ([vol. 12, p. 402](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=402) and [p. 415](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=415)) record that third-century AH compilers assembled their canonical collections by winnowing vast pools of circulating material. **Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Bukhārī (d. 256 AH)** reported sifting 600,000 traditions over sixteen years to compile *al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaḥīḥ*, while **Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj (d. 261 AH)** reported extracting his *Musnad al-Ṣaḥīḥ* from 300,000 heard narrations ([*Siyar* vol. 12, p. 565](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=565)), **Abū Dāwūd** selected ~4,800 from 500,000, and **Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal** sifted *al-Musnad* from over 750,000 reports.

According to Ibn Ḥajar's canonical audit in *Hady al-Sārī* ([p. 468](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/463) and [p. 477](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/472)), *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* contains 7,397 connected (*mawṣūl*) entries with repetitions (7,563 in ʿAbd al-Bāqī's numbering; 7,275 per Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ and al-Nawawī), which reduce to **2,602 unique connected Prophetic texts** once duplicates across legal chapters are consolidated. Whether taking the larger repeated figure against the 600,000 evaluated base pool, al-Bukhārī set aside 98.74% to 99.57% of the material circulating two centuries after the Prophet's death. Furthermore, his companion statement in *Siyar* ([vol. 12, p. 415](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=415)) and *Hady al-Sārī* ([p. 487](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/482); cf. [Fatwa #129325](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/129325/) and [Fatwa #31442](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/31442/)) claiming retention of 100,000 authentic reports alongside 200,000 defective ones—while omitting other authentic reports lest the book grow long ([*Siyar* vol. 12, p. 402](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=402))—leaves roughly 92,400 to 97,400 authentic units outside his canon, a figure exceeding the total number of unique Prophetic *mutūn* across all Six Canonical Books combined.

#### 2. Technical *Ṭuruq* Counting vs. Diachronic Chain Proliferation

To resolve this numerical gap, classical authorities—including **al-Bayhaqī**, **Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ**, **al-Nawawī**, and **Ibn Ḥajar** (*Hady al-Sārī* [p. 487](https://shamela.ws/book/1224/482))—explain that early traditionists (*al-mutaqaddimūn*) applied the term *ḥadīth* not to a distinct Prophetic text (*matn*), but to every individual chain of transmission (*ṭarīq* / *isnād*) as well as Companion and Successor statements (*mawqūf* and *maqṭūʿ*). Under this accounting, a single saying transmitted through 30 chains counted as 30 aḥādīth, allowing a critic to evaluate hundreds of derivative branches by auditing a core teacher's notebook (*juzʾ*). Historically, however, this definition underscores the scale of second- and third-century *isnād* multiplication: a core repertoire of a few thousand Prophetic sayings generated 600,000 competing transmission pathways within two hundred years, of which two-thirds in al-Bukhārī's own memory were defective and nearly 99% were excluded from his canonical text alongside biographical reports of his juvenile memorization of 70,000 traditions ([*Siyar* vol. 12, p. 417](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/pageno_redirect.php?part=12&bk_no=60&pageno=417)). The scale of this ninth-century filtering process underscores how vast quantities of circulating oral traditions were left outside the canonical collections.

evidence_items.label: Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah's Note on Chain Attachment in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5765 and the Disconnected Precursor in Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq 19764
evidence_items.content_markdown: At the conclusion of the bewitchment narrative in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5765](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5765) (analyzed in [*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 10/244](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/10534/)), **Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah** (d. 198 AH) records how **Hishām ibn ʿUrwah** (61–146 AH) supplied a continuous Companion chain to a previously disconnected family report: *"The first one who narrated it to us was Ibn Jurayj, saying: 'The family of ʿUrwah (Āl ʿUrwah) narrated to me from ʿUrwah.' Then I asked Hishām about it, and he narrated it to us from his father, from ʿĀʾishah!"* Pre-Hishām disconnected (*mursal*) precursors survive in [*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* (11/14, #19764)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/18818/) (via `Maʿmar ← al-Zuhrī ← Ibn al-Musayyab and ʿUrwah`, lacking both **ʿĀʾishah** in the *isnād* and the individual name **Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam** in the *matn*) and [*al-Muṣannaf* (#19765)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/18819/) (via `Maʿmar ← ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī ← Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar`, lacking ʿĀʾishah, Labīd, and any mention of a Jewish actor).

evidence_items.label: Classical Rijāl Assessments of Hishām's Late-Life Iraqi Memory Decline and Tadlīs & Exclusive Iraqi Transmission Bottlenecks
evidence_items.content_markdown: **Yaʿqūb ibn Shaybah** (cited in Ibn Ḥajar's [*Hady al-Sārī* p. 631 / Fatwa #36550](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/36550/) and al-Dhahabī's [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 6/35–36](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/937/)) and **Ibn Kharrāsh** record that **Imām Mālik** and Medinan scholars criticized Hishām's late-life Iraqi transmissions (after 131 AH, age 71+) because in Kūfa he attributed reports directly to his father that he had heard through intermediaries—a practice **Ibn Ḥajar** classified as *tadlīs* (`قُلْتُ: هَذَا هُوَ التَّدْلِيسُ`), **Ibn al-Qaṭṭān** termed late-life confusion (*ikhtalaṭa wa-taghayyara*), and **al-Dhahabī** described as age-related memory decline (`fī al-kibar tanāqaṣa ḥifẓuhu`). Every canonical chain from Hishām for both the bewitchment narrative ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3175](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3175), [3268](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3268), [5763](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5763), [5765](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5765), [5766](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5766); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2189a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2189a)–[2189b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2189b)) and the marital-age narrative ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3894](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3894), [3896](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3896), [5133](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5133), [5134](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5134), [5158](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5158)) passes exclusively through Iraqi transmitters and is absent from Mālik's Medinan *Muwaṭṭaʾ*.
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «هِشَامٌ ثَبْتٌ، لَمْ يُنْكَرْ عَلَيْهِ إِلَّا بَعْدَمَا صَارَ إِلَى الْعِرَاقِ، فَإِنَّهُ انْبَسَطَ فِي الرِّوَايَةِ، وَأَرْسَلَ عَنْ أَبِيهِ أَشْيَاءَ» — "Hishām is reliable; nothing was criticized in him except after he went to Iraq, for he expanded loosely in narration and sent disconnected reports from his father." ([Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 6/35–36](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/937/))

evidence_items.label: Kūfan Super-Centenarian Bridge Narrators (Muʿammarūn Aged 120–130) Spanning the 64-Year Chronological Gap in the Ṣaḥīḥayn
evidence_items.content_markdown: Because Kūfa's premier Companion **ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd** died early in **32 AH** and Kūfa's leading jurist **Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī** (d. 96 AH) never narrated directly from any of the Companions ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 4/521](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/663/); cf. [*Kitāb al-ʿIlal* 3/380](https://shamela.ws/book/2331/1526) on the late Kūfan demand for *isnāds*), second-century Kūfan transmitters faced a 64-to-90-year chronological interval when collectors required uninterrupted chains. In hundreds of *Ṣaḥīḥayn* traditions, this interval is spanned by a localized Kūfan cluster of super-centenarian narrators (*muʿammarūn*) credited with lifespans of **120 to 130 years**—including **Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh** (d. 82 AH, age 120–127; [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 4976](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4976)), **Suwayd ibn Ghafalah** (d. 82 AH, age 120–130; [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 4/70](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/460/); [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5057](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5057)), **Abū ʿAmr Saʿd ibn Iyās al-Shaybānī** (d. 96 AH, age 120; [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 527](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:527)), **Zayd ibn Wahb al-Juhanī** (d. 83–96 AH, age 120+; [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3208](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3208)), and **al-Maʿrūr ibn Suwayd** (age 120; [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 30](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:30)).

([Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 4/521](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/663/))

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical commentators cite al-Dhahabī ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 6/35–36](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/937/)) and Ibn Ḥajar ([*Hady al-Sārī* p. 631 / Fatwa #36550](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/36550/)) to argue that Hishām never experienced total senility (*ikhtilāṭ*), that his Iraqi *ʿan* formulas summarized earlier Medinan auditions from his father, and that Kūfan *muʿammarūn* ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 4/70](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/460/)) possessed exceptional natural longevity.
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: Even while rejecting total senility, **al-Dhahabī** ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 6/35–36](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/937/)) notes that Hishām's memory diminished in old age such that *"he forgot some of what he had memorized or erred,"* and **Ibn Ḥajar** ([*Hady al-Sārī* p. 631 / Fatwa #36550](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/36550/)) identifies the practice described by Yaʿqūb ibn Shaybah as **omission of intermediaries (*tadlīs*)** (`قُلْتُ: هَذَا هُوَ التَّدْلِيسُ`). Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah's testimony in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5765](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5765) and Ibn Ḥajar's comment in [*Fatḥ al-Bārī* (10/236)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/10530/) (`وَوَقَعَ فِي رِوَايَةِ الْحُمَيْدِيِّ عَنْ سُفْيَانَ عَنِ ابْنِ جُرَيْجٍ حَدَّثَنِي بَعْضُ آلِ عُرْوَةَ عَنْ عُرْوَةَ وَظَاهِرُهُ أَنَّ غَيْرَ هِشَامٍ أَيْضًا حَدَّثَ بِهِ عَنْ عُرْوَةَ`) corroborate this mechanism in primary texts, showing that the bewitchment report circulated through an unspecified *Āl ʿUrwah* informant and as a disconnected *mursal* tradition (cf. [*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* #19764](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/18818/)) prior to Hishām supplying the connected `ʿUrwah ← ʿĀʾishah` chain.

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
#### 1. Diachronic Shift Between Medinan and Late-Life Iraqi Transmissions

Born in 61 AH, the prominent Hijazi Successor **Hishām ibn ʿUrwah** spent his first seven decades in Medina before relocating to the Abbasid court and Kūfa around 131–132 AH, dying in Baghdad in 146 AH at age eighty-five. Classical *jarḥ wa-taʿdīl* literature preserves a sharp geographical and chronological divide in his output. As documented by **Ibn Ḥajar** in [*Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb* (11/50) and *Hady al-Sārī* (p. 631)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/36550/) and by **al-Dhahabī** in *Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* ([vol. 6, pp. 35–36](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/937/)), early critics **Yaʿqūb ibn Shaybah** and **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Kharrāsh** noted that Hishām's Medinan contemporaries and his chief Hijazi pupil **Imām Mālik** rejected his Iraqi corpus. Across three successive trips to Kūfa, Hishām progressively relaxed his transmission formulas—shifting from explicit audition (`ḥaddathanī abī`) to ambiguous `ʿan` links—while attributing directly to his father ʿUrwah reports that he had acquired through unnamed family or Medinan intermediaries.

Within *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* ([no. 5765](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5765); see *Fatḥ al-Bārī* [vol. 10, p. 244](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/10534/)), the Meccan authority **Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah** provides a primary-source witness to this elevation process. Sufyān recalls that the bewitchment narrative first reached Kūfan circles via **Ibn Jurayj** as an anonymous family tradition (`Āl ʿUrwah ← ʿUrwah`), a disconnected (*mursal*) stratum independently preserved in *Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* ([report #19764](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/18818/)) without ʿĀʾishah or the name Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam. Only when Sufyān later queried Hishām in Iraq did Hishām supply the continuous `ʿUrwah ← ʿĀʾishah` *isnād*. Consistently, every canonical pathway from Hishām for both the bewitchment traditions ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2189a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2189a); *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* nos. [5763](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5763), [3268](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3268), and [3175](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3175)) and the marital-age reports (*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* nos. [5134](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5134), [5133](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5133), and [3894](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3894)) branches exclusively through Iraqi pupils such as Abū Usāmah, Sufyān al-Thawrī, and ʿAlī ibn Mushir.

#### 2. Prosopographical Function of Kūfan *Muʿammarūn*

A second structural feature of Kūfan *isnāds* stems from the early death of Kūfa's foundational Companion **ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd** in 32 AH, compounded by the absence of direct Companion auditions for the prominent Kūfan Successor **Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī** (died 96 AH; [*Siyar* 4:521](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/663/)) and the delayed emergence of chain requirements in Iraq ([Aḥmad's *ʿIlal* #5673](https://shamela.ws/book/2331/1526)). To connect mid-second-century Kūfan common links like al-Aʿmash directly to first-generation authorities without multi-link gaps, hundreds of *Ṣaḥīḥayn* chains rely on a localized Kūfan cohort of super-centenarians (*muʿammarūn*) assigned lifespans of 120 to 130 years—including **Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh** ([*Bukhārī* 4976](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4976)), alongside **Suwayd ibn Ghafalah** ([*Siyar* 4/70](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/460/)), **Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī** ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 527](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:527)), and **al-Maʿrūr ibn Suwayd** ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 30](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:30)). These biographical records highlight the chronological and geographical vulnerabilities underlying both late-life Medinan transmissions and Kufan centenarian chains.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «هِشَامٌ ثَبْتٌ، لَمْ يُنْكَرْ عَلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ إِلاَّ بَعْدَ مَا صَارَ إِلَى الْعِرَاقِ، فَإِنَّهُ انْبَسَطَ فِي الرِّوَايَةِ عَنْ أَبِيهِ، فَأَنْكَرَ ذَلِكَ عَلَيْهِ أَهْلُ بَلَدِهِ، وَالَّذِي رَأَى هِشَامٌ يَرْسِلُ عَنْ أَبِيهِ أَشْيَاءَ مِمَّا كَانَ قَدْ سَمِعَهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ أَبِيهِ عَنْ أَبِيهِ. قُلْتُ: هَذَا هُوَ التَّدْلِيسُ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Hishām is reliable (thabt); nothing was criticized in him except after he went to Iraq, for he expanded loosely (inbasaṭa) in narrating from his father [ʿUrwah], and the people of his homeland [Medina] denounced that in him. What was observed is that Hishām used to send disconnected reports (yursilu) from his father regarding things that he had heard from others besides his father, from his father." (Commenting on this passage in Hady al-Sārī, p. 631, Ibn Ḥajar remarks: "I say: This is tadlīs [omission of an intermediary].")
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Yaʿqūb ibn Shaybah in Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb 11/50 & Hady al-Sārī p. 631

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «كَانَ مَالِكٌ لاَ يَرْضَاهُ، بَلَغَنِي أَنَّ مَالِكًا نَقَمَ عَلَيْهِ حَدِيثَهُ لأَهْلِ الْعِرَاقِ؛ قَدِمَ الْكُوفَةَ ثَلاَثَ مَرَّاتٍ: قَدْمَةً كَانَ يَقُولُ: حَدَّثَنِي أَبِي قَالَ سَمِعْتُ عَائِشَةَ، وَقَدِمَ الثَّانِيَةَ فَكَانَ يَقُولُ: أَخْبَرَنِي أَبِي عَنْ عَائِشَةَ، وَقَدِمَ الثَّالِثَةَ فَكَانَ يَقُولُ: أَبِي عَنْ عَائِشَةَ، يَعْنِي يُرْسِلُ عَنْ أَبِيهِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Mālik was not pleased with him. It reached me that Mālik resented his narrating of hadith to the people of Iraq. He came to Kūfa three times: the first time he used to say, 'My father narrated to me (ḥaddathanī abī), saying: I heard ʿĀʾishah (samiʿtu ʿĀʾishah)'; the second time he came, he used to say, 'My father informed me from ʿĀʾishah (akhbaranī abī ʿan ʿĀʾishah)'; and the third time he came, he used to say, 'My father, from ʿĀʾishah (abī ʿan ʿĀʾishah)'—meaning he was narrating disconnectedly (yursilu) from his father."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Kharrāsh in Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb 11/50 & Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 6/35–36

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «هِشَامُ بْنُ عُرْوَةَ: أَحَدُ الأَعْلاَمِ، حُجَّةٌ إِمَامٌ، لَكِنْ فِي الكِبَرِ تَنَاقَصَ حِفْظُهُ وَلَمْ يَخْتَلِطْ أَبَدًا، وَلاَ عِبْرَةَ بِمَا قَالَهُ أَبُو الحَسَنِ بْنُ القَطَّانِ مِنْ أَنَّهُ وَسُهَيْلَ بْنَ أَبِي صَالِحٍ اخْتَلَطَا وَتَغَيَّرَا. نَعَمْ، الرَّجُلُ تَغَيَّرَ قَلِيلاً وَلَمْ يَبْقَ حِفْظُهُ كَمَا هُوَ فِي حَالِ الشَّبِيبَةِ، فَنَسِيَ بَعْضَ مَحْفُوظِهِ أَوْ وَهِمَ، فَكَانَ مَاذَا؟ أَهُوَ مَعْصُومٌ مِنَ النِّسْيَانِ؟ وَلَمَّا قَدِمَ العِرَاقَ فِي آخِرِ عُمُرِهِ حَدَّثَ بِجُمْلَةٍ كَبِيرَةٍ مِنَ العِلْمِ، فِي غُضُونِ ذَلِكَ يَسِيرُ أَحَادِيثَ لَمْ يُجَوِّدْهَا»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Hishām ibn ʿUrwah: one of the luminaries, a proof and an Imām, but in old age his memory declined (fī al-kibar tanāqaṣa ḥifẓuhu), though he never became senile (wa-lam yakhtaliṭ abadan). No weight is given to what Abū al-Ḥasan ibn al-Qaṭṭān said—that he and Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ became confused and altered (ikhtalaṭā wa-taghayyarā). Yes, the man changed slightly (taghayyara qalīlan) and his memory did not remain as it was in his youth, so he forgot some of what he had memorized or erred (fa-nasiya baʿḍa maḥfūẓihi aw wahima)—and so what? Is he infallible from forgetfulness? When he came to Iraq at the end of his life, he narrated a large body of knowledge, in the course of which are a few hadiths in which he did not excel (lam yujawwidhā)."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Dhahabī, Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl 4/301 (#9232); Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 6/35–36

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «حَدَّثَنِي عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ، قَالَ سَمِعْتُ ابْنَ عُيَيْنَةَ يَقُولُ: أَوَّلُ مَنْ حَدَّثَنَا بِهِ ابْنُ جُرَيْجٍ يَقُولُ: حَدَّثَنِي آلُ عُرْوَةَ عَنْ عُرْوَةَ، فَسَأَلْتُ هِشَامًا عَنْهُ فَحَدَّثَنَا عَنْ أَبِيهِ عَنْ عَائِشَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "ʿAbdullāh ibn Muḥammad narrated to me, saying: I heard Ibn ʿUyaynah say: The first one who narrated it to us was Ibn Jurayj, saying: 'The family of ʿUrwah (Āl ʿUrwah) narrated to me from ʿUrwah.' Then I asked Hishām about it, and he narrated it to us from his father, from ʿĀʾishah!"

arguments.plain_english_hook: In their manuals, classical masters explained when chains were first requested, how 'from' links were treated, and whether single chains yield probable belief. What did critics write about chains?
arguments.title: Classical Chain Criteria, Disputed Narrators, Muʿanʿan Links, and Epistemic Grading
arguments.executive_summary: To see how classical scholars filtered that circulating corpus, this section presents five foundational discussions from the manuals of uṣūl al-ḥadīth: Imām Muslim's Introduction quoting Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān on unintended falsehood among pious narrators and Ibn Sīrīn on when chains were first requested, al-Dhahabī and Ibn Ḥibbān on retaining disputed narrators and single chains, the classical distinction between probable belief (ẓann) in single-chain reports and Qurʾānic certainty (qaṭʿ), Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ and al-Mizzī on 'from' (muʿanʿan) chains by mudallis transmitters in the Ṣaḥīḥayn, and Imām Muslim's argument that contemporaneity suffices without proof of a personal meeting. How do these principles define hadith authentication?
arguments.methodological_significance: Reading the methodological treatises of Muslim, al-Shāfiʿī, Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, al-Nawawī, al-Dhahabī, and Ibn Ḥajar shows that classical scholars viewed chain criticism as a rigorous human discipline operating under defined assumptions. How do those classical definitions compare with popular modern assumptions about what a ṣaḥīḥ grade entails?

subpoints.short_title: 4 Early Critics on Unintended Falsehood and the First Chain Requests
subpoints.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see al-Qaṭṭān, quoted in Muslim's introduction, on unintended falsehood among the pious, Shuʿbah's estimate of false reports, and Ibn Sīrīn and al-Nakhaʿī dating the first requests for chains.
subpoints.takeaway: Muslim's introduction notes unintended falsehood; Ibn Sīrīn dates the first asking for chains to the fitnah.
subpoints.title: Unintended Falsehood in Pious Reports, Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān, & the Rise of the Isnād

showcase.gap_label: Four early authorities on when chains were first requested and how unintended falsehood entered reports

points.label: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī: 'People began asking about the isnād during the days of al-Mukhtār'
Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn: 'They used not to ask about the isnād; when the Fitnah occurred, they said: Name for us your men'
Shuʿbah ibn al-Ḥajjāj: 'Had I narrated to you solely from trustworthy transmitters, I would not have narrated from thirty [or three]'
Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān: 'We have never seen the righteous more given to unintended falsehood in anything than in Hadith'

subpoints.summary_markdown: Early Hadith critics such as **Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān** (d. 198 AH) and **Imām Muslim** (d. 261 AH) observed that unintentional falsehood (*kadhib*) flowed most frequently upon the tongues of pious transmitters ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 40](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/39); [*al-Kifāyah* §§547–548](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/547)), while **Shuʿbah ibn al-Ḥajjāj** (d. 160 AH) estimated that three-quarters of the Hadith corpus he investigated was false ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 7/226](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1185/شعبة)) yet noted alongside Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān that restricting transmission strictly to fully precise (*thiqah* / *marḍī*) authorities would have reduced their sources to three to five individuals ([*al-Kifāyah* §284](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/284); [*Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī* 1/376](https://shamela.ws/book/9552/321)). Furthermore, **Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn** (d. 110 AH) ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 27](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/26)) and **Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī** (d. 96 AH) ([*Kitāb al-ʿIlal* #5673](https://shamela.ws/book/2331/1526)) attest that systematic inquiry into chains of transmission (*asānīd*) only commenced during the Second Civil War in the era of al-Mukhtār (66–67 AH)—more than 55 years after the Prophet's death.

evidence_items.label: Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān and Imām Muslim on Unintentional Falsehood Flowing on the Tongues of the Righteous
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 40 (`/muslim/introduction/39`)](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/39), **Imām Muslim** records **Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān** (d. 198 AH) stating, *"We have never seen the righteous (al-ṣāliḥīn) [variant: people of goodness (ahl al-khayr)] lie more in anything than they do in Hadith,"* and explains: *"Falsehood (al-kadhib) flows upon their tongues even though they do not intend to lie."* In [*al-Kifāyah* (p. 158, §§547–548)](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/547), **al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī** preserves Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān's related observation: *"I would entrust a man with one hundred thousand [dirhams], yet I would not entrust him with a single hadith."*

primary_references.label: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Muqaddimah 40 (Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān & Imām Muslim on Falsehood Among the Righteous)

evidence_items.label: Shuʿbah's Assessment of the Hadith Corpus and Reliance on Non-Thiqah Narrators
evidence_items.content_markdown: Summarizing his lifelong examination of the Hadith corpus in **al-Dhahabī's** [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* (7/226)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1185/شعبة), **Shuʿbah ibn al-Ḥajjāj** (d. 160 AH) stated: *"I do not know anyone who has investigated Hadith as thoroughly as I have; I have established that three-quarters of it is false (kadhib)."* At the same time, both **Shuʿbah** and **Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān** noted in [*al-Kifāyah* (p. 90, §284)](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/284) and **Ibn Rajab's** [*Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī* (1/376)](https://shamela.ws/book/9552/321) that had they restricted their own transmissions to strictly trustworthy (*thiqah* / *marḍī*) narrators, Shuʿbah *"would not have narrated to you from three [or thirty]"* and Yaḥyā *"would not have narrated from five."*

evidence_items.label: Ibn Sīrīn and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī Dating the First Demand for Isnāds to the Era of al-Mukhtār (66–67 AH)
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 27 (`/muslim/introduction/26`)](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/26), **Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn** (d. 110 AH) attests that transmitters *"used not to inquire about the isnād; but when the Fitnah occurred, they said: 'Name for us your men,'"* accepting reports from *Ahl al-Sunnah* and rejecting those of *Ahl al-Bidaʿ*. In **Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal's** [*Kitāb al-ʿIlal* (3/380, #5673)](https://shamela.ws/book/2331/1526), **Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī** (d. 96 AH) dates this development specifically—*"People only began asking about the isnād during the days of al-Mukhtār"* (66–67 AH / 685–687 AD)—indicating that traditions circulated for more than 55 years after the Prophet's death prior to routine chain verification.

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Traditional commentators note that **Imām Muslim** ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 40](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/39)) contextualized **Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān's** statement as referring to unintentional errors rather than deliberate falsehood (*kadhib*) by pious narrators, and maintain that classical Hadith methodology addressed this issue by requiring retentive precision (*ḍabṭ*) alongside moral probity (*ʿadālah*) when authenticating reports ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 1](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction)).
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: In the primary sources, unintentional errors by pious transmitters ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 40](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/39); [*al-Kifāyah* §§547–548](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/547)) circulated without systematic chain verification during the 55-year pre-*isnād* period (11–67 AH) attested by **Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn** ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 27](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/26)) and **Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī** ([*Kitāb al-ʿIlal* #5673](https://shamela.ws/book/2331/1526)). Furthermore, the early critics who diagnosed the prevalence of error—**Shuʿbah ibn al-Ḥajjāj** ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 7/226](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1185/شعبة)) and **Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān**—explicitly acknowledged in [*al-Kifāyah* (§284)](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/284) and [*Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī* (1/376)](https://shamela.ws/book/9552/321) that had they restricted their own transmissions solely to narrators satisfying strict precision (*thiqah* / *marḍī*), they would not have narrated from more than three to five individuals.

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
#### 1. Inverse Correlation Between Ascetic Piety and Retentive Precision

Formative Hadith critics of the second and third centuries AH repeatedly documented a structural divergence between personal religious devotion (*ṣalāḥ* / *ʿibādah*) and textual accuracy in transmission. In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 40 (`/muslim/introduction/39`)](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/39) ([IslamWeb *Muqaddimah*](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1/38/باب-أن-الإسناد-من-الدين-والرواية-لا-تكون-إلا-عن-الثقات-وجواز-جرح-الرواة-وأنه-ليس-من-الغيبة-المحرمة)), **Imām Muslim** preserves **Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān's** assessment that ascetic and pious figures introduced false attributions into Hadith more frequently than in any other domain, adding the lexical clarification that objective falsehood (*kadhib*) flowed from their tongues without deliberate intent to deceive.

In [*al-Kifāyah fī ʿIlm al-Riwāyah* (p. 158, §547)](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/547) and [§548](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/548), **al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī** pairs Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān's contrast between financial trustworthiness and Hadith unreliability with firsthand Medinan testimonies from **Abū al-Zinād** ([*al-Kifāyah* §549](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/549)) and **Mālik ibn Anas** ([*al-Kifāyah* §552](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/552)), who declined reports from scores of devout worshippers at the pillars of the Prophet's Mosque. Imām Muslim illustrates the concrete mechanics of such errors in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 41 (`/muslim/introduction/40`)](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/40)—where **Khalīfah ibn Mūsā** inspected **Ghālib ibn ʿUbayd Allāh's** written notebook and discovered that traditions Ghālib was dictating as heard from Makḥūl were written as coming from the discarded narrator Abān—and in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 61 (`/muslim/introduction/60`)](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/60), where **Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī** refused to accept the legal testimony of an exceptionally pious neighbor even for two dates.

#### 2. Corpus-Wide Rejection Rates vs. Practical Dependence on Non-*Thiqāt*

The scale of unverified material circulating in the second century AH is reflected in **Shuʿbah ibn al-Ḥajjāj's** (d. 160 AH) audit preserved in [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* (7/226)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1185/شعبة), where he concluded that three-quarters of the traditions he investigated were false. Yet as documented in [*al-Kifāyah* (p. 90, §284)](https://shamela.ws/book/13055/284), **al-Sakhāwī's** [*Fatḥ al-Mughīth* (2/45)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/82/100/التعديل-المبهم), and **Ibn Rajab's** [*Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī* (1/376)](https://shamela.ws/book/9552/321), both **Shuʿbah** and **Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān** conceded that had they restricted their own narration strictly to transmitters meeting full precision (*thiqah* / *marḍī*), their pool of informants would have shrunk to a tiny handful.

#### 3. Chronological Gap Prior to Post-*Fitnah* Chain Inquiry

Compounding these transmission vulnerabilities, the testimonies of **Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn** in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* Introduction 27 (`/muslim/introduction/26`)](https://sunnah.com/muslim:introduction/26) and **Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī** recorded by **Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal** in [*al-ʿIlal* (3/380, #5673)](https://shamela.ws/book/2331/1526) (cf. [*Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī* 1/355](https://shamela.ws/book/9552/302)) establish that systematic demand for *isnāds* only began during the revolt of al-Mukhtār in Kufa (66–67 AH), leaving a half-century window after 11 AH in which traditions circulated without routine chain verification. These statements in Muslim\'s *Muqaddimah* and *Kitāb al-ʿIlal* describe how early critics viewed unintentional error and the history of chain verification.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «لَمْ نَرَ الصَّالِحِينَ فِي شَيْءٍ أَكْذَبَ مِنْهُمْ فِي الْحَدِيثِ» «لَمْ تَرَ أَهْلَ الْخَيْرِ فِي شَيْءٍ أَكْذَبَ مِنْهُمْ فِي الْحَدِيثِ» قَالَ مُسْلِمٌ: «يَقُولُ: يَجْرِي الْكَذِبُ عَلَى لِسَانِهِمْ وَلَا يَتَعَمَّدُونَ الْكَذِبَ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "We have never seen the righteous (al-ṣāliḥīn) lie more in anything than they do in Hadith" [variant wording: "You have never seen the people of goodness (ahl al-khayr) lie more in anything than they do in Hadith"]. Imām Muslim commented: "He means that falsehood (al-kadhib) flows upon their tongues even though they do not intend to lie."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: قَالَ يَحْيَى بْنُ سَعِيدٍ: «مَا رَأَيْتُ الصَّالِحِينَ فِي شَيْءٍ أَشَدَّ فِتْنَةً مِنْهُمْ فِي الْحَدِيثِ» وَقَالَ يَحْيَى بْنُ سَعِيدٍ الْقَطَّانُ: «آتَمِنُ الرَّجُلَ عَلَى مِائَةِ أَلْفٍ، وَلَا أَئْتَمِنُهُ عَلَى حَدِيثٍ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said: "I have never seen the righteous more severely tested (ashadda fitnatan) in anything than they are in Hadith." And Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān said: "I would entrust a man with one hundred thousand [dirhams], yet I would not entrust him with a single hadith."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, al-Kifāyah fī ʿIlm al-Riwāyah, p. 158 (§§547–548).

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: قَالَ خَلِيفَةُ بْنُ مُوسَى: دَخَلْتُ عَلَى غَالِبِ بْنِ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ فَجَعَلَ يُمْلِي عَلَيَّ: «حَدَّثَنِي مَكْحُولٌ، حَدَّثَنِي مَكْحُولٌ»، فَأَخَذَهُ الْبَوْلُ فَقَامَ، فَنَظَرْتُ فِي الْكُرَّاسَةِ فَإِذَا فِيهَا: «حَدَّثَنِي أَبَانُ عَنْ أَنَسٍ، وَأَبَانُ عَنْ فُلَانٍ»، فَتَرَكْتُهُ وَقُمْتُ.
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: Khalīfah ibn Mūsā said: "I entered upon Ghālib ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, and he began dictating to me: 'Makḥūl narrated to me, Makḥūl narrated to me.' Then the call of nature overtook him and he stood up [to leave]. I looked into his notebook (al-kurrāsah), and saw written in it: 'Abān narrated to me from Anas, and Abān from so-and-so.' So I left him and departed."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: عَنْ أَيُّوبَ قَالَ: «إِنَّ لِي جَارًا — ثُمَّ ذَكَرَ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ — وَلَوْ شَهِدَ عِنْدِي عَلَى تَمْرَتَيْنِ مَا رَأَيْتُ شَهَادَتَهُ جَائِزَةً»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: From Ayyūb [al-Sakhtiyānī], who said: "I have a neighbor"—and he went on to praise his great virtue and piety—"yet if he were to testify before me regarding two dates (tamratayn), I would not consider his testimony permissible."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: قَالَ الْأَصْمَعِيُّ: سَمِعْتُ شُعْبَةَ يَقُولُ: «مَا أَعْلَمُ أَحَدًا فَتَّشَ الْحَدِيثَ كَتَفْتِيشِي، وَقَفْتُ عَلَى أَنَّ ثَلَاثَةَ أَرْبَاعِهِ كَذِبٌ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: Al-Aṣmaʿī said: I heard Shuʿbah say: "I do not know anyone who has investigated Hadith as thoroughly as I have; I have established that three-quarters of it is false (kadhib)."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 7/226; Abū Nuʿaym al-Iṣfahānī, Ḥilyat al-Awliyāʾ 7/149.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: سَمِعْتُ عَاصِمَ بْنَ عَلِيٍّ يَقُولُ: سَمِعْتُ شُعْبَةَ يَقُولُ: «لَوْ لَمْ أُحَدِّثْكُمْ إِلَّا عَنْ ثِقَةٍ لَمْ أُحَدِّثْكُمْ عَنْ ثَلَاثِينَ» [وَفِي رِوَايَةِ السَّخَاوِيِّ: «عَنْ ثَلَاثَةٍ»]
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAlī said: I heard Shuʿbah say: "Had I only narrated to you from a trustworthy transmitter (thiqah), I would not have narrated to you from thirty [in al-Sakhāwī's reading: from three; in Ibn Rajab's wording: except from a tiny handful (nafar yasīr)]."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, al-Kifāyah fī ʿIlm al-Riwāyah, p. 90 (§284, https://shamela.ws/book/13055/284); al-Sakhāwī, Fatḥ al-Mughīth 2/45 (https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/82/100/التعديل-المبهم); Ibn Rajab, Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī 1/376 (https://shamela.ws/book/9552/321).

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: قَالَ يَحْيَى الْقَطَّانُ: «إِنْ لَمْ أَرْوِ إِلَّا عَمَّنْ أَرْضَى مَا رَوَيْتُ عَنْ خَمْسَةٍ، أَوْ نَحْوِ ذَلِكَ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān said: "If I only narrated from those with whom I am satisfied, I would not have narrated from five, or thereabouts."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Ibn Rajab al-Ḥanbalī, Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī 1/376.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: عَنْ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ سِيرِينَ قَالَ: «لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَسْأَلُونَ عَنِ الْإِسْنَادِ، فَلَمَّا وَقَعَتِ الْفِتْنَةُ قَالُوا: سَمُّوا لَنَا رِجَالَكُمْ، فَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ فَيُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ، وَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ فَلَا يُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn said: "They used not to inquire about the isnād; but when the Fitnah (civil strife) occurred, they said: 'Name for us your men.' Thus, those who belonged to Ahl al-Sunnah would be looked at and their hadith accepted, while those who belonged to Ahl al-Bidaʿ (sectarian innovators) would be looked at and their hadith rejected."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: حَدَّثَنِي أَبِي قَالَ: حَدَّثَنَا جَابِرُ بْنُ نُوحٍ قَالَ: أَخْبَرَنَا الْأَعْمَشُ عَنْ إِبْرَاهِيمَ قَالَ: «إِنَّمَا سُئِلَ عَنِ الْإِسْنَادِ أَيَّامَ الْمُخْتَارِ»

subpoints.short_title: 3 Classical Statements on Keeping Disputed Narrators and Single Chains
subpoints.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see al-Dhahabī on retaining disputed narrators to preserve the corpus, Ibn Ḥibbān on chains lacking two witnesses at every link, and Judge ʿUmar ibn Ḥabīb on exempting Companions from review.
subpoints.takeaway: Al-Dhahabī and Ibn Ḥibbān gave practical reasons for retaining disputed narrators and single-witness chains.
subpoints.title: Pragmatic Retention of Disputed Narrators & Solitary Reports (Āḥād)

items.arabic: فلو رد حديث هؤلاء لذهب جملة من الآثار النبوية وهذه مفسدة بينة
items.english: If the hadiths of these individuals were rejected, a vast body of Prophetic traditions would be lost, and this would be an evident detriment.

items.arabic: فَأَمَّا الْأَخْبَارُ فَإِنَّهَا كُلُّهَا أَخْبَارُ آحَادٍ
items.english: As for Prophetic reports, they are all solitary reports (akhbār āḥād); whoever refrains from accepting solitary reports has resolved to abandon the Sunnah in its entirety.

items.arabic: لَوْ كَانَ أَصْحَابُهُ كَذَّابِينَ فَبَاطِلَةٌ الشَّرِيعَةُ
items.english: If his Companions were untruthful, then the Sharīʿah would be invalidated.

subpoints.summary_markdown: Classical Sunni authorities documented that strict biographical exclusion and multi-witness corroboration were moderated out of practical necessity so that the legal corpus of the Sunnah and Sharīʿah would be preserved. Consequently, canonical compilers retained disputed and sectarian narrators such as ʿIkrimah ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3017](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3017)) and ʿAbbād ibn Yaʿqūb ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7534](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7534)) as noted by **al-Dhahabī** in [*Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl* (1/5–6)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/11055/من-تقبل-روايته-للحديث-ومن-لا-تقبل), exempted the entire Companion generation from critical vetting lest the legal rulings of the Sharīʿah be invalidated as articulated by Judge **ʿUmar ibn Ḥabīb** in [*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* (21/294–295)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/5269/عمر-بن-حبيب-العدوي-القاضي), and grounded jurisprudence on solitary (*āḥād*) chains that **Ibn Ḥibbān** in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān* (1/145–146)](https://shamela.ws/book/9247/110) acknowledged do not meet the two-witness-per-tier standard analogous to [Qurʾān 2:282](https://quran.com/2/282).

evidence_items.label: Al-Dhahabī on Retaining Sectarian and Disputed Narrators (ʿIkrimah and ʿAbbād ibn Yaʿqūb) to Preserve the Prophetic Corpus
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl* (1/5–6)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/11055/من-تقبل-روايته-للحديث-ومن-لا-تقبل), **al-Dhahabī** explains that **al-Bukhārī** and **Muslim** transmitted from numerous sectarian innovators because ***"if the hadiths of these individuals were rejected, a vast body of Prophetic traditions would be lost."* ** Accordingly, **al-Bukhārī** relies approximately 139 times on the Khārijite-linked transmitter **ʿIkrimah**—including the foundational solitary report for capital punishment in apostasy cases ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3017](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3017), [6922](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6922))—even though classical biographical dictionaries record that Ibn ʿAbbās's son ʿAlī bound him for *"attributing falsehoods to my father,"* that Ibn ʿUmar, Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, and Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī impugned his veracity, and that **Imām Mālik** declined to accept his transmissions ([*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 20/279–280](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/5058/عكرمة-البربري-مولى-ابن-عباس); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 5/20–24](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/707/عكرمة)). Similarly, [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7534](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7534) transmits directly from the Shīʿī narrator **ʿAbbād ibn Yaʿqūb al-Rawājinī**, who was documented as reviling ʿUthmān and was characterized as *"suspect in his religious views"* by Ibn Khuzaymah ([*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 14/175–179](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/3364/عباد-بن-يعقوب-الأسدي-الرواجني-الكوفي); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 11/536–538](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/2116/الرواجني)).

evidence_items.label: Ibn Ḥibbān and Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ on the Absence of Two-Witness-Per-Tier Chains and the Scarcity of Verbatim Tawātur
evidence_items.content_markdown: Addressing jurists who stipulated two upright witnesses at every generational link (`عَدْلَيْنِ عَنْ عَدْلَيْنِ`) by analogy with the two witnesses required for recording a financial debt in [Qurʾān 2:282](https://quran.com/2/282), **Ibn Ḥibbān** (d. 354 AH) explained in his introduction to [*Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān* (1/145–146)](https://shamela.ws/book/9247/110) why requiring every narrator in every tier to have two witnesses is impossible, observing that **no hadith in the Prophetic corpus** satisfies that condition since *"all Prophetic reports are solitary reports (akhbār āḥād)"* and requiring two witnesses per tier would entail *"abandoning the Sunnah in its entirety."* Similarly, **Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ** (d. 643 AH) noted in his [*Muqaddimah* (pp. 16–17)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/90/5/ابن-الصلاح-يمنع-المتأخرين-من-تصحيح-الأحاديث) the Category 1 definition of *ṣaḥīḥ* chains and why later scholars rely on canonical compilations, while in [*Muqaddimah* (pp. 268–269)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/90/137/) and al-Suyūṭī's [*Tadrīb al-Rāwī* (2/628–632)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/88/498/) he notes that searching for verbatim *mutawātir* hadiths exhausts the researcher (*aʿyāhu taṭallubuhu*).

evidence_items.label: Methodological Exemption of the Companion Generation (ʿAdālat al-Ṣaḥābah) to Preserve the Legal Framework of the Sharīʿah
evidence_items.content_markdown: Although [Qurʾān 9:101](https://quran.com/9/101) attests that unrecognized hypocrites resided among the inhabitants of Medina (`مَرَدُوا عَلَى النِّفَاقِ لَا تَعْلَمُهُمْ`), classical Sunni hadith methodology exempted the entire Companion generation from individual biographical criticism (*kulluhum ʿudūl*). When scholars at the court of Caliph Hārūn al-Rashīd questioned solitary reports transmitted via Abū Hurayrah, Judge **ʿUmar ibn Ḥabīb** articulated the foundational rationale for this collective exemption (**al-Dhahabī**, who summarizes Hārūn's anger in [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 9/491](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1626/عمر-بن-حبيب), and **al-Mizzī**, who preserves the full dialogue in [*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 21/294–295](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/5269/عمر-بن-حبيب-العدوي-القاضي)): ***"If his Companions were impugned as untruthful, then the entire Sharīʿah would be invalidated (fa-l-sharīʿatu bāṭilah), and the religious obligations and legal rulings regarding prayer, fasting, divorce, marriage, and penal laws would all be rejected."***

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical and modern Sunni methodologists maintain that heterodox narrators such as ʿIkrimah and ʿAbbād ibn Yaʿqūb were retained only when their personal honesty and memory were independently verified (**al-Dhahabī**, [*Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl* 1/5–6](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/11055/من-تقبل-روايته-للحديث-ومن-لا-تقبل)), noting that Khārijite doctrine strictly prohibited lying (**al-Mizzī**, [*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 20/279–280](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/5058/عكرمة-البربري-مولى-ابن-عباس)) and that later scholars identified numerous *mutawātir* traditions beyond the restrictive threshold described by [*Tadrīb al-Rāwī*](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/88/498/).
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: In the primary biographical sources, however, the criticisms of **ʿIkrimah** specifically concerned his reliability in hadith transmission rather than merely his theological views: Ibn ʿAbbās's son ʿAlī physically restrained him for *"attributing falsehoods to my father,"* while Ibn ʿUmar, Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī, and **Imām Mālik** impugned his veracity and declined his reports ([*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 20/279–280](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/5058/عكرمة-البربري-مولى-ابن-عباس); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 5/20–24](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/707/عكرمة)). Likewise, **Ibn Ḥibbān** criticized **ʿAbbād ibn Yaʿqūb** for transmitting anomalous and rejected (*munkar*) reports from famous authorities ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 11/537](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/2116/الرواجني); [*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 14/175–179](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/3364/عباد-بن-يعقوب-الأسدي-الرواجني-الكوفي)). Furthermore, **Ibn Ḥibbān's** introduction in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān* (1/145–146)](https://shamela.ws/book/9247/110) explains why requiring two witnesses is impossible, addressing the earliest tiers of transmission: because canonical chains pass through single-strand Companion and Successor links, no hadith in the corpus possesses two independent witnesses at every generational tier analogous to [Qurʾān 2:282](https://quran.com/2/282), and **al-Dhahabī** explicitly grounded the retention of disputed innovators in the practical necessity of preserving the Prophetic corpus ([*Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl* 1/5–6](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/11055/من-تقبل-روايته-للحديث-ومن-لا-تقبل)).

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
#### 1. Al-Dhahabī on Retaining Disputed Narrators (*Mubtadiʿah*)

While theoretical treatises on *uṣūl al-ḥadīth* define narrator acceptability through strict adherence to Sunni orthodoxy and impeccable retention, classical prosopographers documented that enforcing those standards without exception would have excluded many reports relied upon in canonical collections. In [*Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl* (1/5–6)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/11055/من-تقبل-روايته-للحديث-ومن-لا-تقبل), **Shams al-Dīn al-Dhahabī** (d. 748 AH) observed that because sectarian commitments were widespread among Kufan and Basran Successors, rejecting their transmissions would have caused the loss of a vast portion of Prophetic reports.

This pragmatic accommodation operated across opposite poles of early sectarian conflict inside *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī*. In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7534](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7534), al-Bukhārī narrates directly from the Kufan Shīʿī teacher **ʿAbbād ibn Yaʿqūb al-Rawājinī** (d. 250 AH), despite biographical records in [*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* (14/175–179)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/3364/عباد-بن-يعقوب-الأسدي-الرواجني-الكوفي) and [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* (11/536–538)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/2116/الرواجني) documenting his denigration of ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥah, and al-Zubayr and **Ibn Ḥibbān's** charge that he narrated rejected traditions (*manākīr*). Conversely, al-Bukhārī cites the Khārijite-aligned transmitter **ʿIkrimah** (d. 105 AH) in roughly 139 places—including the primary solitary chain for capital punishment in apostasy at [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3017](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3017) and [6922](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6922)—notwithstanding eyewitness reports in [*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* (20/279–280)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/5058/عكرمة-البربري-مولى-ابن-عباس) and [*Siyar* (5/20–24)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/707/عكرمة) recording **ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās**, **Ibn ʿUmar**, **Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī**, and **Imām Mālik** impugning his attributions.

#### 2. Collective Companion Probity and Judge ʿUmar ibn Ḥabīb's Statement

A second institutional accommodation exempted the entire first generation (*al-Ṣaḥābah*) from biographical criticism. Primary sources preserve three lines of counter-evidence: [Qurʾān 9:101](https://quran.com/9/101) attests to unidentifiable hypocrites among the Medinan population; senior Companions challenged solitary reports of peers in **Ibn Qutaybah's** [*Taʾwīl Mukhtalif al-Ḥadīth* (1/72–73)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/83/4/); and aged Companions such as **Zayd ibn Arqam** acknowledged memory loss in [*Sunan Ibn Mājah* 25](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:25), paralleling **Ibn Ḥibbān's** category of late-life senility (*ikhtilāṭ*). As recorded in [*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* (21/294–295)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/5269/عمر-بن-حبيب-العدوي-القاضي) and [*Siyar* (9/491)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1626/عمر-بن-حبيب), Judge **ʿUmar ibn Ḥabīb** defended collective Companion immunity before Caliph Hārūn al-Rashīd not on empirical grounds, but because questioning Companion transmitters would nullify the legal rulings of the Sharīʿah.

#### 3. Structural Absence of Multi-Witness Chains

Finally, when Muʿtazilite jurists demanded two upright witnesses at every generational link by analogy with debt contracts in [Qurʾān 2:282](https://quran.com/2/282), **Ibn Ḥibbān** explained in his introduction ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān* 1/145–146](https://shamela.ws/book/9247/110)) the impossibility of demanding dual corroborating witnesses at every generational link, conceding that no Prophetic tradition satisfies a strict two-witness threshold. Alongside this, **Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ** documented in his [*Muqaddimah* (pp. 16–17)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/90/5/ابن-الصلاح-يمنع-المتأخرين-من-تصحيح-الأحاديث) why later scholars rely on canonical collections, while [*Tadrīb al-Rāwī*](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/88/498/) records the scarcity of verbatim *mutawātir* traditions. Classical theorists thus recognized that strict evidentiary thresholds had to be relaxed in practice to preserve the transmitted legal and doctrinal corpus.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «فَلِقَائِلٍ أَنْ يَقُولَ: كَيْفَ سَاغَ تَوْثِيقُ مُبْتَدِعٍ وَحَدُّ الثِّقَةِ الْعَدَالَةُ وَالْإِتْقَانُ؟ فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ عَدْلًا مَنْ هُوَ صَاحِبُ بِدْعَةٍ؟ وَجَوَابُهُ أَنَّ الْبِدْعَةَ عَلَى ضَرْبَيْنِ: فَبِدْعَةٌ صُغْرَى كَغُلُوِّ التَّشَيُّعِ، أَوْ كَالتَّشَيُّعِ بِلَا غُلُوٍّ وَلَا تَحَرُّقٍ، فَهَذَا كَثِيرٌ فِي التَّابِعِينَ وَتَابِعِيهِمْ مَعَ الدِّينِ وَالْوَرَعِ وَالصِّدْقِ، فَلَوْ رُدَّ حَدِيثُ هَؤُلَاءِ لَذَهَبَ جُمْلَةٌ مِنَ الْآثَارِ النَّبَوِيَّةِ، وَهَذِهِ مَفْسَدَةٌ بَيِّنَةٌ... فَقَدِ احْتَجَّ الْبُخَارِيُّ وَمُسْلِمٌ بِجَمَاعَةٍ كَثِيرَةٍ مِنَ الْمُبْتَدِعَةِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Someone might ask: 'How is it permissible to declare an innovator (mubtadiʿ) trustworthy when the definition of trustworthiness (thiqah) is religious rectitude (ʿadālah) and precision (itqān)? How can a proponent of heresy be considered upright?' The answer is that innovation is of two types: first, minor innovation, such as extreme Shi'ism (ghulūw al-tashayyuʿ), or Shi'ism without extremism or rancor; this was widespread among the Successors (Tābiʿūn) and their successors alongside religiosity, piety, and truthfulness. If the hadiths of these individuals were rejected, a vast body of Prophetic traditions would be lost, and that would be a manifest harm (mafsadah bayyinah)... Indeed, al-Bukhārī and Muslim relied as authoritative proof (iḥtajja) upon a large group of innovators."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Shams al-Dīn al-Dhahabī, Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl fī Naqd al-Rijāl 1/5–6.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «حَدَّثَنَا الثِّقَةُ فِي رِوَايَتِهِ، الْمُتَّهَمُ فِي دِينِهِ، عَبَّادُ بْنُ يَعْقُوبَ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "The one trustworthy in his narration, yet suspect in his religion, ʿAbbād ibn Yaʿqūb, narrated to us."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Ibn Khuzaymah, in al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl 14/175–179 and al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 11/536–538.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «دَخَلْتُ عَلَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، وَعِكْرِمَةُ مُقَيَّدٌ عَلَى بَابِ الْحَشِّ، قَالَ: قُلْتُ: مَا لِهَذَا كَذَا؟ قَالَ: إِنَّهُ يَكْذِبُ عَلَى أَبِي»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "I entered upon ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās while ʿIkrimah was tied up at the door of the latrine. I asked: 'Why is this man being treated like this?' He replied: 'Because he lies against my father.'"
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl 20/279; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 5/20–24.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «سَمِعْتُ يَحْيَى بْنَ مَعِينٍ يَقُولُ: إِنَّمَا لَمْ يَذْكُرْ مَالِكُ بْنُ أَنَسٍ عِكْرِمَةَ، لِأَنَّ عِكْرِمَةَ كَانَ يَنْتَحِلُ رَأْيَ الصُّفْرِيَّةِ. وَقَالَ الرَّبِيعُ بْنُ سُلَيْمَانَ، عَنِ الشَّافِعِيِّ: وَهُوَ ـ يَعْنِي مَالِكَ بْنَ أَنَسٍ ـ سَيِّئُ الرَّأْيِ فِي عِكْرِمَةَ، قَالَ: لَا أَرَى لِأَحَدٍ أَنْ يَقْبَلَ حَدِيثَهُ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "I heard Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn say: 'Mālik ibn Anas refrained from citing ʿIkrimah only because ʿIkrimah adhered to the doctrine of the Ṣufriyyah [Khārijites].' And al-Rabīʿ ibn Sulaymān reported from al-Shāfiʿī: 'He—meaning Mālik ibn Anas—held a low opinion of ʿIkrimah, and said: I do not consider it permissible for anyone to accept his hadith.'"

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «كَبِرْنَا وَنَسِينَا، وَحَدِيثُ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ شَدِيدٌ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "We have grown old and forgotten, and narrating from the Messenger of God ﷺ is a weighty [or severe] matter."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Zayd ibn Arqam, in Sunan Ibn Mājah 25; Ibn Ḥibbān, Kitāb al-Majrūḥīn 1/39.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «وَمِنْهُمْ جَمَاعَةٌ مِنَ الثِّقَاتِ اخْتَلَطُوا فِي آخِرِ أَعْمَارِهِمْ حَتَّى اخْتَلَطَ صَحِيحُ حَدِيثِهِمْ بِسَقِيمِهِ فَلَمْ يَتَمَيَّزْ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "And among them is a group of trustworthy narrators (al-thiqāt) whose memories deteriorated in the final years of their lives, until their sound hadiths became mixed with their unsound ones and could no longer be distinguished."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Ibn Ḥibbān, Kitāb al-Majrūḥīn min al-Muḥaddithīn 1/64.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «قُلْتُ: يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ، إِنَّ الَّذِي قُلْتَهُ وَجَادَلْتَ عَلَيْهِ فِيهِ إِزْرَاءٌ عَلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ وَعَلَى مَا جَاءَ بِهِ، إِذَا كَانَ أَصْحَابُهُ كَذَّابِينَ فَالشَّرِيعَةُ بَاطِلَةٌ، وَالْفَرَائِضُ وَالْأَحْكَامُ فِي الصَّلَاةِ وَالصِّيَامِ وَالطَّلَاقِ وَالنِّكَاحِ وَالْحُدُودِ كُلُّهُ مَرْدُودٌ غَيْرُ مَقْبُولٍ. فَرَجَعَ إِلَى نَفْسِهِ، ثُمَّ قَالَ لِي: أَحْيَيْتَنِي يَا عُمَرُ بْنُ حَبِيبٍ أَحْيَاكَ اللَّهُ... ثُمَّ أَمَرَ لِي بِعَشَرَةِ آلَافِ دِرْهَمٍ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "I said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, that which you have stated and argued for constitutes a disparagement of the Messenger of God ﷺ and of what he brought: if his Companions were liars, then the entire Sharīʿah would be nullified (fa-l-sharīʿatu bāṭilah), and the religious obligations and legal rulings regarding prayer, fasting, divorce, marriage, and penal laws (ḥudūd) would all be rejected and unacceptable.' So [al-Rashīd] came to his senses and said to me: 'You have restored me to life, O ʿUmar ibn Ḥabīb, may God give you life!' ... and he ordered ten thousand dirhams for me."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: ʿUmar ibn Ḥabīb al-ʿAdawī, in al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl 21/294–295; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 9/491.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «وَمَنْ سُئِلَ عَنْ إِبْرَازِ مِثَالٍ لِذَلِكَ فِيمَا يُرْوَى مِنَ الْحَدِيثِ أَعْيَاهُ تَطَلُّبُهُ، وَحَدِيثُ: (إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ) لَيْسَ مِنْهُ بِنَحْوٍ مِمَّا ذَكَرْنَاهُ، نَعَمْ حَدِيثُ: (مَنْ كَذَبَ عَلَيَّ مُتَعَمِّدًا فَلْيَتَبَوَّأْ مَقْعَدَهُ مِنَ النَّارِ) نَرَاهُ مِثَالًا لِذَلِكَ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Whoever is asked to produce an example of that [verbatim mutawātir] among what is narrated of hadith will be exhausted by the search for it. Even the hadith 'Actions are only by intentions' does not belong to it, as we have mentioned. Yes, the hadith 'Whoever lies about me intentionally, let him take his seat in the Fire' we regard as an example of that."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddimah Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth, Type 30, pp. 268–269 (https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/90/137/); al-Suyūṭī, Tadrīb al-Rāwī 2/628–632 (https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/88/498/).

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «فَأَمَّا الْأَخْبَارُ فَإِنَّهَا كُلُّهَا أَخْبَارُ آحَادٍ؛ لِأَنَّهُ لَيْسَ يُوجَدُ عَنِ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ خَبَرٌ مِنْ رِوَايَةِ عَدْلَيْنِ، رَوَى أَحَدُهُمَا عَنْ عَدْلَيْنِ، وَكُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمَا عَنْ عَدْلَيْنِ، حَتَّى يَنْتَهِيَ ذَلِكَ إِلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ، فَلَمَّا اسْتَحَالَ هَذَا وَبَطَلَ، ثَبَتَ أَنَّ الْأَخْبَارَ كُلُّهَا أَخْبَارُ الْآحَادِ، وَأَنَّ مَنْ تَنَكَّبَ عَنْ قَبُولِ أَخْبَارِ الْآحَادِ فَقَدْ عَمَدَ إِلَى تَرْكِ السُّنَنِ كُلِّهَا، لِعَدَمِ وُجُودِ السُّنَنِ إِلَّا مِنْ رِوَايَةِ الْآحَادِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "As for Prophetic reports, they are all solitary reports (akhbār āḥād); because there does not exist from the Prophet ﷺ a single report narrated by two upright witnesses, each of whom narrated from two upright witnesses, and each of those from two upright witnesses, until it reaches the Messenger of God ﷺ. Since this is impossible and non-existent, it is established that all reports are solitary reports, and that whoever refrains from accepting solitary reports has effectively resolved to abandon the Sunnah in its entirety (tark al-sunan kullihā), due to the non-existence of the Sunnah except through solitary transmission."

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «فَقَدْ تَعَذَّرَ فِي هَذِهِ الْأَعْصَارِ الِاسْتِقْلَالُ بِإِدْرَاكِ الصَّحِيحِ بِمُجَرَّدِ اعْتِبَارِ الْأَسَانِيدِ، لِأَنَّهُ مَا مِنْ إِسْنَادٍ مِنْ ذَلِكَ إِلَّا وَنَجِدُ فِي رِجَالِهِ مَنِ اعْتَمَدَ فِي رِوَايَتِهِ عَلَى مَا فِي كِتَابِهِ عَرِيًّا عَمَّا يُشْتَرَطُ فِي الصَّحِيحِ مِنَ الْحِفْظِ وَالضَّبْطِ وَالْإِتْقَانِ، فَآلَ الْأَمْرُ إِذًا فِي مَعْرِفَةِ الصَّحِيحِ وَالْحَسَنِ إِلَى الِاعْتِمَادِ عَلَى مَا نَصَّ عَلَيْهِ أَئِمَّةُ الْحَدِيثِ فِي تَصَانِيفِهِمُ الْمُعْتَمَدَةِ الْمَشْهُورَةِ... وَصَارَ مُعْظَمُ الْمَقْصُودِ بِمَا يُتَدَاوَلُ مِنَ الْأَسَانِيدِ خَارِجًا عَنْ ذَلِكَ إِبْقَاءَ سِلْسِلَةِ الْإِسْنَادِ الَّتِي خُصَّتْ بِهَا هَذِهِ الْأُمَّةُ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "In these eras, it has become impossible to independently determine the authentic (al-ṣaḥīḥ) merely by examining chains of transmission (bi-mujarrad iʿtibār al-asānīd); for there is not a single chain among them except that we find among its transmitters someone who relied in his narration upon what was in his written book, devoid of what is required for the Ṣaḥīḥ regarding memorization (ḥifẓ), precision (ḍabṭ), and mastery (itqān). Consequently, the matter of knowing the Ṣaḥīḥ and the Ḥasan has been reduced to relying upon what the Imāms of hadith stipulated in their well-known, authoritative compilations... and the primary purpose of the chains circulated outside of that has become merely the ceremonial preservation of the chain of transmission (ibqāʾ silsilat al-isnād) with which this community was uniquely distinguished."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddimah Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth, Type 1, pp. 16–17.
