evidence_items.label: ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd (d. 127 AH), Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh / Shuʿbah (d. 193 AH), and al-Bazzī (d. 250 AH): Memory Critiques, 500+ Intra-School Variants, and Chain Connecting
evidence_items.content_markdown: **ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd** (d. 127 AH) was assessed by **Ibn Saʿd** as *"making frequent errors in his hadith (kathīr al-khaṭaʾ fī ḥadīthihi),"* by **Ibn ʿUlayyah** and **al-ʿUqaylī** as having *"poor memory (sayyiʾ al-ḥifẓ),"* and by **al-Nasāʾī** as *"not a memorizer"* ([*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 13/476–478](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/3252/); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 5/256–261](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/825/)). Meanwhile, ʿĀṣim's second canonical transmitter, **Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh (Shuʿbah)** (d. 193 AH), was graded by **Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal** as *"trustworthy, perhaps he erred (thiqah, rubbamā ghaliṭa)... Abū Bakr makes very many errors (kathīr al-ghalaṭ jiddan),"* noted for frequent errors by **Abū Nuʿaym**, recounted learning ʿĀṣim's reading with difficulty five verses at a time (`تَعَلَّمْتُ مِنْ عَاصِمٍ الْقُرْآنَ كَمَا يَتَعَلَّمُ الصَّبِيُّ مِنَ الْمُعَلِّمِ، فَلَقِيَ مِنِّي شِدَّةً، فَمَا أُحْسِنُ غَيْرَ قِرَاءَتِهِ`), and differed from his fellow transmitter **Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān** in **over 500 letters** of ʿĀṣim's reading ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 8/496–502](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1431/); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 5/259–260](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/825/)). Likewise, **Ibn Kathīr's** primary Meccan transmitter **al-Bazzī** (d. 250 AH) was graded by **Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī** as *"weak (ḍaʿīf)"* and by **al-ʿUqaylī** as *"munkar al-ḥadīth (transmitting uncorroborated reports); he connects [interrupted] hadiths (yūṣilu al-aḥādīth)"* ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 12/51](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/2138/)).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «قَرَأَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ الْقُرْآنَ، وَجَوَّدَهُ ثَلَاثَ مَرَّاتٍ عَلَى عَاصِمِ بْنِ أَبِي النَّجُودِ» — "Abū Bakr [ibn ʿAyyāsh / Shuʿbah] recited the Qurʾān and perfected it three times under ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd." ([Al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 8/495](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1431/))

primary_references.label: Al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl 13/476–478 (no. 3002, ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd)
Al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 5/256–261 (ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd)

evidence_items.label: Qālūn (ʿĪsā ibn Mīnā, d. 220 AH — Canonical Rāwī of Nāfiʿ): Profound Hearing Loss and Auditing Oral Recitation Visually
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Maʿrifat al-Qurrāʾ al-Kibār* (1/93)](https://shamela.ws/book/8349/88) and [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* (10/327)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1754/), **ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan al-Hisinjānī** reported that **Nāfiʿ's** canonical Medinan transmitter **Qālūn** (d. 220 AH) *"was profoundly deaf (shadīd al-ṣamam); even if you raised your voice to the utmost limit he would not hear, so he would look at the lips of the reciter and correct his solecisms and errors,"* while **al-Dāraquṭnī** deemed Qālūn subject to error (*fa-wahhamahu*) in Hadith transmission (`قالون الأصم نافع قيل له: يعتبر بحديثه؟ فوهّمه`) and the edition's footnote (citing *Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl* 3/327 and *Lisān al-Mīzān* 4/407) records **Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ's** dismissal of writing his hadith ([*Suʾālāt al-Barqānī li-l-Dāraquṭnī* p. 72, no. 43 & n. 4](https://shamela.ws/book/1060/69)). Because key Arabic phonetic features in *tajwīd*—such as pharyngealization (*tafkhīm*), glottal stops (*hamzah*), and nasalization (*ghunnah*)—are articulated in the throat and nasal cavity rather than on the lips, auditing oral recitation visually presents a notable phonetic constraint ([*Maʿrifat al-Qurrāʾ al-Kibār* 1/93](https://shamela.ws/book/8349/88); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 10/327](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1754/)).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «كان قالون شديد الصمم فلو رفعت صوتك لا إلى غاية لا يسمع فكان ينظر إلى شفتي القارئ فيرد عليه اللحن والخطأ» — "Qālūn was profoundly deaf; he would look at the reciter's lips to correct his errors." ([Maʿrifat al-Qurrāʾ al-Kibār 1/93](https://shamela.ws/book/8349/88))

primary_references.label: Al-Dāraquṭnī, Suʾālāt al-Barqānī p. 72 (no. 43 & n. 4 citing Mīzān 3/327 and Lisān 4/407, Qālūn)

key_arabic_quote_structured.arabic: كان قالون شديد الصمم فلو رفعت صوتك لا إلى غاية لا يسمع فكان ينظر إلى شفتي القارئ فيرد عليه اللحن والخطأ
key_arabic_quote_structured.english: Qālūn was profoundly deaf; he would look at the reciter's lips to correct his errors.

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Traditional scholars harmonize these accounts by citing **Abū ʿAlī al-Muqriʾ's** statement that people transmitted from **Hishām ibn ʿAmmār** early (`fa-akhadha al-nās ʿanhu qadīman`) and that **al-Bukhārī** relied on his sound narrations ([*Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb* 11/54](https://shamela.ws/book/3310/4837); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 11/424–425](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/2059/)), and by explaining that **Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān** and **Shuʿbah** differed in over 500 letters only because **ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd** transmitted the reading of **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib** (via Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī) to Ḥafṣ while transmitting the reading of **ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd** (via Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh) to Shuʿbah ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 5/259–260](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/825/)).
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: In the primary biographical record, however, **Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī** explicitly rejected Abū ʿAlī al-Muqriʾ's harmonization regarding Hishām ibn ʿAmmār, writing: *"This Abū ʿAlī is al-Awzāʿī [al-Aṣbahānī], who is not trustworthy in transmission (laysa bi-thiqah fī al-naql); I had intended to discard his statement, then I cited it and clarified his status"* ([*Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb* 11/54](https://shamela.ws/book/3310/4837)), while **Abū Dāwūd** documented Hishām's own admission when accepting prompted reports (`قد روي فلا أبالي من حمل الخطأ` — [*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 30/248–249](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/7879/)). Furthermore, the report stating that ʿĀṣim intentionally taught Ḥafṣ the reading of ʿAlī and Shuʿbah the reading of Ibn Masʿūd is narrated solely by **Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān** himself ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 5/259–260](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/825/)), rendering the harmonization dependent on the uncorroborated testimony of the very transmitter whose precision and reliability are under examination ([*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 7/10–16](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/1479/); [*Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb* 2/400–402](https://shamela.ws/book/3310/915)).

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
#### 1. Sensory and Cognitive Vulnerabilities Among Canonical *Ruwāt*

Biographical dictionaries by al-Mizzī, al-Dhahabī, and Ibn Ḥajar show that *ʿilm al-rijāl* critiques recur across multiple canonical Qurʾānic transmitters (*ruwāt*). In the case of Nāfiʿ's Medinan transmitter **Qālūn** (ʿĪsā ibn Mīnā, d. 220 AH), **al-Dhahabī** ([*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 10/327](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1754/قالون); [*Maʿrifat al-Qurrāʾ al-Kibār* 1/93](https://shamela.ws/book/8349/88)) preserves contemporary testimonies that Qālūn could not hear a trumpet blast and corrected students' recitation by watching their lip movements, while **al-Dāraquṭnī** ([*Suʾālāt al-Barqānī* p. 72, no. 43 & n. 4](https://shamela.ws/book/1060/69)) judged him subject to error in Hadith (*fa-wahhamahu*) and footnote 4 quotes **Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ** laughing at transcribing his narrations. Non-labial phonetic distinctions central to *tajwīd*—including velarization, glottal stops, pharyngeal constriction, and nasal duration—occur inside the vocal tract and nasal cavity where visual observation of the lips does not distinguish the articulation.

In Damascus, Ibn ʿĀmir's canonical transmitter **Hishām ibn ʿAmmār** (d. 245 AH)—whose narrations also appear in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī*—is documented in [*Siyar* (11/424–425)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/2059/هشام-بن-عمار), [*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* (30/248–250)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/7879/هشام-بن-عمار-أبو-الوليد-الدمشقي), and [*Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb* (11/53–54)](https://shamela.ws/book/3310/4836) as charging monetary fees per sheet of Hadith and undergoing late-life cognitive decline (*taghayyur*), during which he uncritically repeated over four hundred baseless traditions fed to him (*talqīn*) by Faḍlak al-Rāzī.

#### 2. Intra-School Divergence in Kufa and Chain Modification in Mecca

In Kufa, the Eponymous Reader **ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd** (d. 127 AH) was criticized for frequent Hadith errors, inconsistency (*iḍṭirāb*), and weak memory by **Ibn Saʿd**, **Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān**, **Ibn ʿUlayyah**, **al-ʿUqaylī**, and **al-Nasāʾī** ([*Tahdhīb al-Kamāl* 13/476–478](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/3252/عاصم-بن-بهدلة-وهو-ابن-أبي-النجود); [*Siyar* 5/256–261](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/825/عاصم-بن-أبي-النجود)). Furthermore, ʿĀṣim's two canonical transmitters—**Ḥafṣ** and **Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh (Shuʿbah)** (d. 193 AH)—diverged from one another in more than five hundred letters ([*Siyar* 8/496–502](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/1431/أبو-بكر-بن-عياش)), a discrepancy harmonized solely through an uncorroborated report narrated by Ḥafṣ himself claiming that ʿĀṣim taught him the reading of ʿAlī while teaching Shuʿbah the reading of Ibn Masʿūd. Similarly, in Mecca, Ibn Kathīr's primary transmitter **al-Bazzī** (d. 250 AH) was rejected by **Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī** and **al-ʿUqaylī** for transmitting uncorroborated traditions and attaching continuous chains to interrupted reports ([*Siyar* 12/51](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/2138/البزي)).

#### 3. Pre-Canonization Philological Rejection by Imām al-Ṭabarī

Prior to **Ibn Mujāhid's** (d. 324 AH) administrative canonization of the Seven Readings in Baghdad, **Imām al-Ṭabarī** (d. 310 AH) treated Eponymous Readings as fallible scholarly transmissions open to grammatical and historical refutation. In *Jāmiʿ al-Bayān*, al-Ṭabarī rejected **Ibn ʿĀmir's** construct separation at [Qurʾān 6:137](https://quran.com/6/137) as syntactically invalid ([*Jāmiʿ al-Bayān* 12/137–138](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/50/1901/القول-في-تأويل-قوله-تعالى-وكذلك-زين-لكثير-من-المشركين-قتل-أولادهم-)), censured **Ḥamzah's** genitive conjunction at [Qurʾān 4:1](https://quran.com/4/1) as defective prose inflection ([*Jāmiʿ al-Bayān* 7/520–523](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/50/1161/القول-في-تأويل-قوله-تعالىواتقوا-الله-الذي-تساءلون-به-والأرحام)), and dismissed **Ibn Kathīr's** case assignment at [Qurʾān 2:37](https://quran.com/2/37) as the solitary error of a transmitter susceptible to forgetfulness ([*Jāmiʿ al-Bayān* 1/542](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/50/138/القول-في-تأويل-قوله-تعالى-فتلقى-آدم-من-ربه-كلمات)). The biographical records of the canonical readers confirm that scriptural transmission operated under validation criteria distinct from hadith narrator criticism.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «قَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ الْحَسَنِ الْهِسِنْجَانِيُّ: كَانَ عِيسَى بْنُ مِينَا قَالُونُ أَصَمَّ لَا يَسْمَعُ الْبُوقَ، فَكَانَ إِذَا قَرَأَ عَلَيْهِ الْقَارِئُ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ يَنْظُرُ إِلَى شَفَتَيِ الْقَارِئِ فَيَرُدُّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّحْنَ وَالْخَطَأَ. وَسَأَلْتُ أَحْمَدَ بْنَ صَالِحٍ عَنْ حَدِيثِهِ، فَضَحِكَ وَقَالَ: تَكْتُبُونَ عَنْ كُلِّ أَحَدٍ!»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan al-Hisinjānī said: 'ʿĪsā ibn Mīnā Qālūn was deaf (aṣamm) and could not hear a trumpet (lā yasmaʿu al-būq); when a reciter recited to him, he would look at the lips of the reciter and correct his solecisms and mistakes. And I asked Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ [al-Miṣrī] about his Hadith, so he laughed and said: "Do you write down [Hadith] from just anyone?" (taktubūna ʿan kulli aḥad!)'"
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Dhahabī, Maʿrifat al-Qurrāʾ al-Kibār 1/93 and Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 10/327; Ibn Ḥajar, Lisān al-Mīzān 6/316.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «هِشَامُ بْنُ عَمَّارٍ لَمَّا كَبِرَ تَغَيَّرَ فَكُلُّ مَا دُفِعَ إِلَيْهِ قَرَأَهُ، وَكُلَّمَا لُقِّنَ تَلَقَّنَ، وَكَانَ قَدِيمًا أَصَحَّ، كَانَ يَقْرَأُ مِنْ كِتَابِهِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "When Hishām ibn ʿAmmār grew old, he deteriorated (lammā kabira taghayyara); everything that was handed to him he would read out, and whatever was fed to him (luqqina) he would accept and repeat (talaqqana). Formerly he was more sound, when he used to read from his own book."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī, in al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl 30/248–249 and al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 11/424.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «حَدَّثَ هِشَامٌ بِأَرْجَحَ مِنْ أَرْبَعِ مِائَةِ حَدِيثٍ لَيْسَ لَهَا أَصْلٌ، مُسْنَدَةٌ كُلُّهَا، كَانَ فَضْلَكُ يَدُورُ عَلَى أَحَادِيثِ أَبِي مُسْهِرٍ وَغَيْرِهِ، يُلَقِّنُهَا هِشَامَ بْنَ عَمَّارٍ، يَجِيءُ بِالْحَدِيثِ لَيْسَ لَهُ أَصْلٌ، فَيُلَقِّنُهُ إِيَّاهُ، سَمِعْتُ أَبَا حَاتِمٍ الرَّازِيَّ يَحْكِي ذَلِكَ، وَحَدَّثَنَا أَبُو دَاوُدَ قَالَ: أَرْجَحَ مِنْ أَرْبَعِ مِائَةِ حَدِيثٍ لَيْسَ لَهَا أَصْلٌ مُسْنَدَةٌ كُلُّهَا»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Hishām narrated more than four hundred hadiths that have no basis whatsoever (bi-arjaḥ min arbaʿi miʾati ḥadīthin laysa lahā aṣl), all of them with full chains (musnadah kulluhā). Faḍlak [al-Rāzī] used to go around with the hadiths of Abū Mushir and others, feeding them to Hishām ibn ʿAmmār; he would bring a hadith that had no basis and feed it to him—I heard Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī recounting that, and Abū Dāwūd narrated to us saying: more than four hundred baseless hadiths, all with full chains."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī, in al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl 30/249–250; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 11/425; Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb 11/53–54.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «سَمِعْتُ ابْنَ وَارَةَ يَقُولُ: عَزَمْتُ زَمَانًا أَنْ أُمْسِكَ عَنْ حَدِيثِ هِشَامِ بْنِ عَمَّارٍ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ يَبِيعُ الْحَدِيثَ. وَقَالَ صَالِحُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الْأَسَدِيُّ الْحَافِظُ: كَانَ هِشَامُ بْنُ عَمَّارٍ يَأْخُذُ عَلَى الْحَدِيثِ، وَلَا يُحَدِّثُ مَا لَمْ يَأْخُذْ... وَقَالَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ سَيَّارٍ: كَانَ يَأْخُذُ عَلَى كُلِّ وَرَقَتَيْنِ دِرْهَمًا. وَقَالَ الْمَرُّوذِيُّ: ذَكَرَ أَحْمَدُ هِشَامَ بْنَ عَمَّارٍ، فَقَالَ: طَيَّاشٌ خَفِيفٌ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "I heard Ibn Wārah say: 'I resolved for a period of time to abstain from the Hadith of Hishām ibn ʿAmmār because he used to sell Hadith.' And Ṣāliḥ ibn Muḥammad al-Asadī the Ḥāfiẓ said: 'Hishām ibn ʿAmmār used to take payment for narrating Hadith, and would not narrate unless he was paid.' ... And ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn Sayyār said: 'He used to charge one dirham for every two sheets.' And al-Marrūdhī said: Aḥmad [ibn Ḥanbal] mentioned Hishām ibn ʿAmmār and said: 'Flighty and light [in reliability] (ṭayyāsh khafīf).'"

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «ذَكَرَهُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ سَعْدٍ فِي الطَّبَقَةِ الثَّانِيَةِ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكُوفَةِ... قَالَ: وَكَانَ ثِقَةً، إِلَّا أَنَّهُ كَانَ كَثِيرَ الْخَطَأِ فِي حَدِيثِهِ. وَقَالَ يَعْقُوبُ بْنُ سُفْيَانَ: فِي حَدِيثِهِ اضْطِرَابٌ، وَهُوَ ثِقَةٌ... قَدْ تَكَلَّمَ فِيهِ ابْنُ عُلَيَّةَ، فَقَالَ: كَانَ كُلُّ مَنْ كَانَ اسْمُهُ عَاصِمٌ سَيِّئَ الْحِفْظِ... وَقَالَ ابْنُ خِرَاشٍ: فِي حَدِيثِهِ نَكَرَةٌ. وَقَالَ أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ الْعُقَيْلِيُّ: لَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهِ إِلَّا سُوءُ الْحِفْظِ. وَقَالَ الدَّارَقُطْنِيُّ: فِي حِفْظِهِ شَيْءٌ... قَالَ النَّسَائِيُّ: عَاصِمٌ لَيْسَ بِحَافِظٍ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Muḥammad ibn Saʿd mentioned him in the second layer of the people of Kufa... and said: 'He was trustworthy, except that he made many errors in his Hadith (kāna kathīr al-khaṭaʾ fī ḥadīthihi).' Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān [al-Fasawī] said: 'In his Hadith there is inconsistency (fī ḥadīthihi iḍṭirāb), though he is trustworthy.' ... Ibn ʿUlayyah criticized him, saying: 'Everyone whose name was ʿĀṣim had a poor memory (sayyiʾ al-ḥifẓ).' ... Ibn Khirāsh said: 'In his Hadith there is unacceptability (nakārah).' Abū Jaʿfar al-ʿUqaylī said: 'There was nothing against him except poor memory (sūʾ al-ḥifẓ).' Al-Dāraquṭnī said: 'There is some weakness in his memory (fī ḥifẓihi shayʾ).' ... Al-Nasāʾī said: 'ʿĀṣim is not a memorizer (laysa bi-ḥāfiẓ).'"
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl 13/476–478; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 5/256–261.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «ذَكَرَهُ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ فَقَالَ: ثِقَةٌ، رُبَّمَا غَلِطَ، صَاحِبُ قُرْآنٍ وَخَيْرٍ... وَقَالَ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ: أَبُو بَكْرٍ كَثِيرُ الْغَلَطِ جِدًّا... فَأَمَّا حَالُهُ فِي الْقِرَاءَةِ، فَقَيِّمٌ بِحَرْفِ عَاصِمٍ، وَقَدْ خَالَفَهُ حَفْصٌ فِي أَزْيَدَ مِنْ خَمْسِمِائَةِ حَرْفٍ... قَالَ يَحْيَى بْنُ آدَمَ: قَالَ لِي أَبُو بَكْرٍ: تَعَلَّمْتُ مِنْ عَاصِمٍ الْقُرْآنَ كَمَا يَتَعَلَّمُ الصَّبِيُّ مِنَ الْمُعَلِّمِ، فَلَقِيَ مِنِّي شِدَّةً، فَمَا أُحْسِنُ غَيْرَ قِرَاءَتِهِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal mentioned him [Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh / Shuʿbah] and said: 'Trustworthy, perhaps he erred (rubbamā ghaliṭa), a man of the Qurʾān and goodness'... And Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: 'Abū Bakr makes very many errors (kathīr al-ghalaṭ jiddan)'... As for his status in recitation, he is the custodian of the reading of ʿĀṣim, yet Ḥafṣ differed from him in more than five hundred letters... Yaḥyā ibn Ādam said: Abū Bakr said to me: 'I learned the Qurʾān from ʿĀṣim just as a child learns from a teacher; he faced difficulty with me, so I do not master any reading other than his.'"

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «وَصَحَّحَ لَهُ الْحَاكِمُ حَدِيثَ التَّكْبِيرِ وَهُوَ مُنْكَرٌ. وَقَدْ قَالَ أَبُو حَاتِمٍ: ضَعِيفُ الْحَدِيثِ، لَا أُحَدِّثُ عَنْهُ. وَقَالَ الْعُقَيْلِيُّ: مُنْكَرُ الْحَدِيثِ، يُوصِلُ الْأَحَادِيثَ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Al-Ḥākim authenticated for him [al-Bazzī] the hadith of al-takbīr, though it is rejected (munkar). Abū Ḥātim said: 'Weak in Hadith (ḍaʿīf al-ḥadīth); I do not narrate from him.' And al-ʿUqaylī said: 'Rejected in Hadith (munkar al-ḥadīth); he connects [interrupted] hadiths (yūṣilu al-aḥādīth).'"
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ 12/51; Ibn Ḥajar, Lisān al-Mīzān 1/631–633.

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «فَفَرَّقُوا بَيْنَ الْخَافِضِ وَالْمَخْفُوضِ بِمَا عَمِلَ فِيهِ مِنَ الِاسْمِ. وَذَلِكَ فِي كَلَامِ الْعَرَبِ قَبِيحٌ غَيْرُ فَصِيحٍ... قَالَ أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ: وَالْقِرَاءَةُ الَّتِي لَا أَسْتَجِيزُ غَيْرَهَا: (وَكَذَلِكَ زَيَّنَ لِكَثِيرٍ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ قَتْلَ أَوْلَادِهِمْ شُرَكَاؤُهُمْ)... لِإِجْمَاعِ الْحُجَّةِ مِنَ الْقَرَأَةِ عَلَيْهِ، وَأَنَّ تَأْوِيلَ أَهْلِ التَّأْوِيلِ بِذَلِكَ وَرَدَ، فَفِي ذَلِكَ أَوْضَحُ الْبَيَانِ عَلَى فَسَادِ مَا خَالَفَهَا مِنَ الْقِرَاءَةِ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Thus they separated the genitive governing noun from the genitive governed noun by inserting the direct object between them. And that, in the speech of the Arabs, is ugly and uneloquent (qabīḥ ghayr faṣīḥ)... Abū Jaʿfar [al-Ṭabarī] said: The reading other than which I do not deem permissible to recite is 'wa-kadhālika zayyana li-kathīrin mina al-mushrikīna qatla awlādihim shurakāʾuhum'... due to the consensus of the authoritative reciters upon it and the agreement of the exegetes; in that is the clearest proof of the invalidity (fasād) of whatever reading contradicts it."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Imām al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān ʿan Taʾwīl Āy al-Qurʾān 12/137–138 (on Qurʾān 6:137).

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «وَذَلِكَ غَيْرُ فَصِيحٍ مِنَ الْكَلَامِ عِنْدَ الْعَرَبِ، لِأَنَّهَا لَا تَنْسُقُ بِظَاهِرٍ عَلَى مَكْنِيٍّ فِي الْخَفْضِ، إِلَّا فِي ضَرُورَةِ شِعْرٍ... وَأَمَّا الْكَلَامُ، فَلَا شَيْءَ يَضْطَرُّ الْمُتَكَلِّمَ إِلَى اخْتِيَارِ الْمَكْرُوهِ مِنَ الْمَنْطِقِ، وَالرَّدِيءِ فِي الْإِعْرَابِ مِنْهُ... قَالَ: وَالْقِرَاءَةُ الَّتِي لَا نَسْتَجِيزُ لِقَارِئٍ أَنْ يَقْرَأَ غَيْرَهَا فِي ذَلِكَ، النَّصْبُ: (وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ الَّذِي تَسَاءَلُونَ بِهِ وَالْأَرْحَامَ)»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "And that is uneloquent (ghayr faṣīḥ) speech among the Arabs, because they do not conjoin an explicit noun onto a pronominal suffix in the genitive except under poetic license... whereas in prose speech, nothing compels a speaker to choose what is disliked in expression and defective in grammatical inflection (al-radīʾ fī al-iʿrāb)... And the reading other than which we do not permit any reciter to recite in that [verse] is the accusative: 'wa-ittaqū Allāha alladhī tasāʾalūna bihi wa-al-arḥāma'."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Imām al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān ʿan Taʾwīl Āy al-Qurʾān 7/520–523 (on Qurʾān 4:1).

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «فَغَيْرُ جَائِزٍ عِنْدِي فِي الْقِرَاءَةِ إِلَّا رَفْعُ آدَمَ عَلَى أَنَّهُ الْمُتَلَقِّي الْكَلِمَاتِ، لِإِجْمَاعِ الْحُجَّةِ مِنَ الْقَرَأَةِ وَأَهْلِ التَّأْوِيلِ مِنْ عُلَمَاءِ السَّلَفِ وَالْخَلَفِ، عَلَى تَوْجِيهِ التَّلَقِّي إِلَى آدَمَ دُونَ الْكَلِمَاتِ. وَغَيْرُ جَائِزٍ الِاعْتِرَاضُ عَلَيْهَا فِيمَا كَانَتْ عَلَيْهِ مُجْمِعَةً، بِقَوْلِ مَنْ يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ السَّهْوُ وَالْخَطَأُ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: "Yet in my view, nothing is permissible in reciting this verse except placing Ādamu in the nominative as the one who received the words, due to the consensus of the authoritative reciters and exegetes among the scholars of the salaf and khalaf on directing the action of receiving to Adam rather than the words. And it is impermissible to object to what they have agreed upon based on the statement of one who is subject to forgetfulness and error (bi-qawli man yajūzu ʿalayhi al-sahw wa-al-khaṭaʾ)."
arabic_blockquotes.citation: Imām al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān ʿan Taʾwīl Āy al-Qurʾān 1/542 (on Qurʾān 2:37).

arguments.header: Does a Report Keep Its Wording From Book to Book?
arguments.short_title: Does a Report Keep Its Wording From Book to Book?
arguments.reader_question: What do earlier and later versions of the same report show side by side?
arguments.plain_english_hook: When the same account appears across eighth- and ninth-century collections, its wording and attribution sometimes differ across chains. What do earlier and later versions show?
arguments.title: Parallel Texts, Variant Phrases, and Attribution Across Early Compilations
arguments.executive_summary: Turning from biographical grading to textual comparison across eighth- and ninth-century compilations, parallel chains preserve distinct readings of key phrases: Mount Thawr in Muslim 1370a alongside 'such-and-such' (kadhā) in Bukhārī 1870, al-Zuhrī's phrase 'according to what reached us' in Bukhārī 6982 compared with Bukhārī 3, the desert-army reports naming Ibn al-Zubayr in Muslim 2882a–2884 alongside Bukhārī 2118, sayings attributed to Successors in earlier works that appear with prophetic chains in later collections, and eschatological reports on Arabia and Constantinople. How did classical commentators explain these textual variations?
arguments.methodological_significance: Placing early and later recensions side by side allows readers to observe how transmitters handled geographical names, narrative interpolations (idrāj), and elevated chains (rafʿ), as documented by scholars such as Ibn Ḥajar, al-Bazzār, and al-Dāraquṭnī. When two authentic chains preserve different wordings of the same report, which version reflects the earlier form?

subpoints.short_title: 5 Versions of ʿAlī's Scroll and the Name “Thawr” as a Medina Boundary
subpoints.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see five chains giving different contents for the one short scroll in ʿAlī's scabbard, and Muslim 1370a naming Thawr as a Medina boundary where Bukhārī 1870 reads “such-and-such.” How do the versions compare?
subpoints.takeaway: Ibn Ḥajar cited a small Thawr near Uḥud; Abū ʿUbayd said Medina had no mountain of that name.
subpoints.title: The 'Scroll of ʿAlī' Reports and 'Mount Thawr' Across Parallel Versions

a.text: Medina is sacred [[from ʿAyr to Thawr]].

b.text: Medina is a sanctuary [[from the ʿAyr Mountain to such-and-such a place (kadhā)]].

showcase.note: Abū ʿUbayd and later commentators noted that Mount Thawr is in Mecca, not Medina; al-Bukhārī's version replaces the name with 'such-and-such' (kadhā).

subpoints.summary_markdown: Across the canonical collections, five chains report ʿAlī stating that he possessed no written document from the Prophet apart from the Qurʾān and a short scroll (*ṣaḥīfah*) in his sword scabbard ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 111](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:111); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1370a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1370a)), with each chain listing different contents for the scroll. In al-Aʿmash's Kūfan chain ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1370a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1370a); [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6755](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6755)), the text defines Medina's sanctuary as 'between ʿAyr and Thawr,' whereas parallel versions in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 1870](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1870), [3172](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3172), and [7300](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7300) read 'from ʿAyr to such-and-such' (`إِلَى كَذَا`).

evidence_items.label: Five Distinct Legal and Political Texts Inside the Same Sword-Scabbard Scroll Across 2nd-Century Regional Common Links
evidence_items.content_markdown: Although every chain describes a single small scroll suspended inside ʿAlī's sword scabbard, five regional common links report divergent contents: **(1)** `Muṭarrif ← al-Shaʿbī` (**0 overlap**: states the scroll contained *nothing* except blood-money, captive release, and non-retaliation against a Muslim for a disbeliever; [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 111](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:111), [3047](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3047), [6903](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6903)); **(2)** `Qatādah ← al-Ḥasan / Abū Ḥassān` (equal blood-valuation among believers, mutual protection, and asylum granted by the humblest Muslim; [*Sunan al-Nasāʾī* 4734](https://sunnah.com/nasai:4734), [*Musnad Aḥmad* 991](https://sunnah.com/ahmad:991)); **(3)** `Abū al-Ṭufayl` (four maledictions upon whoever sacrifices to anyone other than God, curses his parents, alters boundary stones, or shelters an offender; [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1978a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1978a)); **(4)** `ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal ← Fuḍayl` (joins the Abrahamic haram of Mecca to the Medinan sanctuary; [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1370c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1370c)); and **(5)** `al-Aʿmash ← Ibrāhīm al-Taymī` (camel-age schedules, Medina's sanctuary between ʿAyr and *Thawr*, client allegiance, and collective Muslim protection; [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7300](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7300); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1370a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1370a); cf. [*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 12:42](https://shamela.ws/book/1673/7029)).

key_arabic_quote_structured.arabic: الْمَدِينَةُ حَرَمٌ مَا بَيْنَ عَيْرٍ إِلَى ثَوْرٍ
key_arabic_quote_structured.english: Medina is a sacred sanctuary from ʿAyr to Thawr.

evidence_items.label: Muslim 1370a ('From ʿAyr to Thawr') Compared with Bukhārī 1870, 3172, and 7300 ('To Such-and-Such')
evidence_items.content_markdown: Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām (d. 224 AH; cited in Ibn Ḥajar's [*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 4:82–83](https://shamela.ws/book/1673/2372) and al-Nawawī's [*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 9:143](https://shamela.ws/book/1711/2022)) and al-Samhūdī ([*Wafāʾ al-Wafāʾ* 1:77–79](https://shamela.ws/book/23695/73)) noted that the inhabitants of Medina knew no mountain called Thawr, and noted that parallel transmissions in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 1870](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1870), [3172](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3172), and [7300](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7300) read *'between ʿAyr and such-and-such'* (`مَا بَيْنَ عَيْرٍ إِلَى كَذَا`) or left a blank space (`بَيَاضًا`).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «الْمَدِينَةُ حَرَمٌ مَا بَيْنَ عَائِرٍ إِلَى كَذَا مَنْ أَحْدَثَ فِيهَا حَدَثًا أَوْ آوَى مُحْدِثًا» — "Medina is a sanctuary between ʿĀʾir and such-and-such [in place of 'Thawr']; whoever introduces an innovation therein or shelters an innovator..." ([Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1870](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1870))

comparison_tables.title: Five Divergent 2nd-Century Regional Clusters of the 'Scroll of ʿAlī (Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī)' Tradition
headers: Reported Contents Inside ʿAlī's Sword-Scabbard Scroll
rows: Blood-money (*al-ʿaql*), ransoming captives (*fakāk al-asīr*), and *"a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever"*
2. Baṣran: Qatādah ← al-Ḥasan ← Qays ibn ʿUbād / Qatādah ← Abū Ḥassān al-Aʿraj
Equal blood-valuation of believers, collective solidarity against outsiders, and safe-conduct (*dhimmah*) granted by the lowest believer
3. Meccan / Kūfan: Abū al-Ṭufayl ʿĀmir ibn Wāthilah
Four liturgical curses (sacrificing to other than God, cursing parents, altering land boundary-markers, sheltering an offender)
4. Baṣran: ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal ← Fuḍayl ibn Zayd
Appends Abraham's sanctification of Mecca to the Medinan sanctuary ruling
Camel-age brackets, ban on *mawālī* switching clientage, and **"Medina is a sanctuary between ʿAyr and Thawr"** (reading *"such-and-such"* [`إِلَى كَذَا`] in *Bukhārī* 1870, 3172, 7300)

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical commentators sought to resolve the geographical anomaly by suggesting that a small hill behind Mount Uḥud in Medina was also called 'Thawr'—a conjecture attributed to **al-Nawawī** in [*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 9:143](https://shamela.ws/book/1711/2022) and to **ʿAbd al-Salām al-Baṣrī** and **al-Marāghī** by Ibn Ḥajar in [*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 4:82](https://shamela.ws/book/1673/2372)–[83](https://shamela.ws/book/1673/2373). Ibn Ḥajar further cites **Abū Bakr al-Ḥāzimī** for the scribal emendation to 'Uḥud', while acknowledging that early authorities like **Abū ʿUbayd** and **Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr** rejected the existence of any Medinan Thawr. Others proposed the divergent versions represent partial excerpts from a longer composite scroll.
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: Each regional narrator introduces his respective clauses with restrictive phrasing indicating the complete contents of a brief note (`فَإِذَا فِيهَا` / `مَا فِيهَا إِلَّا`), and early authorities—including Abū ʿUbayd as cited in [*Fatḥ al-Bārī* (4:82)](https://shamela.ws/book/1673/2372) and [*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* (9:143)](https://shamela.ws/book/1711/2022) and Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr, as well as al-Samhūdī in [*Wafāʾ al-Wafāʾ* (1:77–79)](https://shamela.ws/book/23695/73)—attested that the people of Medina knew no mountain called Thawr, where transmitters in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 1870](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1870), [3172](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3172), and [7300](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7300) read *"such-and-such"* (`إِلَى كَذَا`) in place of *"Thawr"*.

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
### 1. Five Second-Century Regional Common Links for One Sword-Scabbard Scroll
Every canonical version of the *Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī* tradition shares an identical four-step literary skeleton: a questioner asks **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib** whether the Prophet confided secret written teachings to the *Ahl al-Bayt* beyond the Qurʾān; ʿAlī swears an emphatic denial; he draws a small scroll (*ṣaḥīfah*) from the scabbard of his sword (*qirāb al-sayf*); and he introduces its contents with restrictive particles (`مَا فِيهَا إِلَّا` / `فَإِذَا فِيهَا`). Applying *isnād-cum-matn* analysis across Kūfa, Baṣra, and Mecca reveals that five second-century AH common links used this fixed anti-esoteric frame as a vessel for divergent local rulings:
* **Cluster I (`al-Shaʿbī`, d. c. 103 AH, Kūfa):** Circulated after Mukhtār al-Thaqafī's Kūfan uprising, restricting the scroll to three clauses: bloodwit (*al-ʿaql*), ransoming prisoners (*fakāk al-asīr*), and *"a Muslim is not executed for a disbeliever"* ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 111](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:111), alongside [3047](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3047) and [6903](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6903)).
* **Cluster II (`Qatādah ibn Diʿāmah`, d. 117 AH, Baṣra):** Drops bloodwit and ransom, substituting equal blood-worth among believers and collective protection (*dhimmah*; [*Sunan al-Nasāʾī* 4734](https://sunnah.com/nasai:4734); [*Musnad Aḥmad* 991](https://sunnah.com/ahmad:991)).
* **Cluster III (`Abū al-Ṭufayl`, d. c. 100–110 AH):** Replaces the legal statutes entirely with four liturgical curses (`لَعَنَ اللَّهُ...`) against sacrificing to idols, cursing parents, shifting land markers, and harboring an offender ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1978a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1978a)).
* **Cluster IV (`ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal ← Fuḍayl ibn Zayd`, Baṣra):** Inserts Abraham's sanctification of Mecca alongside Medina's sanctuary ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1370c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1370c)).
* **Cluster V (`al-Aʿmash ← Ibrāhīm al-Taymī`, d. 92 AH, Kūfa):** Amalgamates camel-age brackets, a Medinan sanctuary clause (*mā bayna ʿAyrin ilā Thawr*), safe-conduct, and a curse on *mawālī* who switch tribal patrons ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1370a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1370a); [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6755](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6755)).

### 2. The Name 'Thawr' as a Medinan Boundary and the Variant 'Such-and-Such' (`إِلَى كَذَا`)
In Cluster V, the scroll defines Medina's sanctuary boundaries as *"between ʿAyr and Thawr."* While Mount ʿAyr borders Medina on the south (paired in Medinan traditions with Mount Uḥud on the north; [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1362](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1362)), **Mount Thawr lies in Mecca**, some 450 km south. In *Fatḥ al-Bārī* ([4/82–85](https://shamela.ws/book/1673/2373)) and *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* ([9:143](https://shamela.ws/book/1711/2022); cf. al-Samhūdī, *Wafāʾ al-Wafāʾ* [1:77–79](https://shamela.ws/book/23695/73)), **Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām**, **al-Nawawī**, and **Ibn Ḥajar** confirm that Medinans knew no mountain called Thawr and identify the wording as an Iraqi transmitter error. In parallel canonical versions of the same tradition (*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 1870, 3172, and 7300), the name *Thawr* does not appear, and the boundary reads *kadhā* ('such-and-such'), which Ibn Ḥajar notes some transmitters used when hesitating over the wording.

subpoints.summary_markdown: Parallel chapters of *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* preserve different lengths and phrasing for the Cave Ḥirāʾ narrative: [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6982](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6982) includes the phrase `فِيمَا بَلَغَنَا` (*'according to what has reached us'*) inside al-Zuhrī's transmission, whereas [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3) ends before that clause. Alongside early accounts in [Ibn Saʿd's *al-Ṭabaqāt* (1:153)](https://shamela.ws/book/1686/151) and [al-Ṭabarī's *Tārīkh* (2:300)](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/925), the case also compares the two versions of the 'Ten Promised Paradise' report evaluated by al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī in [*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 3747–3748](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3747).

evidence_items.label: The Phrase 'According to What Reached Us' («فِيمَا بَلَغَنَا») in Bukhārī 6982 Compared with Bukhārī 3 and Early Sīrah Accounts
evidence_items.content_markdown: Whereas [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3) (cf. [*Bukhārī* 4953](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4953); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 160a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:160a)) presents the Cave Ḥirāʾ onset-of-revelation narrative under a continuous `al-Zuhrī ← ʿUrwah ← ʿĀʾishah` chain despite ʿĀʾishah being unborn at the event, the `Maʿmar ← al-Zuhrī` transmission in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6982](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6982) includes the phrase **«فِيمَا بَلَغَنَا»** (*"according to what has reached us"*) introducing the account of the Prophet ascending mountain peaks during the pause in revelation (*fatrat al-waḥy*). Earlier biographical and historical sources record parallel forms of the account: ʿUrwah's son Hishām transmitted his father's account as a *mursal* report stopping at ʿUrwah without ʿĀʾishah ([Ibn Saʿd, *al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā* 1:153](https://shamela.ws/book/1686/151)), while eyewitness Zubayrid client Wahb ibn Kaysān ([Ibn Hishām, *al-Sīrah al-Nabawiyyah*](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/58/264/); [al-Ṭabarī, *Tārīkh* 2:300](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/925)–[301](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/926)) records ʿUrwah's brother ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr hearing the narrative from Meccan preacher (*qāṣṣ*) **ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī** (d. 68 AH)—where, as in al-Nuʿmān ibn Rāshid's recension from al-Zuhrī ([*Tārīkh al-Ṭabarī* 2:298](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/923)), the Prophet answers Gabriel's *"Iqraʾ!"* with *"What shall I recite?"* (`مَا أَقْرَأُ؟ / مَاذَا أَقْرَأُ؟`) rather than [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3)'s *"I am not one who reads"* (`مَا أَنَا بِقَارِئٍ`).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «حَزِنَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فِيمَا بَلَغَنَا حُزْنًا غَدَا مِنْهُ مِرَارًا كَىْ يَتَرَدَّى مِنْ رُءُوسِ شَوَاهِقِ الْجِبَالِ» — "The Prophet grieved—according to what has reached us—going out repeatedly in order to throw himself from the summits of high mountains." ([Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6982](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6982))

evidence_items.label: Comparing Bukhārī 6982, 4953, and 3 Alongside al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī on Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 3747–3748
evidence_items.content_markdown: Comparing the three canonical recensions of the Cave Ḥirāʾ narrative inside *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* shows three distinct forms across his chapters: in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6982](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6982), Maʿmar includes al-Zuhrī's phrase `فِيمَا بَلَغَنَا` (*"according to what has reached us"*) introducing the mountain-ascent episode; in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 4953](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4953) (*Kitāb al-Tafsīr*), the narrative stops at the pause of revelation (*fatrat al-waḥy*) and the Prophet's grief (`وَفَتَرَ الْوَحْىُ فَتْرَةً حَتَّى حَزِنَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ`) while omitting the mountain-ascent sequel; and in the opening chapter ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3); cf. [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 160a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:160a)), `ʿUqayl ← al-Zuhrī` truncates the entire pause and grief sequence after `وَفَتَرَ الْوَحْىُ`. Analogously, in the Kūfan versus Medinan transmission of the "Ten Promised Paradise" roster ([*Sunan Abī Dāwūd* 4649](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4649)–[4650](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4650); [*Sunan Ibn Mājah* 133](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:133); [*Musnad Aḥmad* #1631](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/6/1545/) vs. [*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 3747](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3747)–[3748](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3748)), **Imām al-Bukhārī** and **al-Tirmidhī** ruled that Saʿīd ibn Zayd's Kūfan transmission (which counts the Prophet himself as the first of the ten and omits Abū ʿUbaydah) is more authentic (`أَصَحُّ`) than the ten-Companion transmission.
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «ثُمَّ لَمْ يَنْشَبْ وَرَقَةُ أَنْ تُوُفِّيَ وَفَتَرَ الْوَحْىُ فَتْرَةً حَتَّى حَزِنَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ» — "Soon Waraqah died and revelation paused for a period until the Messenger of God grieved [stopping before the mountain-ascent sequel of Bukhārī 6982]." ([Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4953](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4953))

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical commentators such as **Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī** ([*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 1:23–27](https://shamela.ws/book/1673/27), [12:359–361](https://shamela.ws/book/1673/7346)) propose that ʿĀʾishah's pre-birth Cave Ḥirāʾ report ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3)) represents a valid Companion *mursal* while the `fīmā balaghanā` mountain-ascent passage ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6982](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6982)) constitutes al-Zuhrī's separable sub-commentary, and that the Prophet delivered two distinct ten-man Paradise lists on separate occasions ([*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 3747](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3747)–[3748](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3748)).
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: Neither ʿUrwah's son Hishām ([*Ṭabaqāt Ibn Saʿd* 1:153](https://shamela.ws/book/1686/151)) nor the eyewitness Zubayrid court account ([*Tārīkh al-Ṭabarī* 2:300](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/925)–[301](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/926)) traces the Cave Ḥirāʾ narrative to ʿĀʾishah, and comparing [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3) with [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6982](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6982) shows that al-Zuhrī integrated anonymous *balāghāt* directly into a composite *sīrah* narrative beneath the `ʿUrwah ← ʿĀʾishah` header. Similarly, the two-occasions harmonization for the Ten Promised Paradise tradition is complicated by the fact that both versions converge on the same Medinan father-son transmission node (`ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥumayd ← Ḥumayd`), leading **al-Bukhārī** and **al-Tirmidhī** ([*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 3747](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3747)–[3748](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3748)) to evaluate them as competing variants of a single hadith (`هَذَا الْحَدِيثُ`) and judge the Saʿīd ibn Zayd version more authentic (`وَهَذَا أَصَحُّ مِنَ الْحَدِيثِ الأَوَّلِ`).

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
### 1. Comparing Bukhārī 3 and Bukhārī 6982 in the Cave Ḥirāʾ Account
In the opening chapter of [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3) (and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 160a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:160a)), the narrative of the Prophet's call at Cave Ḥirāʾ reads as a seamless monologue transmitted via `Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī (d. 124 AH) ← ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr (d. 94 AH) ← ʿĀʾishah`. Yet when al-Bukhārī cites Maʿmar ibn Rāshid's fuller transmission from al-Zuhrī in the Book of Dream Interpretation ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 6982](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6982)), the exact point where *Bukhārī* 3 truncates the pause of revelation (*fatrat al-waḥy*) preserves the phrase (*fīmā balaghanā*, meaning what reached the compilers), introducing an unchained report of the Prophet repeatedly ascending mountain peaks in distress.

Two independent early controls corroborate that al-Zuhrī combined disparate *sīrah* reports beneath a single `ʿUrwah ← ʿĀʾishah` header:
* **Hishām ibn ʿUrwah's *Mursal* Transmission:** In Ibn Saʿd's *al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā* ([1:153](https://shamela.ws/book/1686/151)), when ʿUrwah's own son Hishām transmits his father's Cave Ḥirāʾ account (`via Ḥammād ibn Salamah`), the chain stops at ʿUrwah without mentioning ʿĀʾishah.
* **The Zubayrid Storyteller (*Qāṣṣ*) Performance:** In al-Ṭabarī's *Tārīkh* ([2:300](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/925), [2:301](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/926); cf. Ibn Hishām's *Sīrah* [1:235–236](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/58/264/)), the Zubayrid client Wahb ibn Kaysān describes ʿUrwah's brother ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr listening to the Meccan preacher **ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī** (d. 68 AH) recount the Ḥirāʾ narrative (glossing pre-Islamic *taḥannuth* as *al-tabarrur*, `وَالتَّحَنُّثُ: التَّبَرُّرُ`). In ʿUbayd's oral performance—as well as in al-Nuʿmān ibn Rāshid's branch from al-Zuhrī in *Tārīkh al-Ṭabarī* ([2:298](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/923))—the Prophet responds to Gabriel's command *"Iqraʾ!"* with the question *"What shall I recite?"* (*mā aqraʾu / mādhā aqraʾu*), whereas [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3) reads *"I am not one who reads"* (*mā anā bi-qāriʾ*).

### 2. The Two Transmissions of the "Ten Promised Paradise" Roster (*Tirmidhī* 3747–3748)
A parallel textual divergence appears in the *ʿAsharah al-Mubashsharūn* tradition. In its earliest Kūfan stratum—transmitted from **Saʿīd ibn Zayd** through two Kūfan sub-transmitters, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Akhnas (in [*Sunan Abī Dāwūd* 4649](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4649) and *Musnad Aḥmad* [#1631](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/6/1545/)) alongside Riyāḥ ibn al-Ḥārith (in [*Sunan Abī Dāwūd* 4650](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4650) and [*Sunan Ibn Mājah* 133](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:133))—Saʿīd rebukes Kūfan detractors of ʿAlī by enumerating ten men in Paradise: **the Prophet himself as the first of the ten**, followed by eight senior Companions while **omitting Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ** and naming himself tenth. When the tradition passed through the Medinan family link `ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥumayd ← his father Ḥumayd`, one branch ([*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 3748](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3748)) preserved Saʿīd's roster, whereas `al-Darāwardī` ([*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 3747](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3747)) shifted the Companion attribution to the narrator's ancestor **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf** and substituted Abū ʿUbaydah in place of the Prophet to produce ten Companions—an alteration that both **al-Tirmidhī** and **al-Bukhārī** judged less authentic than Saʿīd ibn Zayd's original report.

subpoints.short_title: 3 Reports on the Desert-Army Prophecy: 2 Name Ibn al-Zubayr, 1 Omits
subpoints.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Muslim 2882–2883, where people in Ibn al-Zubayr's Mecca apply a prophecy of an army swallowed by the desert to the Syrian forces of their day, and Bukhārī 2118, which omits that setting.
subpoints.takeaway: Commentators refer the prophecy to a future army; narrators in Muslim applied it to Ibn al-Zubayr's war.
subpoints.title: The Desert-Swallowing Report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2882–2884 and Bukhārī 2118

showcase.gap_label: Three canonical transmissions of the Baidāʾ army report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī

points.label: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2882a: Names Ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca during the dialogue with Umm Salamah
Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2883a: Ibn Ṣafwān cites Ḥafṣah's report regarding the army sent against Mecca
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2118: Records the shorter general wording ('An army will attack the Kaʿbah') without naming Ibn al-Zubayr

subpoints.summary_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2882a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2882a)–[2884](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2884), narrators during the **Second Fitnah (60–73 AH / 680–692 AD)** connected the report of an army being swallowed by the desert (*khasf*) at al-Baidāʾ to the Syrian expeditions sent against **ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr** in Mecca. When the Syrian forces crossed al-Baidāʾ without being swallowed ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2883b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2883b); [*Sunan Ibn Mājah* 4063](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:4063)), Ibn Ṣafwān remarked, *'By God, it is not this army!'* A shorter version of the report in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 2118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2118) does not include the Ibn al-Zubayr setting or the Meccan sanctuary-seeker clause.

evidence_items.label: The Desert-Swallowing (Khasf) Report Discussed During Ibn al-Zubayr's Caliphate (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2882a–2883a)
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2882a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2882a) (`ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rufayʿ ← ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Qibṭiyyah`), Ibn al-Zubayr's governor **al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Rabīʿah** and chief supporter **ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān** visit **Umm Salamah** specifically *"during the days of Ibn al-Zubayr"* (`وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ فِي أَيَّامِ ابْنِ الزُّبَيْرِ`) to ask about the army destined to be swallowed by the earth (*al-jaysh alladhī yukhsafu bihi*). Umm Salamah replies that a refugee will seek sanctuary at the Sacred House (`يَعُوذُ عَائِذٌ بِالْبَيْتِ`) and an army sent against him will be swallowed at al-Baidāʾ (`فَإِذَا كَانُوا بِبَيْدَاءَ مِنَ الأَرْضِ خُسِفَ بِهِمْ`, identified by Abū Jaʿfar as Baidāʾ of Medina)—an expectation that remained unfulfilled when al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf's Syrian army marched through al-Baidāʾ unharmed and killed Ibn al-Zubayr in 73 AH / 692 AD ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2545](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2545); cf. [*Sunan Ibn Mājah* 4063](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:4063)).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: يَعُوذُ عَائِذٌ بِالْبَيْتِ فَيُبْعَثُ إِلَيْهِ بَعْثٌ فَإِذَا كَانُوا بِبَيْدَاءَ مِنَ الأَرْضِ خُسِفَ بِهِمْ — "A refugee will seek refuge at the Sacred House, an expedition will be sent against him, and when they are at al-Baidāʾ of the earth, they will be swallowed up." (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2882a)

key_arabic_quote_structured.arabic: يَعُوذُ عَائِذٌ بِالْبَيْتِ فَيُبْعَثُ إِلَيْهِ بَعْثٌ فَإِذَا كَانُوا بِبَيْدَاءَ مِنَ الأَرْضِ خُسِفَ بِهِمْ
key_arabic_quote_structured.english: A refugee will seek refuge at the Sacred House, an expedition will be sent against him, and when they are at al-Baidāʾ of the earth, they will be swallowed up.

evidence_items.label: Ḥafṣah's Parallel Second-Fitnah Recension via ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān and His Explicit Identification of the Umayyad Army (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2883a–2883b)
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2883a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2883a)–[2883b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2883b) (`Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah ← Umayyah ibn Ṣafwān ← his grandfather ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān ← Ḥafṣah`), **ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān**—who died clinging to the curtains of the Kaʿbah alongside **ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr** in 73 AH / 692 AD—narrates from **Ḥafṣah** that an army marching to attack the Sacred House (`لَيَؤُمَّنَّ هَذَا الْبَيْتَ جَيْشٌ يَغْزُونَهُ`) will have its middle ranks swallowed at al-Baidāʾ until only a lone survivor (*al-sharīd*) remains to report their destruction. When the Umayyad army from Syria marched on Mecca without being swallowed, Ibn Ṣafwān exclaimed in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2883b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2883b): *"By God, it is not this army!"* (`أَمَا وَاللَّهِ مَا هُوَ بِهَذَا الْجَيْشِ`), while Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Taymī confessed in [*Sunan Ibn Mājah* 4063](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:4063): *"When the army of al-Ḥajjāj came, we thought that they were [the ones]!"* (`فَلَمَّا جَاءَ جَيْشُ الْحَجَّاجِ ظَنَنَّا أَنَّهُمْ هُمْ`).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: لَيَؤُمَّنَّ هَذَا الْبَيْتَ جَيْشٌ يَغْزُونَهُ حَتَّى إِذَا كَانُوا بِبَيْدَاءَ مِنَ الأَرْضِ يُخْسَفُ بِأَوْسَطِهِمْ — "An army will surely head toward this House in order to attack it, until when they are at al-Baidāʾ of the earth, their middle ranks will be swallowed up." (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2883a–2883b)

key_arabic_quote_structured.arabic: لَيَؤُمَّنَّ هَذَا الْبَيْتَ جَيْشٌ يَغْزُونَهُ حَتَّى إِذَا كَانُوا بِبَيْدَاءَ مِنَ الأَرْضِ يُخْسَفُ بِأَوْسَطِهِمْ
key_arabic_quote_structured.english: An army will surely head toward this House in order to attack it, until when they are at al-Baidāʾ of the earth, their middle ranks will be swallowed up.

evidence_items.label: Comparing ʿĀʾishah's Short Version (Bukhārī 2118) with the Full Versions in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2882a–2884
evidence_items.content_markdown: Whereas the Umm Salamah, Ḥafṣah, and `Ibn al-Zubayr ← ʿĀʾishah` chains in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2882a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2882a)–[2884](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2884) preserve the explicit Second-Fitnah frame (`فِي أَيَّامِ ابْنِ الزُّبَيْرِ` and the Qurashī *ʿāʾidh* seeking refuge in the Kaʿbah, `بِرَجُلٍ مِنْ قُرَيْشٍ قَدْ لَجَأَ بِالْبَيْتِ`), the parallel recension transmitted via `Muḥammad ibn Sūqah ← Nāfiʿ ibn Jubayr ← ʿĀʾishah` in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 2118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2118) records the report without Ibn al-Zubayr's name or the seventh-century Mecca dialogue, presenting it in general future wording (`يُخْسَفُ بِأَوَّلِهِمْ وَآخِرِهِمْ`). This difference between parallel transmissions compares with how the Second-Fitnah Ḥijāz Fire report ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7118); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2902](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2902)) and twelve-caliph / thirty-year caliphate traditions ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1821d](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1821d); cf. [*Sunan Abī Dāwūd* 4646](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4646); [*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 2226](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:2226)) were re-anchored in later commentary.
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: يَغْزُو جَيْشٌ الْكَعْبَةَ فَإِذَا كَانُوا بِبَيْدَاءَ مِنَ الأَرْضِ يُخْسَفُ بِأَوَّلِهِمْ وَآخِرِهِمْ — "An army will attack the Kaʿbah, and when they are at al-Baidāʾ of the earth, they will be swallowed up from the first of them to the last of them." (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2118)

key_arabic_quote_structured.arabic: يَغْزُو جَيْشٌ الْكَعْبَةَ فَإِذَا كَانُوا بِبَيْدَاءَ مِنَ الأَرْضِ يُخْسَفُ بِأَوَّلِهِمْ وَآخِرِهِمْ
key_arabic_quote_structured.english: An army will attack the Kaʿbah, and when they are at al-Baidāʾ of the earth, they will be swallowed up from the first of them to the last of them.

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical commentators propose that although the Companions in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2882a–2883b applied the Baidāʾ army-swallowing prophecy to the Umayyad expeditions against ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr during the Second Fitnah, the prophecy itself refers to a future end-times army marching against the Mahdī, while the Ḥijāz Fire in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7118 was fulfilled by the 654 AH (1256 AD) Medinan volcanic eruption.
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2882a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2882a)–[2884](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2884) (as well as [*Sunan Ibn Mājah* 4063](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:4063)), the Companions and Meccan officials themselves—Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Rabīʿah, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān—invoked the report specifically *"during the days of Ibn al-Zubayr"* regarding the Syrian army marching on a Qurashī refugee in Mecca, before the recension in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 2118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2118) omitted both the Zubayrid frame and the *ʿāʾidh* (sanctuary-seeker) clause. Similarly, the canonical Ḥijāz Fire report ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7118); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2902](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2902)) appears in its earliest pre-canonical stratum ([*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* 20788](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19829/)) as al-Zuhrī's own unattributed (*maqṭūʿ*) statement rather than a Prophetic prediction.

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
### 1. The *Baidāʾ* Army Reports During the Second Fitnah (*Muslim* 2882a–2884; *Bukhārī* 2118)
The canonical traditions regarding an army swallowed by the desert at *al-Baidāʾ* ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2882a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2882a)–[2884](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2884); [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 2118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2118)) record both the seventh-century Mecca dialogue naming Ibn al-Zubayr and the shorter general wording:
* **Explicit Second-Fitnah Anchoring:** In [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2882a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2882a), the sub-narrator ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Qibṭiyyah records that the Meccan governor **al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Rabīʿah** alongside **ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān** questioned Umm Salamah about *"the army that will be swallowed by the earth"* specifically *"during the days of Ibn al-Zubayr"* (*wa-kāna dhālika fī ayyām Ibn al-Zubayr*), when Umayyad forces marched from Syria via Medina to besiege Ibn al-Zubayr (*ʿāʾidh al-Bayt*, the refugee of the Kaʿbah) in 64 AH (683 AD) and 72–73 AH (692 AD). Likewise, in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2883a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2883a)–[2883b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2883b), **ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān** himself serves as the sole Companion-level link transmitting the identical prophecy from **Ḥafṣah**.
* **Ibn Ṣafwān's Reaction in Muslim 2883b and the Shorter Version in Bukhārī 2118:** When the Umayyad army traversed *al-Baidāʾ* without being swallowed and killed both Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn Ṣafwān inside the Meccan sanctuary ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2545](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2545)), Ibn Ṣafwān remarked in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2883b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2883b) (via *Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah ← Umayyah ibn Ṣafwān ← ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān*): *"By God, it is not this army!"* (*amā wa-Llāhi mā huwa bi-hādhā al-jaysh*), while al-Taymī recorded in [*Sunan Ibn Mājah* 4063](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:4063) that the Meccans had expected al-Ḥajjāj's troops to be that very force (*ẓanannā annahum hum*). Whereas [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2884](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2884) (via *Ibn al-Zubayr ← ʿĀʾishah*) retains the Qurashī refugee clause, the recension in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 2118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2118) omits both Ibn al-Zubayr's frame and the refugee at the Kaʿbah, presenting a general future wording (*yaghzū jayshun al-Kaʿbata*).

### 2. Parallel Second-Fitnah Controls in the Canonical Corpus
A parallel trajectory governs two companion traditions from the same era. First, the canonical hadith predicting a fire in the Ḥijāz illuminating camel necks at Buṣrā ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7118); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2902](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2902)) is preserved in its earliest second-century source ([*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* 20788](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19829/)) as **Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī's** own unattributed (*maqṭūʿ*) saying. Second, the Kūfan tradition limiting the Prophetic Caliphate (*khilāfat al-nubuwwah*) to thirty years ([*Sunan Abī Dāwūd* 4646](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4646); [*Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī* 2226](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:2226), alongside the twelve-caliph tradition in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1821d](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1821d)) bottlenecks exclusively through `Saʿīd ibn Jumhān ← Safīnah` to terminate right-guided rule at **al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī's** abdication to Muʿāwiyah in Rabīʿ I 41 AH (661 AD).

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «دَخَلَ الْحَارِثُ بْنُ أَبِي رَبِيعَةَ وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ صَفْوَانَ وَأَنَا مَعَهُمَا عَلَى أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ أُمِّ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ فَسَأَلاَهَا عَنِ الْجَيْشِ الَّذِي يُخْسَفُ بِهِ وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ فِي أَيَّامِ ابْنِ الزُّبَيْرِ فَقَالَتْ قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: يَعُوذُ عَائِذٌ بِالْبَيْتِ فَيُبْعَثُ إِلَيْهِ بَعْثٌ فَإِذَا كَانُوا بِبَيْدَاءَ مِنَ الأَرْضِ خُسِفَ بِهِمْ»
arabic_blockquotes.english_translation: *"Al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Rabīʿah and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān entered upon Umm Salamah, Mother of the Believers, and I was with them, and they asked her about the army that would be swallowed by the earth—and that was during the days of Ibn al-Zubayr. She said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'A refugee will seek refuge at the Sacred House, an expedition will be sent against him, and when they are at al-Baidāʾ of the earth, they will be swallowed up.'"*

arabic_blockquotes.arabic_text: «أَخْبَرَتْنِي حَفْصَةُ أَنَّهَا سَمِعَتِ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ يَقُولُ: لَيَؤُمَّنَّ هَذَا الْبَيْتَ جَيْشٌ يَغْزُونَهُ حَتَّى إِذَا كَانُوا بِبَيْدَاءَ مِنَ الأَرْضِ يُخْسَفُ بِأَوْسَطِهِمْ وَيُنَادِي أَوَّلُهُمْ آخِرَهُمْ ثُمَّ يُخْسَفُ بِهِمْ فَلاَ يَبْقَى إِلاَّ الشَّرِيدُ الَّذِي يُخْبِرُ عَنْهُمْ»

subpoints.summary_markdown: In Hadith historiography, *rafʿ* (retrojection) denotes the upward elevation of a Successor statement (*maqṭūʿ*), Companion maxim (*mawqūf*), or Late Antique homily into a Prophetic narration (*marfūʿ*). Earlier and supplementary compilations—specifically *Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* ([#20788](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19829/)) and al-Ṭabarānī's *al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr* ([#8670](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/84/8550/))—preserve the non-prophetic intermediate strata for traditions subsequently canonized as Prophetic speech in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7118) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5427](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5427).

evidence_items.label: The Fire from the Ḥijāz Illuminating Camels at Buṣrā (Bukhārī 7118; Muslim 2902): Attested Earlier as al-Zuhrī's Own Unattributed (Maqṭūʿ) Statement in Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq (#20788)
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* #20788](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19829/), the statement that a fire from the Ḥijāz will illuminate the necks of camels in Buṣrā is recorded by Maʿmar ibn Rāshid as the unchained remark (*maqṭūʿ*) of his teacher Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī. In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7118) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2902](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2902), the same Arabic wording appears via other students of al-Zuhrī with a full chain back to the Prophet.

([Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7118))

evidence_items.label: The Four-Plant Citron Parable (Bukhārī 5427; Muslim 797a): From Vayikra Rabbah 30:12 through Ibn Masʿūd's Mawqūf Homily (al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr #8670) to Qatādah's Marfūʿ Hadith
evidence_items.content_markdown: In [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5427](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5427), [5020](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5020), [7560](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7560), and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 797a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:797a), a Prophetic parable classifies four types of people by fragrance (*rīḥ*) and taste (*ṭaʿm*) led by the citron (`الأُتْرُجَّةِ`) and date (`التَّمْرَةِ`), paralleling the 5th-century Palestinian Midrash *Vayikra Rabbah* 30:12 on the Four Species of Sukkot—starting with the citron (*etrog*, Aramaic *utrūgā*) and date palm (*lulav*)—comparing Torah learning (taste) and good deeds (fragrance). Crucially, al-Ṭabarānī's [*al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr* (#8670)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/84/8550/) preserves the intermediate Kūfan stratum as a non-prophetic (*mawqūf*) statement of **ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd** retaining the Midrashic contrast between scripture recitation and action (`مَثَلُ الَّذِي يَقْرَأُ الْقُرْآنَ وَلَا يَعْمَلُ بِهِ...`), before every canonical Prophetic *isnād* converged upon the Basran *mudallis* **Qatādah ibn Diʿāmah** (d. 117 AH).
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «مَثَلُ الْمُؤْمِنِ الَّذِي يَقْرَأُ الْقُرْآنَ كَمَثَلِ الأُتْرُجَّةِ، رِيحُهَا طَيِّبٌ وَطَعْمُهَا طَيِّبٌ» — "The example of a believer who recites the Qurʾān is like a citron: its fragrance is good and its taste is good." ([Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5427](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5427))

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Classical commentators propose that al-Zuhrī ([*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* #20788](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19829/)) and Ibn Masʿūd ([*al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr* #8670](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/84/8550/)) abbreviated existing Prophetic hadiths by omitting the upward chain (*ikhtiṣār*), and maintain that the 654 AH / 1256 AD Medina lava flow ([*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 13:84–85](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/13020/)) fulfilled the Buṣrā fire tradition ([*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7118)) while viewing the Midrashic citron parallel to [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5427](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5427) as coincidental.
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: In our earliest extant compilation ([*Muṣannaf ʿAbd al-Razzāq* #20788](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19829/)), al-Zuhrī's premier student Maʿmar records the Buṣrā fire as al-Zuhrī's own *maqṭūʿ* words alongside its circulation as an *Isrāʾīliyyah* of Kaʿb al-Aḥbār ([*Kitāb al-Fitan* #1754](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/102778)), and the localized 1256 AD Medina eruption ([*Fatḥ al-Bārī* 13:84–85](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/13020/)) could not physically illuminate camel necks in Buṣrā (~1,000 km away) across the Earth's curvature. Likewise, [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5427](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5427) parallels the Jewish Sukkot four-plant matrix of *Vayikra Rabbah* 30:12 (*etrog*/citron and *lulav*/date), whose intermediate Kūfan *mawqūf* stage under Ibn Masʿūd ([*al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr* #8670](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/84/8550/)) still preserved the Midrashic 'study vs. deeds' axis before the Basran *mudallis* Qatādah transmitted it as a Prophetic tradition.

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
### 1. Stratigraphic Comparison of the Ḥijāz Fire Tradition (*Muṣannaf* #20788 vs. *Bukhārī* 7118)
When a saying originates with an early scholar or folkloric tradition and only acquires a Prophetic chain (*isnād*) in later generations, cross-checking pre-canonical compilations against the ninth-century *Ṣaḥīḥayn* exposes the intermediate layers of *rafʿ* (retrojection). A clear empirical case is the apocalyptic prediction in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 7118](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7118) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 2902](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2902) that a fire emerging from the Ḥijāz will illuminate the necks of camels at Buṣrā in Syria. Every canonical Prophetic route pivots on the Medinan jurist **Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī** (died 124 AH), who linked the report through Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib back to Abū Hurayrah.

However, in the earliest surviving pre-canonical collection—the *Muṣannaf* of ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī ([#20788](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/73/19829/))—al-Zuhrī's closest pupil **Maʿmar ibn Rāshid** recorded the exact sentence solely as al-Zuhrī's own unchained (*maqṭūʿ*) remark, without either Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib or Abū Hurayrah. Moreover, *Kitāb al-Fitan* by Nuʿaym ibn Ḥammād ([entry #1754](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/102778), discussed in IslamWeb Fatwā [#60848](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/60848/)) preserves the identical camel-neck hyperbole at Buṣrā (*tuḍīʾu minhā aʿnāqu al-ibili bi-Buṣrā*) as an *Isrāʾīliyyāt* saying of **Kaʿb al-Aḥbār** describing a fire driven from Yemen. Although medieval chroniclers cited by Ibn Ḥajar in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* ([13:84–85](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/52/13020/)) later linked the canonized report to the 654 AH / 1256 AD Medina volcanic eruption (*Ḥarrat Rahaṭ*), a localized basaltic flow in Medina could never physically illuminate camel necks 1,000 km north in Syrian Buṣrā beyond the Earth's horizon.

### 2. From Rabbinic Midrash and *Mawqūf* Homily to *Marfūʿ* Parable (*Bukhārī* 5427)
A second three-stage trajectory is preserved for the botanical parable in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5427](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5427) (alongside [5020](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5020), [7560](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7560), and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 797a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:797a)), which categorizes believers and hypocrites across a fourfold grid of scent (*rīḥ*) and taste (*ṭaʿm*) anchored by the citron (*al-utrujjah*) and date (*al-tamrah*). As Wilhelm Bacher demonstrated, this exact four-plant matrix parallels the homiletic structure of *Vayikra Rabbah* (30:12), a fifth-century Palestinian Midrash expounding the Sukkot Four Species (led by the citron/*etrog* and date palm/*lulav*), where taste represents scriptural study and fragrance represents righteous deeds. Remarkably, in *al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr* ([report #8670](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/84/8550/)), al-Ṭabarānī records the transitional Kūfan stage as a non-prophetic (*mawqūf*) saying of **ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd** that still retains the Midrashic contrast between reciting scripture and acting upon it (*yaqraʾu al-Qurʾāna wa-lā yaʿmalu bihi*), before the Basran *mudallis* **Qatādah ibn Diʿāmah** (d. 117 AH) popularized the fully elevated Prophetic version via Anas and Abū Mūsā. Diachronic comparison across eighth- and ninth-century compilations provides documentary evidence of regional legal maxims ascending into Prophetic statements.

subpoints.short_title: “Arabia Will Become Meadows”: 1 Chain and 2 Translations of a Verb
subpoints.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see Muslim 157c and its single narrator Suhayl, Sufyān al-Thawrī's doubt that Suhayl attributed it to the Prophet, classical readings of taʿūd as “becomes,” and sunnah.com's 2020 change to “reverts to.”
subpoints.takeaway: Sufyān al-Thawrī doubted the attribution; classical commentators read taʿūd as “becomes.”
subpoints.title: The 'Green Arabia' Hadith: Attribution Doubts & 2020 Translation Shift

a.text: The Last Hour will not come... [[and till the land of Arabia becomes]] meadows and rivers.

b.text: The Last Hour will not come... [[and till the land of Arabia reverts to]] meadows and rivers.

showcase.note: Sufyān al-Thawrī also expressed doubt over whether Suhayl originally attributed this wording to the Prophet.

subpoints.summary_markdown: The single-strand report in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 157c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:157c)—stating that the Hour will not come until Arabian land *"becomes (`taʿūd`) meadows and rivers"*—exhibits documented classical retrojection (*rafʿ*) doubt at its lone transmitter Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ in *Musnad al-Bazzār* ([#9071](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1000/4414/)) and *al-Mustadrak* ([#8472](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/8349/)). Furthermore, pre-modern commentators consistently defined `تَعُودَ` as an auxiliary verb of transformation (*"becomes"*, *Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān* [#6700](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/314/6708/); *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* [7:97](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/53/2839/)), matching `sunnah.com`'s English rendering before a mid-2020 update changed *"becomes"* to *"reverts to."*

evidence_items.label: Al-Bazzār on the Single Chain Through Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ and Sufyān al-Thawrī's Note in al-Mustadrak #8472
evidence_items.content_markdown: As **al-Bazzār** (d. 292 AH) established in [*al-Baḥr al-Zakhkhār* (#9071)](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1000/4414/), the "meadows and rivers" clause in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 157c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:157c) is a solitary (*gharīb*) narration transmitted exclusively through **Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ** from his father (`وَلَا نَعْلَمُ أَخَذَهُ إِلَّا سُهَيْلٌ عَنْ أَبِيهِ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ`). Classical *rijāl* authorities ([al-Dhahabī, *Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 5:458–461](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/915/)) documented that Suhayl suffered a severe illness that impaired his memory, and **al-Ḥākim al-Naysābūrī** ([*al-Mustadrak* #8472 / IslamWeb #8519, 5:674](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/8349/)) preserves the statement of Suhayl's direct student **Sufyān al-Thawrī** expressing uncertainty as to whether Suhayl elevated (*rafaʿa*) the saying to the Prophet (`قَالَ سُفْيَانُ: لَا أَعْلَمُ إِلَّا قَدْ رَفَعَهُ`).

evidence_items.label: Classical Commentaries Defining «تَعُودَ» (Taʿūd) as Auxiliary Transformation (Ṣāra = "Becomes") Under Paraphrastic Transmission (al-Riwāyah bi-l-Maʿnā)
evidence_items.content_markdown: Because classical hadith transmission operated by non-verbatim paraphrase (*al-riwāyah bi-l-maʿnā*—e.g., rendering one marriage pronouncement with different verbs: `زَوَّجْتُكَهَا` in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5029](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5029) and [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1425b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1425b), `مَلَّكْتُكَهَا` in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5030](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5030) and [5087](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5087), and `أَمْكَنَّاكَهَا` / `أَنْكَحْتُكَهَا` in [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5149](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5149)), resting a prehistoric paleoclimatic interpretation on the single verb `تَعُودَ` (*taʿūd*) exceeds the verbal precision of hadith transmission. Pre-modern authorities defined `تَعُودَ` here as an auxiliary verb of transformation (*ṣayrūrah* = *ṣāra*, "becomes"): **Ibn Ḥibbān** ([*Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān* #6700](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/314/6708/)) paraphrased it as *kawn* (*"the coming into being of cultivation and rivers"*), **Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qurṭubī** ([*al-Mufhim*](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/article/182849/)) explained it as future agricultural planting and canal irrigation, and **al-Nawawī** ([*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 7:97](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/53/2839/)) read it as abandoning irrigated lands—while even a restorative reading parallels Qurʾānic accounts of lush ancient Arabian gardens in Sabaʾ ([Q. 34:15](https://quran.com/34/15)), ʿĀd ([Q. 26:134](https://quran.com/26/134)), and Thamūd ([Q. 26:147](https://quran.com/26/147)).

([Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān #6700](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/314/6708/))

evidence_items.label: The 2020 Digital Translation Shift on sunnah.com from "Becomes" to "Reverts To" as a Modern Exegetical Corollary
evidence_items.content_markdown: Between April and June 2020, the English translation of [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 157c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:157c) on `sunnah.com` was updated from *'until the land of Arabia becomes meadows and rivers'* (Abdul Hamid Siddiqui's printed translation) to *'reverts to meadows and rivers.'* The case compares this modern English rendering with the definitions of `تَعُودَ` (*taʿūd*) given by Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Nawawī.
evidence_items.key_arabic_quote: «حَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا» — "Until the land of the Arabs becomes meadows and rivers." ([Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 157c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:157c))

primary_references.label: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 157c (Book 12, Hadith 76 — Current Digital Text and Translation)
Ibn Ḥibbān, Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān #6700 (Classical Rendering of taʿūd as kawn / 'Becoming')

key_arabic_quote_structured.english: Until the land of the Arabs becomes meadows and rivers.

scholarly_discussion.classical_harmonization: Modern commentators note that a primary lexical meaning of the root *ʿ-w-d* is 'to return/revert' (treating the 2020 `sunnah.com` update on [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 157c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:157c) as a literal rendering) and contend that Imām Muslim's inclusion of Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ's narration in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 157c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:157c) supports its Prophetic attribution and wording.
scholarly_discussion.primary_source_evaluation: Inclusion in [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 157c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:157c) stands alongside the classical *ʿilal* record showing that the clause rests on a single-strand (*gharīb*) bottleneck through the memory-impaired Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ ([*Musnad al-Bazzār* #9071](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1000/4414/); [*Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* 5:458–461](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/915/)) and that his student **Sufyān al-Thawrī** expressed doubt whether Suhayl elevated (*rafaʿa*) it to the Prophet ([*al-Mustadrak* #8472](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/8349/)). Furthermore, pre-modern commentators—**Ibn Ḥibbān** ([#6700](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/314/6708/)), **al-Qurṭubī** ([*al-Mufhim*](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/article/182849/)), and **al-Nawawī** ([*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 7:97](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/53/2839/))—explicitly defined `تَعُودَ` here in its auxiliary sense of *kawn* / *ṣayrūrah* ("becoming" via agricultural irrigation), showing that classical exegesis did not read the Arabic verb as requiring prehistoric reversion.

subpoints.deep_dive_markdown:
### 1. Classical Lexicography and Commentaries on the Verb `تَعُودَ` (*Taʿūd*)
Modern scientific-miracle (*iʿjāz ʿilmī*) literature frequently cites [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 157c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:157c) to argue that the verb `تَعُودَ` (*taʿūd*) encodes prehistoric knowledge of the Holocene Humid Period by predicting that Arabia will *"revert"* to a primordial green state. In classical Arabic syntax, however, *ʿāda* functions both as a full verb meaning *"to return"* and as an incomplete auxiliary verb (*min akhawāt kāna*) denoting simple transition (*ṣayrūrah*) synonymous with *ṣāra* (*"to become"*), regardless of any prior condition. Pre-modern Hadith compilers and commentators uniformly understood the passage in this agricultural, transformative sense:
* **Ibn Ḥibbān** (d. 354 AH) placed the tradition in his *Ṣaḥīḥ* ([#6700](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/314/6708/)) under a chapter heading using the verbal noun *kawn* (*"coming into existence / becoming"*): *Dhikru al-ikhbār ʿan kawn al-ʿumrān wa-kathrat al-anhār fī arāḍī al-ʿArab*.
* **Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qurṭubī** (d. 656 AH) in *al-Mufhim* ([IslamWeb](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/article/182849/)) explained the clause as describing future agricultural irrigation, canal-digging, and land cultivation (*bi-ghirāsati al-arḍi wa-ʿimāratihā wa-ijrāʾi miyāhihā*), while **al-Nawawī** (d. 676 AH) in *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* ([7:97](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/53/2839/)) interpreted it as people abandoning the land unplanted and unirrigated due to warfare and turmoil, without suggesting a paleoclimatic cycle. Even if a restorative sense were assumed, the seventh-century Hijazi audience already possessed Qurʾānic descriptions of ancient Arabian realms—including Sabaʾ ([Qurʾān 34:15](https://quran.com/34/15)), ʿĀd ([Qurʾān 26:134](https://quran.com/26/134)), and Thamūd ([Qurʾān 26:147](https://quran.com/26/147))—as former lands of gardens and flowing springs (`جَنَّاتٍ وَعُيُونٍ`).

### 2. The Solitary Bottleneck of `Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ` and the 2020 Website Edit
From an *isnād* standpoint, **Abū Bakr al-Bazzār** (d. 292 AH) demonstrated in *al-Baḥr al-Zakhkhār* ([#9071](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1000/4414/)) that this wording is a single-strand (*gharīb*) report transmitted solely by **Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ** from his father Dhakwān (`Abū Ṣāliḥ ← Abū Hurayrah`). Biographical dictionaries such as al-Dhahabī's *Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ* ([5:458–461](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/915/)) record that a severe illness damaged Suhayl's memory in later life, while **al-Ḥākim** in *al-Mustadrak* ([#8472](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/74/8349/)) preserves a direct expression of doubt from Suhayl's student **Sufyān al-Thawrī** over whether Suhayl elevated (*rafaʿa*) the report to the Prophet (*lā aʿlamu illā qad rafaʿahu*). Because early transmitters routinely paraphrased reports according to general meaning (*al-riwāyah bi-l-maʿnā*; cf. [*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* 5029](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5029), [5030](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5030), [5087](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5087), [5149](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5149); [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 1425b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1425b)), building a geological proof on a single ambiguous verb exceeds the precision of solitary chains. On `sunnah.com`, the English rendering by Abdul Hamid Siddiqui for [*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* 157c](https://sunnah.com/muslim:157c) translated `تَعُودَ` as ***"becomes"*** before a mid-2020 update changed the online text to read ***"reverts to."***

subpoints.short_title: 2 Prophecy Groups on Constantinople and Basra With 8th-Century Details
subpoints.plain_english_hook: Here you'll see reports in Muslim and Bukhārī on taking Constantinople, Musnad Aḥmad 18957 being cited for Maslamah's 717 AD siege, and Basra reports that run through Saʿīd ibn Jumhān (d. 136 AH).
subpoints.takeaway: Commentators link some reports to 1453; others carry 8th-century details such as Maslamah's 717 AD siege.
subpoints.title: Eighth-Century Constantinople and Basra Contexts Preserved in Hadiths
